The learning activities and submissions are team-based experiences and for that reason, it is important to participate in class at DTU Campus.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the importance between Feasibility, Viability, Desirability, Responsibility and Sustainability of an innovation content, - Identify different team dynamics and apply relevant iniciatives to their innovation process, - Explain relevant approaches in the facilitation of teamwork, - Explain methods for leading and facilitating the different stages of an innovation process e.g., exploration, ideation, iteration, designing, and building, - Apply methods to support and maintain a collaborative environment in the processes of exploration, ideation, iteration, designing, and building, - Guide team dicussions on group dynamics and teamwork with regards to the division of tasks and responsibilities, - Identify and increase the inclusion of diverse disciplinary backgrounds in the different stages of the innovation process, - Apply methods to facilitate constructive teamwork in a context where the decision-making process is characterized by high uncertainty and risk of being led astray, - Support the making of informed and qualified decisions in an innovation process with regards to Feasibility, Viability, Desirability, Sustainability, and Responsibility, - Reflect on their role, ways of working, and value as an innovation facilitator in the innovation process., - Keep the end in mind with regards to deliver and argue to the relevant stakeholders the design choices of an explored concept in relation to both the value creation and limitations, - Give and receive constructive and appropriate feedback to and from team members and other teams.
42543:
Name English: Management of organizational change
Danish Title: Ledelse af organisatorisk forandring
General Course Objectives: This course encompasses the process of managing sustainable organisational change and transitions. It enables students to learn how to manage change processes and how to navigate individual, group, and organisational perspectives to safeguard both organizational performance and sustainability. This is achieved by introducing theories and models of change management, applying these to practice cases and planning an organizational change intervention in relation to a specific case.
Content: The course focuses on leading organizational change and transition processes. It introduces core theories and models for organizational change processes, from understanding the change to implementing the change and sustaining it. Throughout the course, you work with different cases of organizational change where you use theories and models to analyze and make recommendations with concern for both people and performance. In addition, concrete examples are presented through guest lectures.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Demonstrate an understanding of the concepts, theories and perspectives introduced throughout the course - Critically evaluate, and apply relevant theories and models to complex real-life management challenges related to change - Analyze an organizational change related case or topic, while determining key problem areas, selecting and applying relevant theories, tools and methods to propose potential solutions - Understand organizational change and change management, as an interplay among several organizational key actors, including employees, managers and other organizational stakeholders - Assess and discuss technological change within an organizational and societal context, and explain how relevant actions support implementation - Discuss and reflect on the use of digital technologies in managing and coordinating companies’ activities across local and global operations - Develop and plan an organizational change intervention in a simulated or practical context - Formulate recommendations with concern for society, people, and performance
42554:
Name English: Social Entrepreneurship: Theory and Practice
Danish Title: Social Entrepreneurship: Theory and Practice
General Course Objectives: The purpose of the course is to help students learn to combine insights about real-world management and leadership issues with practical consulting experience. The course consists of scheduled class meetings, client meetings, a class presentation and final individual report related to the consulting experience. DTU students will work together with visiting students from Johns Hopkins University to develop solutions for a specific client, and have the opportunity to interact with its stakeholders such as clients and managers in the Copenhagen area, reflect on organizational processes, and receive on-going guidance and formal end-of-experience feedback.
Content: 1. Relationship Building 2. Dimensions of Social Entrepreneurship 3. Identification of Social Entrepreneurs (Characteristics & Skills) 4. Building Resiliency 5. The Dynamics of Social Change 6. Leading Social Change – required competencies 7. Using technology to create social values 8. Business planning for social ventures 9. Social/Innovation site visit 10. Team work - working in cross cultural or cross disciplinary teams
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Apply relevant leadership theories and concepts to the development of social ventures - Define the dimensions of Social Entrepreneurship - Discuss the dynamics of social changes - Identify key competences required to lead social change - Generate insightful and actionable solutions for a social business venture - Work in a multi-cultural team environment - Communicate the thought verbally and in written form effectively - Evaluate own preferences in terms of leadership style, conflict resolution, and values.
42575:
Name English: Technology and Innovation Management
Danish Title: Teknologi og Innovationsledelse
General Course Objectives: The primary goal of the course is to expose students to a variety of perspectives on technological corporate innovation, building on an active learning process and preparing for work challenges in the future.
Content: This course approaches the management of technological innovation from a resource/knowledge based view, which sees technological innovations as a driving force of competitive advantage of organizations through a combination of internal resources and external linkages. Students are introduced to the theories, models, tools and practical cases from industries by understanding what technological innovations are, why they are important, and what are needed to enable and manage technological innovations within and outside of the boundary of organizations. Although most attention will be paid to innovations made by industrial firms, relevant issues of innovations at levels of individual, team, network of organizations, and industry will be addressed as well. The weekly readings consist of a mixture of book chapters, journal articles, and cases. In addition to ‘understanding’ technological innovations, students are also required to ‘practice’ innovations by developing a case study throughout the course and applying the knowledge learned from the course to the innovation case.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Define what innovation is and what different types of innovations are and explain why innovation is important. - Pinpoint the role of technology in innovation both in theory and in practice. - Identify relevant issues about innovation when exposed to a real-life situation. - Explain the key concepts of Schumpeterian theory and technology in relation to techno-logical innovation. - Explain the key concepts of resource-based view and its relevance to innovation strategy. - Explain the key concepts of knowledge and learning and its relevance to innovation. - Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of the theoretical perspectives form the course curriculum. - Analyze the innovation process within an organization. - Evaluate the organizational implications with regard to different methods of innovation. - Contrast how value is created and captured by different innovative organizations with regard to an open or closed environment of innovation. - Collect relevant and adequate empirical material for a case study of a specific innovation. - Develop a specific innovation case using the theoretical perspectives and innovation tools learned from the course curriculum.
42576:
Name English: From Analytics to Action
Danish Title: From Analytics to Action
General Course Objectives: The general purpose of the course is to qualify the student to understand and handle problems and opportunities in data analysis projects from a management perspective. The student will be able to identify and assess challenges in connection with the commercial and organizational value of data projects as well as challenges in connection with their implementation, including collection, analysis and visualization of data, involved, processes, technology and organization. In this regard, there will be a special focus on communicating the results and prerequisites of data projects, including various strategies for data visualization and involvement of stakeholders, as well as translation of the data project's potential to the business context of the company or organization in question. As a team, the students must be able to find solutions to identified challenges and communicate them clearly in a management perspective.
Content: The role of data analysis projects in different organizational contexts. Challenges in connection with the implementation of data analysis projects in companies. Different types of data visualization and strategies for their use. Different theories about data and the effects of data analysis on markets and organizations. Involvement of stakeholders in analyses of data. Assessment of the business value of data projects. Discussion of data quality issues. Typical data analysis process models. Technological challenges. Analysis of actors. Data analysis strategy. Discussions, articles and mini-cases will give participants the opportunity to discuss individual aspects of management challenges and solutions. Within a project based on a case study, participants will apply their knowledge in a team and deliver solutions.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - analyze challenges and opportunities in a specific data analysis project - identify the project's stakeholders - define the project's commercial value - compare and assess potential pitfalls and barriers for the project - develop a realistic and well-thought-out plan for the implementation of the project in a concrete company - visualize the project's prerequisites, processes and results. - discuss the project's possible consequences for the market and organisation. - design a strategy for the involvement of actors who are relevant to the implementation and impact of the project - prepare a presentation of the project's opportunities and challenges to senior management - communicate the project's results and relevance to the company's business in clear and well-argued language
42577:
Name English: Introduction to Business Analytics
Danish Title: Introduktion til Business Analytics
General Course Objectives: Business Analytics is about exploring and analysing data to gain insight into past business performance in order to guide future business planning. This course introduces the portfolio of data science tasks and techniques necessary for exploring, manipulating, visualizing and analysing data (descriptive analytics), as well as for building prediction models using machine learning (predictive analytics) that can be used to gain insights and support decisions (prescriptive analytics). It is designed with Business Analytics students in mind (i.e. some Python programming background is required), particularly – but not exclusively - those related to studies on mobility and logistics and business analytics. Therefore, it contains a strong hands-on component, with specific real-world cases coming mainly from mobility and transportation. The course also includes an introduction to data wrangling, problem formulation, and the basic suite of machine learning algorithms.
Content: The classes are taught in an interactive manner, with theoretical parts, intermingled with practice with Jupyter Notebooks. Main topics are: data visualisation, forecasting and regression models, classification, clustering, dimensionality reduction and time-series. The methods will be exemplified through different cases within e.g. transportation and management. Introduction to Python programming and Pandas is provided as supplementary material (requirement of the course/self learning)
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Design and implement Python-based data analysis workflows, ensuring reproducibility and efficiency - Formulate and operationalize business-related problems as data-driven analytical tasks - Select and apply appropriate data structures, algorithms, and analytical techniques to address complex business problems - Analyse, interpret, and synthesize results from descriptive and predictive models into actionable business insights and recommendations - Develop and evaluate visualizations that reveal complex temporal and spatial patterns for decision-making - Design, train, and validate statistical and machine learning models using appropriate evaluation strategies - Critically assess data science methodologies, model performance, and underlying assumptions, including bias, variance, and overfitting - Explain and critically reflect on key data mining and machine learning concepts in practical and business contexts
42578:
Name English: Advanced Business Analytics
Danish Title: Advanced Business Analytics
General Course Objectives: Business Analytics (BA) concerns the use of data and models to understand organisational systems and support decisions. This course covers advanced data-centric methods across the three main directions in BA: descriptive (“what happened?”), predictive (“what will happen?”), and prescriptive (“what should happen?”). Emphasis is on connecting modelling choices to decision contexts: problem formulation, data management, model evaluation and validation, and communicating results under uncertainty. Methods are applied to business cases to illustrate how data and machine learning can be used for decision support, including modern approaches where relevant. Throughout, the course highlights how responsible analytics can contribute to societal good—by improving decisions in areas such as sustainability, public services, and equitable outcomes—while recognising limitations, risks, and trade-offs. The course relies on advanced machine learning techniques; students are therefore expected to have prior knowledge of data science and machine learning fundamentals, as well as solid programming skills.
Content: The course is delivered in two main blocks. The first half of the semester focuses on advanced business analytics techniques and is taught in an intensive format. This block combines multiple teaching approaches, including interactive lectures integrated with hands‑on Python exercises as well as flipped‑classroom sessions supported by pre‑recorded video lectures and practical in‑class activities. The second half of the semester is dedicated to project work and includes a series of invited talks from industry, the public sector and academia. The main topics covered in the course includes web data mining; Augmented/Virtual reality; natural language processing; Large Language Models; recommender systems; explainable AI; deep learning; reinforcement learning; spatio-temporal prediction models; ensemble models; survival analysis; prediction uncertainty and computer vision.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Identify business and societal impact opportunities related to effective data utilization - Summarize the identifying characteristics of advanced machine learning approaches for descriptive, predictive and prescriptive analytics - Select and apply appropriate machine learning (regression, classification, reinforcement learning, clustering, recommender systems, computer vision, LLMs) - Conduct machine learning experiments in complex settings (e.g. noisy data, high uncertainty, combination with optimization components, parametric and non-parametric models) - Apply one or more explainable AI techniques (e.g SHAP, Lime) in data-driven decision advisory situations - Understand the technical principles and potential of foundation models (e.g. LLMs) - Build on the latest LLM techniques (RAG, LoRA, Chain-of-Thought reasoning) to develop application-ready tools for business and society - Quantify uncertainties in predictive modelling, through quantile regression and heteroskedasticity modelling - Understand and be able to explain causal vs correlational relationships between variables, endogeneity, intervention and counterfactual reasoning - Be able to provide a clear and informative summary (executive summary) for data-driven analyses and tools, including insights for business and critical questions
42580:
Name English: Introduction to Data Science
Danish Title: Introduktion til Data Science
General Course Objectives: To give participants a basic insight into: • Basic data science concepts and selected methods • Communication of data science analyses • Group project work in connection with data science
Content: The course is an introduction to data science with the aim of developing the students' understanding of what it means to work with data science in a societal context. The course introduces different kinds of basic data science methods (multiple linear regression, logistic regression, and cluster analysis) but also aims to give the students opportunities to acquire relevant generic engineering skills, such as working in a group and disseminating results both written and orally. The courses focuses on how engineers work with data science in practice, so that the students gain an understanding of societal applications of data science outside of the university. The course consists of a mix of project work and interactive class sessions based on active learning with a maximal focus on hands-on experience, discussions and peer-feedback. The students have allocated time to work on their projects during classes, but independent further work on the projects between classes is expected.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the data science processes of the Statistical Enquiry Cycle - Choose suitable data for analysing a self-selected topic of societal relevance - Communicate data science analyses to a non-technical audience through an oral presentation with appropriately designed data visualisations - Provide relevant peer-feedback based on predefined criteria and use the feedback constructively to improve a data science analysis - Describe and reflect on their own role in a project-based group work - Apply basic data science methods and assess their suitability for a given problem and dataset - Argue for chosen variables and their functional forms in a regression model based on statistical measures and visualisations - Carry out relevant scenario analyses based on model predictions in Python and interpret the results for the purpose of qualifying the public debate of a societal matter - Write a coherent technical report that synthetises a data science analysis and its limitations in a well-structured manner
42583:
Name English: Systems design
Danish Title: Systemdesign
General Course Objectives: The course introduces a mind-set (ie knowledge and tools) to address a complex technological project in the societal context. The course focuses on understanding and qualifying the context for technological projects using: i) engineering systems, ii) reflection on own practice, and iii) group work on a project dealing with technological issues. The focus of the course is on transport systems and technologies.
Content: The students are introduced to models and theories within system design and engineering. The course consists of theoretical lectures and group work. It works with general cases, where specific issues are analyzed using theories and models.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - understand the broad principles of systems thinking and systems engineering and key parts of the process - understand the role of systems engineering in modern economies - develop and prepare a problem definition in terms of general requirements and relevant stakeholders - explain and apply selected methods of Systems Design in the context of systems engineering problems - explain and apply selected methods of Project Management in the context of systems engineering problems - explain functions and properties of a system as relating to system requirements/needs - perform a system design for a chosen problem and apply the basic principles - explain the complexity and dynamics of a technological system in a wider context - structure and disseminate information, theories and results about technological systems both in writing and orally
42584:
Name English: Project work - Data Science and Management
Danish Title: Fagprojekt - Data Science og Management
General Course Objectives: The purpose of the course is to qualify and train students in project work through planning and implementation of a larger practical and theoretical exercise in team work (typically 3-5 members), and to apply parts of the theoretical contents from other programme specific courses from the Bachelor program Data Science and Management
Content: The topics in the course will depend on the selected project. The detailed contents of the projects are defined in collaboration between the students and the supervisor. Project subjects are published before course start. The students may suggest projects themselves and find supervisors at DTU Management or DTU Compute.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Independently analyze technical and scientific problems and identify, define, and implement solutions in collaboration across both professional and personal competencies. - Conduct relevant and critical information search and review in order to independently increase one's knowledge level in relation to the technical and scientific problem. - Communicate technical information, theories, and results both graphically, in writing, and orally, and present it to different groups of stakeholders. - Evaluate one's own and others' developed solutions in relation to established requirements, including potential sustainability criteria and unintended impacts. - Evaluate any unforeseen challenges in connection with problem-solving of an engineering project. - Select, formulate and define a professionally relevant topic within data science and management. - Set a well-functioning framework for the project work (problem identification, problem formulation, collaboration contract, division of labor, schedule, project management). - Apply quantitative methods for analysis and modeling of technical systems. The methods can be statistical models, differential equations, numerical methods, operations analysis, AI, and more. - Evaluate the validity, assumptions, and sensitivity of the models, and discuss their applicability in an engineering context. - Find relevant literature. Document the project's methods, analyses, and results in a technical report with correct use of references and academic citation.

Name English: Decisions under uncertainty
Danish Title: Beslutninger under usikkerhed
General Course Objectives: To provide students with both a theoretical and practical understanding of how to deal with decision problems characterized by uncertain information.
Content: Students will be introduced to different quantitative methods for decision problems characterised by uncertain information. These methods include decision analysis, Markov chains, simulation, and stochastic programming.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Analyse a decision problem to point out uncertainties and understand what effect these uncertainties have on the decision-making - Describe the procedure in each of the presented methods for decision making based on uncertain information - Design and utilise computational tools to employ the presented methods - Design computational experiments for validating modelling choices for the decision making problem and relevant uncertainties - Apply the presented methods on a specific decision problem characterised by uncertain information - Explain how the different methods can complement one another to gain further insight - Contrast alternative methods for representing uncertainty in decision making from a quantitative standpoint - Deduce recommendation based on the application of the presented methods for decision problems characterised by uncertain information

Name English: Operations and Supply Chain Management
Danish Title: Operations og Supply Chain Management
General Course Objectives: The course aims to introduce the students to the most important planning problems that a company meets across the supply chain. The issues and solution methods treat the strategic, tactical, and operational planning levels. The course provides the students with an introduction to the management and management of supply chains and production planning. Quantitative methods based on e.g., descriptive statistics and mathematical optimization are introduced through exercises that are solved using spreadsheets. Thus, the course provides the students with the first touch of "business intelligence" concepts and motivates later studies within "business analytics."
Content: During the course, the planning problems and corresponding solution methods seen within the primary activities of a company will be discussed. These includes: - Supply chain management (SCM) and operations management (OM) are exemplified through the learning game "The Beer Game" - Production processes, the layout of production systems, and Business Process Management - Quality and capacity management - Management of supplies - Logistics - Forecasting - Sales and Operations Planning - Inventory management - Production Planning The weekly exercises and the mandatory group assignments will be carried out using the Microsoft Excel spreadsheet software. These include basic data management and simple formula expressions, visualization (graphs and figures), and solving simple optimization problems using Microsoft Excel Solver.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain and describe the concepts of value chains, supply chain management and operations management - Explain and describe the concept of processes in the context of production planning and use methods for business process mapping to map the processes in a production in order to improve efficiency - Explain the concept of quality and use quantitative methods of quality management - Explain the concept of capacity and use decision trees for analysis - Explain the concept of management of supplies and use basic methods for analyzing possible suppliers - Explain the concept of logistics and the role of logistics in a supply chain and to be able to solve simple localization problems by mathematical optimization - Describe the concept of forecasting and the most common qualitative forecasting methods and be able to use time series based as well as causal forecasting methods - Explain the concept of "sales and operations planning" and be able to explain the three levels of planning (strategic, tactical and operational planning) and the difference between these - Describe the concept of inventory management and use the most common quantitative methods for inventory management - Explain and make use of the concepts "master schedule record", "material requirement planning" (MRP), "production activity control" (PAC) and vendor order management within production planning - Enter, edit and format data as well as construct and edit formulas and figures/charts in the spreadsheet software used, and solve simple optimization problems in this software - Prepare a concise technical report that describes how qualitative as well as quantitative methods can be used for solving problems within operations and supply chain management

Danish Title: Ingeniørfagets videnskabsteori

Name English: X-Tech Entrepreneurship
Danish Title: X-Tech Entrepreneurship
General Course Objectives: To create a learning environment where students will work on a joint venture with a project submitter. They will work in mixed disciplinary teams to turn technology or market opportunity/need into a product/service and a new business venture. Unlike usual product development or entrepreneurship courses, we have a focus on business to business (B2B), taking students out of their comfort zones, pushing them behind the scenes of unfamiliar technologies and business sectors. The course is set in an accelerator format and emphasizes a learning by doing philosophy. To speed up the learning process, we bring in some of the country’s top X-Tech Entrepreneurs, most of them founders and CEOs. Each of the keynotes will help to emphasis the importance of the methods and theory being taught in the course. The overall course objective is to create a technology demonstrator and a business plan that will be pitched to the examiners (and investors) – with the aim to raise investment and to spinout.
Content: The course covers all of the topics contained within a modern investor pitch deck and business plan. X-Tech cover topics related to technology risk mitigation, product/service-systems, pretotyping and MVPs, IPR, financing, value propositions, business modelling, segmentation & market estimation as well as sustainabliltysustainability and the use of SDGs in a startup business model. The cases are submitted by industry and research departments. The cases are in the form of a patent/technology or a technology related challenge. Every team will be joined by the inventor (project submitter) for the technical development and also a business mentor who will act as the chairperson of the board. The cases/projects fall into different thematic tracks suitable for all different studylines across DTU. The final deliverable of the course is the business pitch deck and business plan. The course ends with X-Tech Finals where the students make a 4 minute business pitch plus 2 minute tech demo in front of your examiners, investors and an audience. There is prototype fund available for each team. There is also a prize fund for the winning teams of X-Tech.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Design with various engineering disciplines (eg. Physics, Electronics, Computer Science, Nano-tech, Mechanical Design, Photonics, Food, Management etc.) - Develop a product or service where the project submitter is not your employer, but instead a customer or stakeholder to your own businessin a joint venture setup. - Apply the principles of effectuation. - Asses the technological risk involved in commercializing X-Tech. - Forecast business potential in the form of market value and projected gross revenue. - Develop and test pretotypes and prototypes. - Design a fitting Minimal Viable Product (MVP). - Asses the implications of IPR. - Create a business plan and make an investment pitch. - Evaluate your business from a sustainability and SDG point of view

Name English: Introduction to Balmorel
Danish Title: Introduktion til Balmorel
General Course Objectives: In this course the students will learn how to perform analyses with the energy system model, Balmorel. Balmorel is a model of a national or international power system including district heating systems. It is implemented as an optimization model, mainly linear with integer elements according to options. The model is an open source model and available on a home page along with a full model description and documentation of analyses (www.balmorel.com). Balmorel has been used for a wide range of analyses documented in project reports available on the model website and in journal papers. Based on the assumption that perfect market conditions exist the model maximizes social welfare, considering operational costs, annualized investment costs and users' utility. Operational costs include fuel costs, CO2 quota costs as well as operation and maintenance costs. Taxes, supports and other policy instruments may be included. Given a number of restrictions, the model may optimize investments in new production as well as transmission capacity and the operation of plants. Prices such as the electricity price can be found from the marginal values of restrictions. The model is designed to cover several countries. Each country consists of one or more regions, between which electricity exchange is restricted due to limited transmission capacities. Each region, in turn, consists of one or more district heating areas, between which no exchange of heat is allowed. The model considers one or more years, and the time resolution within a year may be hourly or using aggregated time segments. Time series on hourly time resolution are given as input for electricity and heat demand, as well as for power production from wind, hydro and other renewable sources. During model run these series may be aggregated to lower time resolution.
Content: The course comprises lectures, student presentations, discussions and assignments. More specifically the course will cover the following themes: - Background and overview of Balmorel - Balmorel and other models – how do we choose - Equations in Balmorel including slack variables - Add-ons - Options and aggregation - Boundaries - Policies - Data structuring - Error search - Input and Output handling - Version tracking
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - to understand and explain the model structure - to interpret and explain the main equations (mathematically and orally) - to understand and explain how add-ons are developed and used - to understand end explain aggregation of time and geography - to choose critically between the many different options when applying the tool - to perform systematic error finding - to apply version management - to analyze energy systems with the model including analysis of economic policy measures - to reflect critically on results and use of model and key assumptions

Name English: Assessing human and ecosystems impacts with the scientific consensus model USEtox
Danish Title: Assessing human and ecosystems impacts with the scientific consensus model USEtox
General Course Objectives: --Human near-field consumer exposure and far-field population exposure/toxicity & ecotoxicity modeling with the global scientific consensus model USEtox-- There is an increasing need for methods to assess impacts of toxic chemical emissions on human health and ecosystems including consumer exposure. This course provides a practical overview of multimedia chemical fate modelling, near-field and far-field multi-pathway human exposure modelling, ecosystem and human health effects dose-response modelling, and comparative indicators for human-toxicological and ecotoxicological impacts. We explain basic concepts of environmental mass balance modelling including partitioning, first order cross-media transport, and persistence. We further introduce the concept of assessing multiple transfers between near-field and far-field environments and resulting exposures for consumers and the general population, discussing data and models available for detergents, building materials, food contact materials and personal care products. Along a series of practical examples, we will illustrate how fate, exposure, effect and damage factors can be combined to construct factors to characterize chemical emissions and chemicals in consumer products, building on the USEtox scientific consensus model and USEtox-compatible near-field models. We will conclude with a demonstration of how the models can be used in various applications, including the prioritization and ranking of chemicals for institutions like the European Commission or the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Teachers will be Peter Fantke (USEtox Managing Director) and members of the USEtox team.
Content: Participants/students will have hands-on access to all model, data, documentation and reading files during the course and will be able to take all files back home. New substances will be characterized and participants/students may bring their own list of substances of interest for the exercises. The course is structured as follows: - Week 1: preparatory reading (reading material will be sent 1 months in advance) - Week 2: virtual, interactive lectures and hands-on exercises - Week 3: preparation of report around own exercise project
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain and apply exposure science methods used in life-cycle impact assessment, chemical substitution, and comparative risk assessment - Use and evaluate basic tools for mass-balance, fate modeling, intake fraction, and effect factor estimation - Review underlying model assumptions and uncertainties - Evaluate data needs along with data and knowledge gaps in toxicity characterization - Explain the scientific fundamentals of chemical impact assessment for a broad range of environmental emissions - Perform your own assessment using the USEtox scientific consensus model and related near-field exposure models and interpret results - Find data sources, implement new substances into USEtox, and modify existing modules - Discuss applicability and limitations of USEtox model, data and results in different application fields including life cycle assessment, product environmental footprinting and comparative risk assessment

Name English: Renewable gas in the energy system
Danish Title: Grøn gas i energisystemet
General Course Objectives: In this course the students will gain an overview of different aspects and stages of the gas chain from supply to regulation: efficient production and use of renewable gases including potential conditioning to natural gas quality, flexible use of gas also for transport, system integration, as well as application of measures to ensure an economically efficient use of gas. The course offers an interdisciplinary approach which will help the students to get a basic understanding of technological, economic and environmental aspects of natural gas and renewable gases in the energy system.
Content: Sessions: 1: Introduction 2: The role of gas in the energy system 3: Regulation 4: Biogas and biological upgrading 5: Power-to-X and the impact/ synergies with the electrical grid 6: Syngas and methanation (Visit to lab at Risø) 7: Hydrogen - overview and current research 8: Gas quality 9: Gas demand and appliances 10: Gas grid and markets
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - explain the main existing and emerging technologies for renewable gas production and conditioning - compare and interpret the role of different future gas technologies in the energy system - synthesize the important interactions between gas, transport and electricity - describe the basic quality requirements for gas to be fed into the Danish gas grid - analyze the impact of current gas regulation and markets on the production and use of gas - understand the basic concepts used for modelling energy systems - develop the specifications for modelling gas systems - provide an overview on how gas can be used in the transport sector and the technologies used for this purpose - give a fundamental introduction to the gas system including gas quality requirements, gas demands and application of gas - explain how the gassystem including storages can contribute in a future with an increasing share of fluctuation electricity production

Name English: Sustainability evaluation and communication
Danish Title: Bæredygtighedsvurdering og kommunikation
General Course Objectives: It is the ambition of the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) that research at the university shall support sustainable development and more explicitly the achievement of the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). All PhD students at DTU must therefore achieve an understanding of sustainability and sustainable development that enables them to position and develop their research in the context of these goals and contribute positively to the achievement of these goals in their research and future professional work. DTU also wants it’s PhD students to be able to reflect on the role of science and research in public debate and develop awareness of how science communication can feed into processes of democratization and sustainable development. All PhD students must therefore train their communication skills and be able to communicate their research to a non-expert audience in a popular science form, as well as reflect on their own responsibility and willingness to communicate with the general public.
Content: The course introduces you to the concept of sustainability and the United Nation’s Sustainable Development Goals (UN SDGs) and to the role of technology in sustainable development. You are introduced to a methodology and guideline in life cycle based evaluation of the sustainability implications of research projects, and you will apply the methodology to your own PhD project to analyse the potential sustainability implications that the outcomes of your research may have. The course also introduces you to theory and practice of communication in general and to a non-expert audience in particular with the aim that you can communicate the potential sustainability implications of your project. Upon completing the course, you will be qualified to understand your own PhD work in relation to the SDGs, be qualified to contribute positively to the achievement of the goals in your future professional life, and be able to communicate the sustainability relevance of your work to a non-expert audience in a popular science form. As part of the course, you are expected to prepare and deliver a presentation at either a Danish high school or to another non-scientific/laymen audience. It is recommended to take the course in the first half of your PhD project (6-18 months into the study period is the optimal time frame and no earlier than 2 months into the study period). The course workload of 2.5 ECTS includes the 4-4.5 in-class days of lectures, exercises and group work (expected 30-34 hours) as well as homework related to both the preparation and finalisation of the SDG evaluation report and communication support (expected 40 hours).
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Know the fundamental principles of sustainability assessment of technologies and be able to use sustainability issues to communicate about research in public. - Be familiar with different prevailing definitions of sustainability and know the history of the sustainability concept and the development of the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). - Be able to interpret the outcome of your project into potential technological and societal changes of relevance for a sustainable development. - Understand the importance of considering the outcomes of your project in a life cycle/system perspective - Understand the importance of considering a broad coverage of impacts within each sustainability dimension - environmental, social, economic - Be able to perform a sustainability screening of your own project against the UN SDGs applying a life cycle perspective - Understand the communication situation and be able to reflect upon the importance of sender, receiver, subject, language and situation (media) - Know how to use central news values (criteria of relevance) and communicate clearly about the relevance of a research project in public - Know how to engage with a non-expert audience and understand the importance of the narrative language - Be familiar with relevant presentation skills and techniques for interacting with an audience - Be able to reflect upon the possible effects of including or excluding risks, uncertainties and private opinion when communicating about your research in public

Name English: Academic Writing and Journal Analysis
Danish Title: Academic Writing and Journal Analysis
General Course Objectives: Academic Writing is an intensive course that: • introduces and explains all the unwritten rules of academic English • covers the primary written rules for analysis, criticism, and rewriting Content includes not only structure, grammar, punctuation, and paragraphing—all of which are critical for publication success—but also the theory of contrastive rhetoric and its implications for all native and non-native writers of English. Participants learn how to say more with fewer words, write with precision, and avoid ambiguity. They also learn to argue according to Anglo-American rhetorical norms, including • establishing the purpose clearly • organizing and focusing content effectively • structuring sentences and paragraphs for greatest impact Furthermore, participants learn techniques for studying journals from a linguistic perspective, so that they may avail themselves of cues and linguistic devices not readily apparent to the untutored eye.
Content: Academic Writing includes not only structure, grammar, punctuation, and paragraphing—all of which are critical for publication success-but also the theory of contrastive rhetoric and its implications for all native and non-native writers of English. Participants learn how to say more with fewer words, write with precision, and avoid ambiguity. They also learn to argue according to Anglo-American rhetorical norms, including • establishing the purpose clearly • organizing and focusing content effectively • structuring sentences and paragraphs for greatest impact Journal Analysis is an intensive course showing participants how to maximize their chances of publication in international journals. It gives participants strategies for analyzing articles (and the journals in which they have been published) for both content and style. The wide range of topics includes such basic strategies as: • analyzing the abstract and introduction for specific linguistic devices • creating abstract models • assessing the ratio of theory to data • determining structural composition and content placement • creating both abstracts and introductions in the most common style of the journal Participants learn techniques for studying journals from a linguistic perspective, so that they may avail themselves of cues and linguistic devices not readily apparent to the untutored eye.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - apply rules of written academic English to their own writing - identify contrastive rhetoric and its implications - create a framework for more precise and short writing of own academic argumentation - structure sentences and paragraphs for greatest impact - organize and focus their own academic writing more effectively - revise their own writing based on the provided feedback - analyze prospective journals for content, focus, orientation, and style before the writing begins - eliminate all journals that are poor matches for their paper - write a paper in the style of a selected journal, including writing and organizational style

42879:
Name English: Decision Support and Strategic Assessment
Danish Title: Beslutningsstøtte og strategisk vurdering
General Course Objectives: The course aims to give the participants a theoretical and practical basis for advanced decision support consisting of cost-benefit analysis, feasibility risk assessment, and strategic analysis using multi-criteria decision analysis. The primary purpose will be to model and establish comprehensive decision support within a specific appraisal study context, emphasizing the strategic impacts and uncertainties involved. The modeling approach will apply cost-benefit analysis, feasibility risk assessment, and multi-criteria decision analysis when setting up and designing the decision support framework.
Content: The course treats basic and advanced theory and methodology in the assessment/​appraisal/​evaluation of major investment projects. An assessment of transport infrastructure projects forms the assignment of the course. However, the methods applied are universal and can be used for other types of projects as well. Knowledge about transport infrastructure projects is not a prerequisite to participating in the course. The course's overall objective is to provide the best possible decision support by applying cost-benefit analysis (CBA), feasibility risk analysis, and strategic analysis using multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) and to combine them into a composite analysis for a pool of investment projects. The following topics will be treated in lectures and exercises, where it is assumed that the student holds some basic knowledge of economics: Socio-economic analysis: The theoretical foundations of the CBA, including social choice mechanisms, market (in)efficiency, social welfare, and the justification of public action. The students will become familiar with the theoretical elements of a CBA both in a static setting and in an intertemporal framework. Risk analysis and uncertainty: Theory and methodology concerning uncertainty and the concept of Optimism Bias. The topic is concerned with determining various uncertain elements in the CBA and treating these using reference class forecasting and Monte Carlo simulation. Strategic analysis: Theory and methodology concerning measuring non-quantifiable impacts, which often are strategic and hold the potential to improve the decision support. The students will get acquainted with different MCDA assessment techniques and how to combine these with the CBA and feasibility risk assessment results. The aim is to include several stakeholder perspectives in the final recommendations. The course participants work in groups to apply and achieve practical knowledge about the analysis methods and concepts. It is expected that the students can clarify/account/argue for the chosen impacts/criteria and the model solutions in connection with the report work and the written examination. The main course content consists of lectures and group exercises with plenary discussions.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Understand the economic foundations of a cost-benefit analysis - Assess a project's intertemporal impacts through discounting and the social cost of carbon - Implement and perform a cost-benefit analysis from a societal perspective on a large investment project - Implement and perform a feasibility risk assessment using Monte Carlo simulation - Identify supplementing criteria to include in a strategic analysis from the perspective of decision-makers and stakeholders - Identify, organize, and assess accessible data material in the context of both a quantitative and a qualitative approach - Apply principles of multi-criteria decision analysis to assess the strategic impacts of a decision problem - Implement and account for the methodology behind a composite analysis based on cost-benefit analysis, feasibility risk assessment, and multi-criteria decision analysis - Design and apply a comprehensive decision support model for a large investment problem - Communicate the chosen solution methods and performed analyses for a given problem area through a technical report
42892:

General Course Objectives: To give the student a cross-disciplinary overview of the main issues associated with shipping and port logistics, as well as to provide insights on what the industry and policy makers are doing to address related challenges.
Content: Overview of the various logistics problems in shipping and ports. The international, regional and sectoral policy context. Innovation drivers and triggers in maritime logistics sectors. Tramp and liner shipping logistics basics. Speed optimization and combined speed-routing models. Weather routing. Liner shipping network design. Balancing environmental vs. economic performance. Greenhouse gas and sulphur abatement and their impact on maritime logistics. Port logistics basics. Port governance models. Generalized costs and hinterland connections. Terminal management problems. Port security. Green ports. Cross-linkages between ship and port logistics. Autonomous shipping and digitalization. Maritime cyber-security. The course assignment will be each student (or student groups) to critically review a number of related papers, and work on a final project that will address a major shipping or port logistics challenge.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: Assess various shipping and port logistics systems according to specified criteria - Analyze the major drivers and triggers of innovation in the shipping and port logistics sectors - Evaluate how one can balance environmental vs economic logistical performance - Review optimisation models and recent literature for this class of problems - Synthesize related policy challenges, in the private industry, the IMO, the EU, and elsewhere - Assess the role of ICT, autonomous shipping and digitalization in maritime logistics - Investigate cross-linkages between shipping and port logistics - Recommend solutions to specific maritime logistics challenges
42973:
Name English: Planning and modelling of infrastructure
Danish Title: Planlægning og modellering af infrastruktur

42B50:
Name English: Strategy
Danish Title: Strategy
General Course Objectives: The aim of this module is to provide the participants with action-learning based knowledge about relevant topics within Strategy that can be applied in the participants’ companies.
Content: This course offers perspectives on the art of strategy and explores how strategy at the business level is conceptualized and practiced. Its design is guided by the premise that the firm is constrained by its environment and the resources it can access but, at the same time, it is also enabled by Management’s ability to leverage and to ultimately change these constraints in ways that create opportunities that may otherwise not exist. Hence, we will be exploring concepts and tools that can help you understand the environment that a company finds itself in, the resources it needs to obtain or create and develop, and the organization it needs to build. The course is built on three pillars: strategic positioning, capabilities, and change. Starting from the analysis of the firm’s external competitive environment, we assess the “structural” attractiveness of the relevant industry and consider how a firm’s position in that industry affects its performance. Then shifting focus internally to an analysis of the firm’s resources and capabilities, we explore how competitive advantage is built and sustained. Finally, we turn to organizational change to explore its drivers, challenges, and implications – particularly in a world that is becoming increasingly volatile, uncertain, complex and ambiguous. We also consider how the organization’s behavioral context both constrains and facilitates our ability to put strategy into action – not only to adapt to a changing world but also to drive some of that change.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Analyze and design business and corporate strategies - Recognize, develop and implement a consistent and coherent strategy in today’s business world - Move beyond conceptual models and analytical techniques to get a more “hands-on” experience through case analysis - Become familiar with and more comfortable in assessing ill-structured competitive situations - Select and apply appropriate tools, concepts and frameworks on real cases and use them effectively - Assess external forces and internal resources to understand and manage the environment that a company faces - Understand the resources companies need to obtain for competitive advantage - Organize deployment of competences and capabilities for achieving competitive advantage

42B54:
Name English: Managerial Economics
Danish Title: Managerial Economics
General Course Objectives: The course aims at giving participants a foundation in basic economic concepts that are essential to understanding the interplay between international economic development, financial markets and business risk.
Content: Today’s business leaders are expected to have an informed, current, and strategic perspective on the economic performance of a wide range of countries. And they are expected to read the forces at play fast, even as economists themselves are not in agreement on the direction of the economy or the decisions that monetary authorities and governments should make. On an industry level, competition takes different shapes and can constraint the strategic options of companies. Executives need a grasp of archetypal industry dynamics, economic methods for optimizing production, costs, pricing to customers as well as transfer pricing to inform their strategic and operational decisions. This course will deepen your understanding of the interplay between international economic developments, financial markets and business risks, and survey various industry dynamics as well as profit optimization principles. It will cover the main issues addressed by economists and the models they use to think them through, giving you a mechanistic understanding rather than a predictive, quantitative set of equations directly applicable to any situation. We will also discuss the impact of AI. Finally, economics as a discipline comes with limitations that should be acknowledged. Some provoking, sometimes controversial ideas proposed as beach heads to renew and expand our economic thinking will be discussed.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Discern key macro- and microeconomic mechanisms and forces, and anticipate their impact on an industry or company - Organize and relate key concepts in macroeconomics, monetary and fiscal policy, and financial markets - Understand the interplay between financial markets, financial institutions, and the business cycle in the real economy - Interpret current developments in economics brought by AI - Apply microeconomic tools to explain industry and competitive dynamics - Appraise decisions on production, pricing, and the value of information from a microeconomic perspective - Reflect on the limitations of economics as a discipline, and discuss forward-looking perspectives that broaden the scope of economic thinking - Become familiar with some of today’s most significant economists and thought-leaders
42B55:
Name English: Problem Solving
Danish Title: Problem Solving
General Course Objectives: The purpose of the module is to equip participants with the knowledge and skills to define, analyze, and solve complex business problems in a structured and evidence-based manner. Through the application of problem-formulation tools, management frameworks, and data analysis techniques, participants will learn to develop actionable solutions, craft clear and persuasive communications, and design realistic implementation plans tailored to diverse organizational contexts.
Content: Problem solving is a fundamental capability for leaders responsible for navigating complex decisions in uncertain and dynamic business environments. This course provides a structured approach to identifying, analyzing, and addressing problems where the appropriate solution is not immediately clear. It emphasizes both the formulation of the right problem and the careful selection of methods and tools for solving it. Throughout the DTU Executive MBA program, participants are introduced to a wide range of frameworks and tools drawn from multiple disciplines. This course helps consolidate that knowledge and trains participants to apply, adapt, and combine these tools effectively when faced with real-world business challenges. The course is organized around four key phases (Figure 1): Statement, Structure, Solve, and Present. Participants will work in groups on their own consultancy projects and use them as live cases for applying each approach. Through lectures, exercises, case examples, and presentations, they will learn how to define and structure problems, collect and analyze data, and develop well-supported, feasible recommendations. Attention is also given to communicating findings effectively, adapting both content and style to different audiences. Three complementary approaches are introduced and practiced: • Constructivist, which emphasizes creativity and contextual adaptation • Hypothesis-driven, which relies on structured logic and testable assumptions; and • Issue-driven, which breaks problems into logically distinct areas of inquiry.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Identify and define complex business problems in structured and actionable terms. - Apply tools and techniques for problem formulation. - Develop structured approaches to solving problems using constructivist, hypothesis-driven, and issue-driven methods. - Select, adapt, and combine management frameworks and tools to fit the nature and context of a specific problem - Design appropriate data collection strategies to support evidence-based problem solving - Analyze and interpret data to support conclusions and develop well-supported recommendations - Prepare clear and logically structured presentations and reports suited to different audiences and purposes - Develop realistic and actionable implementation plans based on the outcomes of analysis
42B56:
Name English: Innovation and Entrepreneurship
Danish Title: Innovation and Entrepreneurship
General Course Objectives: The general purpose of the course is to train MMT participants in the key management and entrepreneurial leadership concepts at the executive level that are relevant to innovation in public and private organizations. The course objectives are to convey judgment and inspire new thought processes about innovation and equip MMT participants with practical use of concepts, frameworks, and analytical tools of entrepreneurship and innovation management.
Content: The focus of this module is to provide students with a holistic overview of how new products and services may be generated effectively. Often described as “innovation” when referring to the activities conducted by large corporates and as “entrepreneurship” to emphasize the agility of new companies, both try to explore the same question: how can firms identify valuable ideas, develop those into promising prototypes for products and services, and eventually make a profit on those on the market? The Innovation and Entrepreneurship module is split into three main units: - Innovation strategy: we will look at how to link innovation to strategy, how to design and implement innovation strategy, key tools in innovation management, and innovation and strategy may shift through collaboration in an increasingly connected world - Where innovation begins: the focus of these sessions is on the first stage of the innovation process, the so called fuzzy-front end, where we will explore systematic ways for idea generation through research-based models for systematic innovation. - Transforming your companies and the world through innovation and entrepreneurship: our study tour takes us to the San Francisco Bay Area to experience a unique innovation ecosystem consisting of world-class research universities, tremendous entrepreneurial activity, an abundance of investment capital, a diverse workforce, social and professional networks, and a risk-friendly business culture. This eclectic mix of innovation components will be studied under the guidance of scholars and entrepreneurs affiliated with UC Berkeley, Haas School of Business; one of the foremost entrepreneurial universities in the world, and visits to companies to meet business leaders from Silicon Valley. The study tour focuses on providing an intense, unique opportunity to capture insights from the Silicon Valley mindset and skillset.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - get to know current trends in innovation and entrepreneurship - recognize and evaluate innovation tasks at the strategic and operational across companies in different sectors and at different maturity levels - develop an appreciation of the high degree of predictability of technical and business evolution discontinuities and what motivates customers across value ecosystems - use selected techniques for idea generation, selection, and development, including those used to identify, evaluate, and implement entrepreneurial opportunities in new and established organizations - identify, frame, analyse, and solve innovation problems and entrepreneurial opportunities strategically and operationally in their companies - design organizational systems and processes necessary for sustained and successful corporate innovation activities - evaluate the potential and design application of new strategies enabled by more holistic approaches to innovation (in particular: open innovation, innovation ecosystems) and capture it in new or revised strategies for innovation and entrepreneurship - describe and analyse the disruptive potential of innovation and describe how it may be strategically exploited by existing competitors, diversifying entrants, entrepreneurs, or their own companies.
42B61:
Name English: Managerial Finance
Danish Title: Managerial Finance
General Course Objectives: Our aim is to enable participants to measure and manage financial information with a focus on long-term value and value creation. This is a “language and tool course” designed to equip participants with the mindset and the skills to develop the financial component of a well-argued business case aligned with strategic objectives, and to deliver a well-founded pitch to management. The course also enhances participants’ ability to communicate effectively—not only with CFOs, treasurers, and controllers, but also with boards, shareholders, and other fund providers.
Content: You will learn how to build a solid financial foundation for your initiatives and how to assess and interpret the strategic and financial performance of your enterprise, its business units, and its projects. As a result, the financial and strategic implications of your decisions will become more transparent, significantly increasing your impact on business management. By the end of the course, you will be able to act as a capable discussion partner for financial colleagues and be better prepared for your next career move, potentially into higher management roles. In sum, the course introduces you to the following learning outcomes in an international context: 1. Demonstrate a thorough knowledge of finance, relevant theories, and methodological skills in an international setting. This includes understanding key financial principles and decision-making tools used to allocate resources and determine value. 2. Adopt strategic perspectives and develop problem-solving abilities in managerial contexts. Students will learn to analyze and provide direction for solving complex issues related to strategy, financing, and investment in international organizations. 3. Collaborate in diverse, cross-cultural teams to discuss, assess, and present financial and investment challenges in companies or projects. The course enhances personal effectiveness by fostering financial literacy and developing the ability to convincingly present and defend financial plans, supported by constructive feedback.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Demonstrate a thorough knowledge of finance, including key theories, methodological skills, and decision-making tools for resource allocation and value determination. - Explain the fundamentals of financial strategy and how financial statements inform managerial decisions. - Apply strategic perspectives, innovative thinking, and analytical skills to solve managerial problems - Address complex issues in strategy, financing, and investment within a global business context - Use systematic approaches, algorithms, and analytical instruments to conduct financial strategy analysis - Practice to collaborate effectively in teams to reflect on, discuss, assess, and present financing and investment challenges in an international setting in class. - Demonstrate leadership and communication skills by presenting, justifying, and defending financial plans, while incorporating feedback to improve effectiveness. - Formulate managerial and strategic decisions that link financial analysis to key performance indicators (KPIs).

42B67:
Name English: Organisational Design and Change
Danish Title: Organisational Design and Change
General Course Objectives: This course focuses on developing the essential skills and tools needed to design and lead effective organisations. By combining Organisational Design and Change Leadership, it equips participants with the knowledge to analyse, design, and implement changes that enhance organisational performance and achieve strategic goals.
Content: Change Leadership This section focuses on the leadership required to navigate and implement strategic change. It goes beyond linear models to address the non-linear and complex realities of organisational change. Key areas of focus include: • Strategic change theories integrated with real-world examples. • Recognising the role of contextual factors in shaping the process. • Internal change factors: Power dynamics, culture, interests, and communication. • External change factors: Political, economic, and social influences. Participants will develop practical insights to: • Design and position effective change interventions. • Work collaboratively in groups to refine strategies. • Present proposals and receive feedback to enhance their approaches. Organisational Design This section introduces practical tools and frameworks to: • Diagnose organisational challenges and identify areas for improvement. • Lead organisational design projects, from understanding problems to developing solutions. • Refine design solutions to align with strategic objectives and improve performance. The organisational design process is structured around the following steps: 1. Strategy: Define what the organisation aims to achieve. 2. Performance Assessment: Evaluate whether strategic goals are being met. 3. Diagnosis: Identify what is working and what needs improvement. 4. Design: Develop solutions to address identified issues. 5. Change Plan: Formulate a plan to implement the solutions. 6. Execution: Carry out the changes effectively. 7. Success: Achieve the desired outcomes.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - understand the tools of organisation diagnosis and how to use them - understand the tools of organisation design and how to use them - assess the alignment between the organizational design and the strategy of the organisation - diagnose why the organisation is underperforming for one or more of its stakeholders - develop options for improving the design of the organisation including structure, processes, decision rights, people models and governance - understand the main theoretical foundations, concepts and the success factors of change management - critically examine the value and limitations of the various approaches to change - assess the different ways to initiate, implement and sustain organizational change
42B68:

42B71:
Name English: Business and Society
Danish Title: Business and Society
General Course Objectives: The aim of this module is to provide the participants with action-learning based knowledge about relevant topics within Internationalization that can be applied in the participants’ companies.
Content: Globalization of markets and business, cultures, values and ethics, the sustainability imperative, and the expectations of society are the cornerstones of this module. The first half of the module explores the opportunities and challenges associated with globalization, cultures, and values; the second part investigates the tension zones, but also enabling relationships, between business and society. The module then concludes with the very practical challenges of managing global teams. Practical experience in handling managerial issues in a foreign culture is a unique supplement to in-class sessions and discussions. Therefore, a consultancy project in a foreign environment is integrated in the course.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - understand the current extent of the globalization of markets, of the potential and challenges they present to businesses, and of the different options businesses have to approach them - understand the specific challenges that emerging-market businesses encounter when entering mature, developed markets in the Western hemisphere - analyse the dilemmas that executives struggle with when their own values (and sometimes their company’s expectations) diverge from the values and expectations of the society around them - apply frameworks to explore how national cultures impact individual preferences in ways of working, communicating, building organizations, and defining oneself in relation to others, and how differences between cultures can represent serious challenges for business executives - understand the personal challenges executives experience when building a business – and an organization – abroad - evaluate environmental, social, and ethical problems associated with foreign direct investment and global supply chains - apply frameworks to explore Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) both as a necessity and constraint for business as well as a potential basis for competitive advantage - understand the complex challenges of working in/leading multicultural teams dispersed across the globe

42B76:
Name English: Leadership
Danish Title: Leadership
General Course Objectives: There is not one way to lead. This course enables you to develop your own leadership style and explores communication in the role of leader. The course lasts 21-months. It is a highly reflective process where development is evaluated on an ongoing basis via a reflective journal. Reflection draws on different inputs: theory, simulations and assignments in other courses. You explore your own values and personality as drivers to increase your performance within teams, in leading teams and in leading the organization. 42B77:
Name English: Operations Management
Danish Title: Operations Management
General Course Objectives: The aim of this module is to provide the participants with action-learning based knowledge about relevant topics within Operations and Supply Chain Management that can be applied in the participants’ companies
Content: The overall logic of the course is that effective operations management is a pre-requisite for all organisations – private or public, manufacturing or service - that seek to create sustainable value. Those organisations that are widely admired all have built their success on exceptional operations capabilities. The course will explore these paragons of operating virtue but also discuss the operational challenges faced by all organizations and introduce a toolbox for participants to make sense of and impact those they face.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - direct an operation by articulating and following an operations strategy. An operations strategy helps to ensure resources and processes are aligned with external-market and internal-functional stakeholders. - design the end-to-end processes that underpin effective delivery systems- avoiding Islands of process excellence – an efficient service centre, a highly automated production cell, an innovative 1st tier supplier, etc. – can help but it is systemic performance that matters. - deliver on organisational promises by planning and controlling resources and processes. For example, for many organisations, the active management of capacity AND demand remains relatively under-developed. It is important to consider both sides of this control ‘equation’ if an operation is to deliver its promises. - develop performance continuously by analysing and improving all processes. No process is perfect! Organisations and their supply networks face ever-changing circumstances. Hence, there is a constant pressure for continuously improved processes. - Understand the role of (digital) technologies and use of these tools for successful operations management - Manage operations in their broader societal context, including dealing with public policy, globalisation pressures, ethical and cultural challenges. - Apply simple systems thinking and analysis concepts to operating problems. - Understand the impact of context conditions (e.g. PESTLE: political, economic, sociological, technological, legal, and environmental) on operations management.
42B82:
Name English: Sustainability Management
Danish Title: Sustainability Management
General Course Objectives: The aim of the course is to introduce how sustainability can be framed and managed at a general level and how it addresses a combination of specific sustainability issues and sectors/ value chains
Content: Sustainability challenges affect all parts of society all over the planet. Sustainability is easy to grasp as a goal but complex to deal with in concrete decision-making. Business, government and civil society have to collaborate and form multi-stakeholder partnerships in order to address them – while applying a holistic perspective. This implies an increasing need for managers, public officials and employees who can address sustainability matters on an informed basis when leading or being part of multidisciplinary teams. The course is seeking to fill this gap by providing participants with frameworks and tools that can help them create value, build business opportunity and adjust corporate strategy to address sustainability challenges. The course will be held by DTU faculty. The format is short lectures followed by group work and reflection rounds in plenum. Participants are encouraged to share experience and practice from their own organisations.
