Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain how the expression of a post-flashover fire temperature can be derived from thermal equilibrium and which parameters the fire curve depends on. - List different design fires based on this model and explain the main differences between nominal fire curves and parametric fires. - Calculate the fire characteristics (fuel load, thermal inertia, and opening factor) of any given compartment and derive the corresponding parametric fire curve. - Predict how the variation of the fire characteristics affects the severity and duration of the fire and, in turn, the heating temperature and fire resistance of the structural elements. - Calculate the reduction of the mechanical design load in fire condition and explain how the mechanical loads influence the critical temperature and the fire resistance of fire-exposed structural elements. - Calculate the reduction of the mechanical properties of steel, concrete, and wood at high temperatures. Calculate the permanent reduction of mechanical properties of cold-worked and presstressed steel and of concrete when they are cooled down to 20 C after being exposed to high temperatures. - Perform the design or verification of uninsulated and insulated steel elements subjected to a parametric or standard fire. - Perform the verification of timber elements exposed to parametric or standard fire - Perform the verification of concrete elemetnts subjected to a parametric or standard fire during and after the fire. - Identify possible weaknesses in the structural fire response of a building elements and indicate measures to improve its fire resistance.
41B02:
Name English: Industrial Fires
Danish Title: Industribrande
General Course Objectives: An introduction of the basic terms, principles and methods for assessment of fire safety of industrial facilities is given. Hereunder the question about the fire emissions fate and effect in the environment, as e.g. the impact to nabors. The starting point are industrial cases and the relevant laws and regualtions, as e.g. the Seveso and ATEX directives.
Content: Industrial fires are an important area within the assessment of fire safety in buildings and facilities. Due to large-scale processes and the associated storage of large quantities of materials and chemicals, a fire would have a different character. For example, greater heat radiation effects could lead to cascade effects and major damage over large distances, which has the potential to also include neighbors to industrial facilities and could cause environmental damage. In addition, such scenarios would make rescue efforts more difficult. Based on the relevant national regulations and legislation based on the Seveso and Atex directives, typical problems and mitigation measures to prevent or reduce the consequences for neighbors and the environment are reviewed. The course introduces distribution calculations of chemical and fire emissions. The students would be able to understand and use key methods, such as emission calculations for liquids and gases, calculate jet fires, gas explosions, etc. and use Probit functions to assess personal injuries. In particular, the students will be introduced to environmental chemical aspects including the release, transport, distribution and degradation of chemical substances in the environment. The students will be able to assess acute toxic effects, chronic effects and ecotoxic effects. Data search is another important part of the course and the students will learn to use various databases and tools, which are made available by, among others, the DTU library. The course concludes with an individualized written group report in which the groups deals with a realistic situation.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Define and describe the basic concepts and terms used in industrial fire risk assessment - Interpret physical-chemical and ecotoxicological data for chemical process in relation to environmental fate and environmental hazard - Perform simple quantitative calculations of substance fate - Collect relevant data on. chemicals, environmental fate and effects of such Internet and databases - Classify chemicals in accordance with regulatory guidelines for risk assessment - Evaluate preventive and mitigative measures to minimize the fire and explosion risks - Plan and carry out a project and formulate hypotheses - Write a technical report, application of the theory in a realistic environment problem with chemicals, including drawing conclusions and making references and citations
41B03:
Name English: Building Fire Technology
Danish Title: Bygningsbrandteknik
General Course Objectives: Void
Content: Void
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain regulations on fire safety - Explain significant parts of the Certification Act - Determine the right usage categories for a building site - Determine the risk class and fire class for a building project - Explain methods concerning active and passive fire safety measures - Assess the building material’s fire behavior properties - Assess the choice of test method and classification for materials and elements - Make an assessment of the fire safety of a building assigned to BK2 - Develop a fire strategy report for a traditional building design - Explain the design process particular to BK2 construction - Document the fire safety for BK2 construction - Make contol plans and control of fire protection
41B04:
Name English: Fire Chemistry
Danish Title: Brandkemi
General Course Objectives: The students vil obtain a basic understanding about fire chemistry and get skills within the most common methods and theories applied in the field. This enables the students, e.g. to predict ignition properties, flame spred characteristics, and the type and yields of combustion products an dother impåortant parameters within Fire safety engineering.
Content: The course Fire Chemistry introduces basic knowledge on the reaction to heat of solid, liquid and gaseous materials typically applied in the built environment. Chemical compositions and chemical structures of a number of materials are reviewed. It is explained how the various materials will generate gaseous species through evaporation and/or pyrolysis. Important parameters herunder are the energy of evaporation, the flammability limits in air and the ignition process. The chemical mechanisms and kinetics behind these processes are introduced. Important terms herunder are the heat of combustion and the Heat release rate under well and poorly ventilated fire conditions. The fire conditions are characterized using the theory of the fuel - oxygen equivalence ratios. Therefore the chemical reaction equations are worked with and the estimation of the heat of combustion using the concept of the Heat of Formation of atoms and molecules is presented. Last not least the generation of toxic combustion products is shown and the toxicity of smoke gases is explained. The course is partly theoretical and partly experimental, as each student will conduct a number of laboratory experiments during the course.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the domains terminology - Calculate the heat of formation, heats of combustion and adiabatic flame temperatures - Explain the assumptions that are the basis for the domain models - Conduct simple calculations for central parameters in fire chemistry, hereunder paramters as ignition, flame spread, explosion limits, flame extinction, selv ignition, amount and types of combustion products. - Conduct evaluation of the obtained results (validity, dimension, units) - Explain and predict the yields of toxic gases and their acute-toxic impacts (smoke poisoning) - Analyse results obtained in laboratory experiments and to evaluate the result's quality - Balance relevant chemical reaction equations and to calculate the fuel- air equivalence ratio
41B05:
Name English: Fire Risk Management
Danish Title: Brandrisikostyring
General Course Objectives: The course introduces the basic concepts and the basic terminology in fire risk analysis and management. Throughout the course, the students will acquire: knowledge on the general approach to fire risk management; understanding of fundamental probability theory, risk analysis and decision theory; and be able to perform practical fire risk assessment. The course will introduce the students to methods for undertaking a rational fire risk assessment and an ensuing fire risk management process for the built environment.
Content: Based on historical fires of relevance the development of fire risk assessment is explained. Both deterministic and probabilistic fire risk methods are introduced. The students will learn about scenario development analysis for e.g. fire and smoke spread. These scenarios are combined with evacuation scenarios as well as acceptance criteria for occupant safety. The students will understand basic probabilistic theory and perform basic probabilistic calculations. Hereunder, an introduction to Bayesian Networks and Monte Carlo methods is given. The differences between qualitative and quantitative risk assessment are introduced and applied by the students based on case studies.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Analyze fire risk using a probabilistic method - Describe physical processes that lead to and are associated with fires - Perform an analysis applying Event- and fault trees - Model stochastic phenomena in fires - Draw a risk profile and explain the profile - Assess the advantages associated with different risk reduction methods related to fire - Perform a sensitivity analysis based on the students own choice of relevant parameters - Perform basic fire risk assessments for a relevant project/case - List stochastic input-variables that are related to fire scenarios in a building - Readily suggest relevant risk-reducing actions or solutions, both related to probability and consequence - Use standard software for probability calculations, risk analysis and decision analysis - Determine input data for a complex fire risk assessment
41B12:
Name English: Fire modelling
Danish Title: Brandmodellering
General Course Objectives: The course is aimed at providing an insight into the most widely used computational tools for fire and evacuation modeling and their possible integration in relation to fire safety design.
Content: The course is organized in three parts, focusing on: i) evacuation modelling; ii) fire modelling; and iii) integration between the two. In the first and second modules the main theoretical aspects related to computational fluid dynamic (CFD) and evacuation algorithms will be presented, respectively. The syntax of FDS as CFD program and of Pathfinder as evacuation program will be introduced and some simple models will be implemented. The simulations will be aimed at highlighting some critical aspects of the modelling, such as validation of the model, objectivity of the solution and sensitivity to uncertainties. As the first homework assignment after the first module, the students must carry out a fire modelling simulation using FDS and assess critical conditions, including temperature and smoke layer height. As the second homework assignment after the second module, the students must conduct an evacuation simulation of a building using Pathfinder and evaluate the evacuation time. Few more advanced functions of FDS and Pathfinder will be introduced and the interaction between fire modelling and evacuation modelling will be presented. Shortly after the end of the third module, a final assignment will be given to the students in the form of an integrated design problem based on the fire and evacuation models implemented in the two previous home assignments. The final models and results should be described in a detailed report.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - list the main types of numerical models for pre- and post-flashover fire - explain the main set of equations and the main solution methods of CFD programs - explain the phenomena influencing evacuation and the analytical and empirical formula describing them - explain the main differences between CFD and evacuation modeling programs and their possible integration implement the necessary sensitivity analyses on the basis of the main model assumptions - identify the main input parameters in FDS and Pathfinder - highlight the main uncertainties in fire and evacuation models and implement the necessary sensitivity analyses - to run analyses in FDS and Pathfinder and interpret the outcomes - recognize the main assumptions of the fire and evacuation models and the limits of validity of the results
41B13:
Name English: Fire safety design
Danish Title: Brandteknisk dimensionering
General Course Objectives: The course aims to provide students with a fundamental understanding of the key principles of the initial, conceptual phase of performance-based fire engineering design. Emphasis is placed on developing the ability to argue for and justify design choices, including why specific fire engineering approaches are applied, and how these choices form part of an integrated whole encompassing fire safety design, evacuation strategies, and the operational capabilities of the emergency response.
Content: The course introduces the fundamental principles of performance-based fire safety design with a specific emphasis on the initial conceptual design phase. Teaching is centred around the development of an initial sketch that forms the basis for discussion and argumentation of key design choices before detailed analyses are undertaken. The course presents international approaches to fire safety design, including the use of conceptual models, engineering judgement, and structured methodologies recognised in the field. Evacuation concepts and strategies are addressed as an integral part of the conceptual design process. Methods for incorporating emergency response considerations into the fire safety design concept (FBIM) are also introduced. Simple analytical methods and calculations are applied where appropriate to support design reasoning, but they are not the primary focus of the course. Emphasis is placed on identifying, evaluating, and justifying possible design solutions and on developing well‑reasoned and clearly documented fire safety design concepts. Practical exercises and discussions constitute a central part of the course, and students work both individually and in groups to develop, analyse, and justify conceptual fire safety solutions.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the principles of performance-based fire safety design and the initial conceptual design phase. - Describe the importance of developing and justifying design concepts before engaging in detailed analyses and calculations. - Outline key international approaches to fire safety design, including the use of conceptual models and engineering judgement. - Explain fundamental principles of evacuation strategies and their role in the conceptual design phase. - Explain methods that can be used to incorporate emergency response into a fire safety design concept (FBIM). - Prepare and discuss an initial sketch as the basis for developing a fire safety design concept. - Identify and argue for essential design choices, including justification of alternative solutions. - Analyse fire safety problems at a conceptual level and evaluate potential design strategies. - Assess the advantages and limitations of different methods for verifying performance-based fire safety requirements. - Apply simple calculations and analyses at appropriate stages to support the argumentation - Document design decisions and justify them professionally in accordance with established practices in performance-based fire safety engineering. - Engage in professional discussion and argue convincingly for selected solutions in both individual and group-based tasks.
41B1B:
Name English: Circular Construction
Danish Title: Cirkulært Byggeri
General Course Objectives: The purpose of the course is to provide the students with the basic skills necessary to understand and discuss the principles of a transformation of construction from a linear to a circular economy. Circular construction involves the use of fewer natural resources, a longer lifespan of the buildings and reuse at the end of their lifespan. Through the course the students learn to incorporate these principles into construction cases in practice. There will be a focus on how we can build for circularity in the future, e.g. through the introduction of material passports and design for separation. Another focus will be on the current building mass with significant topics such as transformation, renovation, reuse of building parts or recycling of building materials in the production of new building materials. The need for competence development and new development at various points in the value chain in the construction industry will be discussed, e.g. selective demolition, recycling platforms, digital tools, circular tenders and documentation of recyclability. Based on the students' own cases, the possibilities for circular construction are analyzed and treated.
Content: - Theory and practice for circular construction - National and international strategies - Transformation of construction and circular renovation - Urban mining. Materials and building parts to be reused or recycled - Selective demolition, recycling platforms, value chains - Design for separation, material and building fit - Technical shared ownership and circular construction (opportunities and challenges) - Context-specific opportunities for circularity - Inspiration from practical examples of circular measures
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain terminology and main principles in circular construction - Compare national and international strategies for circular construction and sustainability - Select ideas for implementing of circular initiatives within construction - Collect and combine ideas for circular solutions in current construction cases - Compare linear and circular value chains - Consider circular solutions at building level, locally, regionally - Discuss the importance of context for possible circular readings - Discuss new construction/renovation based on a circular way of thinking
41B24:
Name English: Building Fire Technology
Danish Title: Bygningsbrandteknik
General Course Objectives: To provide the students with an understanding of building fire protection technology and its importance for securing human, material and economic values ​​that are part of modern construction - and to give participants such insight into the diverse areas of the profession that they will be able to deal with both detailed fire protection problems and cases in a larger context, be they of a practically oriented nature or within research and development.
Content: The course includes learning about the development of fire damage and building fire legislation. The course provides an introduction to fire testing and classification. The course also introduces knowledge about thermal processes, the fire properties of building materials and an introduction to fire design of building structures. The course also includes learning about active and passive fire protection, fire risk and fire protection of different building categories. Finally, the course includes an introduction to fire engineering analysis and planning of construction projects, including through the presentation of case studies.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain current fire safety legislation - Make a choice of use category for a construction project - Explain methods of active and passive fire protection - Assess whether the correct fire testing method has been used for various building materials and building elements - Provide a fire safety assessment of a building - Prepare a fire strategy report for a construction project - Explain the principles of fire ventilation and sprinkler systems - Explain the principles and purpose of a sensitivity analysis in the field of fire - Distinguish projects where the Building Act applies from projects where the Emergency Legislation applies. - Explain risk classes and fire classes
41B25:
Name English: Fire Dynamics
Danish Title: Branddynamik
General Course Objectives: The course aims to provide students with an understanding of the physical laws and relationships that govern fire development and smoke propagation in building fires, as a basis for fire‑dynamic analyses and calculations.
Content: The course includes teaching on primary fire dynamic topics such as heat release rate, flame heights & smoke plumes, ventilation flow, pressure profiles and temperature calculations for gas temperatures. The course also includes topics on heat exchange during fire processes, conservation equations for mass and energy, smoke filling, combustion products and an introduction to fire models, especially the so-called 2-zone models. The course also includes the importance of valid input parameters for use in fire dynamic analyses.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the physical assumptions and principles underlying key models used in fire dynamics. - Describe the theoretical foundations of hand calculation methods, two‑zone models, and CFD models, including their areas of application and limitations. - Apply and perform calculations of central fire dynamic parameters such as heat release rate, temperature, pressure, thermal radiation, smoke production, and toxic effects. - Explain the core terminology and concepts used within the field of fire dynamics. - Evaluate and validate calculated results with respect to order of magnitude, units, and physical plausibility. - Analyse an initial fire compartment and determine relevant input parameters for hand calculation methods and zone models. - Explain the principles of two‑zone models and interpret and assess experimental data from fire tests. - Plan and structure a fire dynamics analysis using both hand calculation methods and simple fire models. - Provide a qualitative and quantitative description of a building fire with a focus on pressure‑ and temperature‑related phenomena.
41B27:
Name English: Fire Safety of Complex buildings
Danish Title: Brandsikring af komplekse bygninger
General Course Objectives: The course is taught in Danish
Content: The course is taught in Danish
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Identify a complex building and explain your choice - Describe the challenges for establishing and maintaining fire safety in a complex building - Independendly search, find and refer to relevant literature - Apply regulations and legislation related to complex buildings - Explain the basic principles of numerical models for complex buildings - Elaborate evacuation strategies of relevance for complex buildings - Elaborate solutions for problems occuring when applying exixting laws and regulations on complex buildings - Elaborate solutions for problems regarding fire installations applied in complex buildings - Explain the basic principles when carrying out numerical evacuation calculations on complex buildings
41E16:
Name English: Engineering mathematics and physics for building constructers
Danish Title: Ingeniørmæssig matematik og fysik for bygningskonstruktører
General Course Objectives: The course aims to provide building designers with the basic engineering skills in mathematics and physics that they may lack in order to follow the Master's degree in Fire Safety at DTU, which otherwise requires an engineering level.
Content: The course presents the basic mathematical disciplines and engineering principles to be able to follow the continuing education for a Master in Fire Safety at DTU. The course therefore includes topics such as geometry, algebra, trigonometry, functions, differential calculus, integral calculus and vector calculus. The course also contains definitions and terminology for work, energy, power and impulse. Finally, the course provides an introduction to basic statics, chemistry and thermodynamics.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Use trigonometry, algebra and vector calculus - Apply functions for curves and surfaces - Set up and solve mathematical equations - Explaining systems of equations - Perform differentiation and integration - Set up and solve differential equations - Determine work, energy, power and impulse - Evaluate basic statics, including static systems, cross-sectional analysis, and section forces - Evaluate and use statistics - Using basic chemistry - Apply thermodynamics
41MIB:
Name English: Fire engineering project task
Danish Title: Brandteknisk projektopgave
General Course Objectives: The fire engineering project concludes the Master’s programme in Fire Safety Engineering and aims to enable the student to independently apply, integrate, and further develop fire engineering knowledge and methods to address a complex, practice‑oriented problem within fire safety. The project shall demonstrate the student’s ability to engage in in‑depth academic work, critical analysis, methodological rigour, and clear, professionally sound documentation.
Content: The course consists of independent individual project work within a fire engineering topic. The project includes formulation and delimitation of a problem, selection and application of relevant fire engineering methods and calculation tools, as well as analysis, evaluation, and documentation of results. The project is carried out under supervision and is concluded with a written report and an oral presentation.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Independently formulate and delimit a fire engineering problem at an academic and professional level. - Select, apply, and combine relevant fire engineering theories, methods, and calculation tools. - Analyse complex fire engineering problems and evaluate alternative solution strategies. - Critically assess assumptions, data, uncertainties, and limitations associated with the applied methods and models. - Integrate knowledge from multiple fire engineering sub‑disciplines into a coherent and comprehensive analysis. - Document results, calculations, and assessments in a clear, structured, and professionally substantiated manner in a technical report. - Communicate the project’s problem formulation, choice of methods, results, and conclusions orally and in writing to a professional audience. - Reflect on the academic contribution of the project and contextualise the results in relation to practice and applicable standards.
42001:
Name English: Large scale energy system analysis
Danish Title: Storskala energisystemanalyse
General Course Objectives: The main purpose of the course is for the students to learn how to perform analysis of future energy system scenarios.
Content: We introduce the concepts of energy system analysis and scenario building. In lectures, exercises and project work the students gradually learn how to build scenarios and analyse future large scale energy systems, as well as assess energy system analyses performed by others. The GAMS based tool, Balmorel, will be applied as an exemplary model.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Collect and evaluate data critically e.g. by comparing production costs of technologies - Develop internally consistent future energy scenarios - Represent energy demand, conversion and resource potentials for future energy systems - Analyse national energy system scenarios - Validate and explain results - Clarify sensitivities of main assumptions through sensitivity analysis - Synthesise the main conclusions and discuss results in relation to results of other energy system analyses and current debate in society - Choose between different types of energy system models for different purposes - Explain the main functionalities of the Balmorel model - Critically reflect on tool functionalities as well as main assumptions and limitations of energy system analyses
42108:
Name English: Advanced Financial Engineering
Danish Title: Advanced Financial Engineering
General Course Objectives: The course covers advanced aspects of financial engineering, such as applying stochastic processes to financial data, analysis, and measurement of financial risk and pricing methods for financial derivatives.
Content: Stochastic processes in finance. Financial Risk Management. Pricing of derivatives.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Apply a number of stochastic processes to financial data - Compute theoretical prices for various financial derivatives - Explain the main types of financial derivatives and their for hedging purposes - Classify financial risks - Measure and analyze market risk using e.g., Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall - Describe and analyse different methods for estimating the probability of counterpart’s default - Describe the principles of counterparty credit risk and calculate Credit Value Adjustment (CVA) for derivatives contracts - Explain some lessons learned from some well known financial crisis
42283:
Name English: Smart Cities
Danish Title: Smarte byer
General Course Objectives: Smart Cities are seen as paramount to rethinking technical infrastructure to meet the anticipated challenges of the 21st century, including digitization, social equality, urban trends and urban quality. The general objective of the course is to explore smart urban systems from a holistic perspective. The course will examine the interconnectedness of various urban systems, the Internet of Things (IoT), their management and their contribution to the quality of life. In particular, the course will emphasize the exploration of the urban mobility system including concepts such as electrical mobility, self-driving vehicles, artificial intelligence, mobility as a service and others; and behavior or usage of urban systems in a smart city, e.g. mobility and activity patterns. Students will adopt a forward-looking approach to technologies in urban environments. Having these in mind, student groups will design projects to solve challenges proposed by course instructors and invited lectures (e.g. industry, public sector, civil organizations, etc.).
Content: The content will be introduced in two stages (approx. 1 week each): concepts and methodologies, provided by instructor and DTU faculty; tools and challenges, provided by invited lecturers from private and public sector. The goal is to design feasible solutions for real-world challenges, using the concepts learned. Stage 1: The concept of the “Smart City” and the interactions between transport and other systems (e.g. energy, environment) through new technologies. Introduction to systems approach, where the inputs, outputs and the ”boundaries” of a system are clearly delineated, with specific focus on decision variables (that effect the system) and system evaluation. Introduction of technical tools that can support the design of smart city solutions (and applicable in the group work). Stage 2: The role of new and mature tools (e.g. software, sensors, new devices) in the future of mobility, including developed (or under development) by industry. Current grand challenges for mobility in our cities, how to approach them, assess the potentials of solutions and design their implementation. The third week of the course will consist of intensive project work.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Compare key smart urban systems, their development, and interconnections; - Analyse the urban environment from a technical perspective; - Be aware of social and ethical issues in smart city technologies - Develop a system-level perspective that takes an integrative approach towards the solution of complex problems in cities; - Evaluate, from a holistic perspective, the impact of smart solutions to specific urban issues on the wider interconnected systems; - Critically evaluate ideas for smart city projects; - Evaluate and critique the implications associated with smart cities; - Evaluate current issues or challenges in urban development by applying smart technology and lessons from case studies; - Create and/or innovate smart solutions to current environmental, social, economic, and governance issues within cities. - Understand and explain the cross-cutting implications of transport decisions to other urban systems (e.g. water, environment, economy); - Present Smart Mobility research and/or development – both orally and in writing.
42501:
Name English: Innovation in Engineering (Polytechnical Foundation)
Danish Title: Innovation in Engineering (Polyteknisk Grundfag)
General Course Objectives: The course introduces students to apply competencies and methods to enable innovation in engineering within multidisciplinary teams. Students will: - Understand how to follow and apply a structure innovation process to a real-life engineering challenge - Experience the varied innovation landscape by navigating and applying their skills in it - Contribute with collaborative initiatives in a team context to allow new perspectives - Combine their disciplines through various methods in a facilitated innovation process - Acquire the DTU's signature Innovation Mindset and application of multidisciplinary teams - Be able to communicate key findings to relevant stakeholders and adjust from their inputs - Acquire a toolkit of structured methods to increase the innovative probability - Create new solution-oriented ideas and mature these into a final concept proposal
Content: Innovation competencies are crucial for future engineers to invigorate new perspectives, particularly to nurture and drive global change in tackling the societal, environmental and health-related challenges we face. Through the course, students acquire applicable experiences and competencies with a systematic approach to innovation in an engineering context. Students are required to develop unique insights into how integrated innovation is practised. They will experience and face challenges with multidisciplinary collaboration while working on a real industry challenge. Each project team will also be assigned a team facilitator (which are students who are taking the course 'Facilitating Innovation in Multidisciplinary Teams'). These facilitators have attained innovation competencies and will guide the team during all project work. With a facilitator at hand, the team will have a 'catalyst' to increase 'Innovation Height'. The course is organized into two main parts. The first week - the BOOST module - is focused on engaging the students with the topic of innovation by an array of speakers, and introducing students to a systematic approach to innovation, including relevant theory. At the start of the first week, the students will be put into project teams based on their chosen innovation challenge as well as their line of study et al. In the second and third weeks - the EXPERIENCE module - the teams's focus is on developing an innovative solution in collaboration with their facilitator. This should result in a concept that must be presented to the stakeholders at the end of the process. The course consists of lectures, reading material, team exercises, assignments, peer-reviews and multiple-choice quizzes. The learning activities and submissions are team-based experiences and for that reason, it is important to participate in class at DTU Campus
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the importance between Feasibility, Viability, Desirability, Responsibility and Sustainability of an innovation context, - Explain the innovation process through the chosen model of the 'Double Diamond', - Explain the different approaches in DTU's Signature Innovation Mindset and practical applications, - Explain methods of working in the different stages of an innovation process e.g., exploration, ideation, iteration, designing, and building, - Apply an innovation process model that encompasses phases of Discover, Define, Develop, Deliver i.e. Double Diamond, - Evaluate and adapt the different phases of the innovation process based on limitations as, resources, time, constraints, data, stakeholders etc., - Contribute activly with your own disciplinary background in the different stages of the innovation process, - Give and receive constructive and appropriate feedback to and from team members and other teams, - Reflect on how to act constructively and proactively in a context where the decision-making process is characterized by high uncertainty and risk, - Make informed and qualified decisions in an innovation process with regards to the Feasibility, Viability, Desirability, Responsibility and Sustainability of a solution, - Reflect on their role, ways of working, and impact as an engineer in the innovation process, - Review and communicate to the relevant stakeholders the design choices of an explored concept in relation to both the value creation and limitations.
42503:
Name English: Facilitating Innovation in Multidisciplinary Teams
Danish Title: Facilitating Innovation in Multidisciplinary Teams
General Course Objectives: The course aims to equip the student with competencies in facilitating innovation in multidisciplinary teams in an engineering context. Students will: - Understand what it takes to facilitate an innovation process in an industry challenge. - Experience the varied innovation landscape by navigating and applying their skills in it given their expanded innovation and facilitation competencies. - Facilitate collaborative initiatives in a group context to develop new perspectives. - Identify value and limitations of new solution-oriented ideas and encourage maturing these into a final concept proposition. - Acquire the DTU's signature Innovation Mindset in the application of multidisciplinary teams and further develop their own approach to innovation. - Expand their toolkit of structured methods to increase the innovative probability.
Content: Facilitating the innovation process can be crucial for future engineers to invigorate new perspectives, particularly to nurture and drive global change in tackling the societal, environmental and health-related challenges we face. Through the course, students acquire experiences and competencies in applying and guiding systematic approaches for facilitating innovation in an engineering context. Students will develop a strong instinct and unique insights into how the facilitation of integrated innovation is practised. They will experience and face challenges through multidisciplinary collaboration while working on a real industry challenge. Each project team (consisting of students who are taking the course 'Innovation in Engineering') will be assigned a team facilitator. As a facilitator, you will bring your experience-based innovation skills into play and guide the multidisciplinary team through the entire project work. The course is organized into two main parts. The first week - the BOOST module - is focused on engaging the students with the topic of innovation by an array of speakers, getting to know the team and introducing students to a systematic approach to facilitating innovation, as well as other relevant theories. At the start of the first week, the students will facilitate up to two teams based on their chosen innovation challenge. The second and third week - the EXPERIENCE module - are focused on facilitating the team through the innovation process. This should result in a concept that must be presented by the team to the stakeholders at the end of the process. The learning activities and submissions are team-based experiences and for that reason, it is important to participate in class at DTU Campus.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the importance between Feasibility, Viability, Desirability, Responsibility and Sustainability of an innovation content, - Identify different team dynamics and apply relevant iniciatives to their innovation process, - Explain relevant approaches in the facilitation of teamwork, - Explain methods for leading and facilitating the different stages of an innovation process e.g., exploration, ideation, iteration, designing, and building, - Apply methods to support and maintain a collaborative environment in the processes of exploration, ideation, iteration, designing, and building, - Guide team dicussions on group dynamics and teamwork with regards to the division of tasks and responsibilities, - Identify and increase the inclusion of diverse disciplinary backgrounds in the different stages of the innovation process, - Apply methods to facilitate constructive teamwork in a context where the decision-making process is characterized by high uncertainty and risk of being led astray, - Support the making of informed and qualified decisions in an innovation process with regards to Feasibility, Viability, Desirability, Sustainability, and Responsibility, - Reflect on their role, ways of working, and value as an innovation facilitator in the innovation process., - Keep the end in mind with regards to deliver and argue to the relevant stakeholders the design choices of an explored concept in relation to both the value creation and limitations, - Give and receive constructive and appropriate feedback to and from team members and other teams.
42588:
Name English: Data and data science
Danish Title: Data og data science
General Course Objectives: This course focuses on the challenges that arise when we try to use data to answer questions. In addition, it establishes various approaches to deal with these challenges. To establish such a focus, the course discusses data types, data collection techniques, and data management. In addition, the course focuses on tools for data processing, exploratory analysis and data visualisations. Finally, the course focuses on how various directions within data science can give different perspectives in a data analysis, e.g. statistical analysis vs. machine learning and exploratory vs. confirmatory data visualisation.
Content: The course covers general aspects of data collection, management and analysis. It classifies various data categories, e.g. revealed preference data, stated preference data as well as data collection through surveys, experiments and online databases. It also covers governance issues such as data management plan and data management principles, such as GDPR and FAIR. Throughout the course, students will work on data to gain experience with data processing (and how time consuming it is). Various tools to do both exploratory analysis as well as data analysis will be covered including descriptive statistics, data scraping, language technology, visualisations, regression and classification tools.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Discuss the relationship between problem, plan and data to answer questions - Describe data types and ways to collect data - Discuss data governance and produce a data management plan - Use data to answer relevant questions - Conduct exploratory data analysis and visualisation - Discuss differences between various approaches in statistics/data science - Apply common techniques to analyse continuous data and interpret the results - Apply common techniques to analyse discrete data and interpret the results - Apply common techniques to analyse textual data and interpret the results - Present focused and concise data analyses
42715:
Name English: Experimenting with ethnography
Danish Title: Eksperimenter i etnografisk analyse
General Course Objectives: Teach participants use of experimental techniques to open new paths of doing ethnographic analysis.
Content: The course introduces the concept of analysis as an experimental practice. By offering the participants the opportunity to themselves use a set of analytic protocols, the effects of which will be discussed and elaborated by peers and experienced scholars, the aim of the course is to open new paths of doing ethnographic analysis. The structure of the course is based on chapters from the anthology Experimenting with Ethnography (Ballestero, Winthereik, eds. 2021) where the writers all use their own practice to suggest ways of experimenting with ethnographic analysis. Rather than approaching analysis as an abstract and solely intellectual practice, the aim of the book and its protocols is to convey a concrete mode of action and creative practice for researchers. An important point of departure for the book is problematizing that a fixed boundary between “the field” (data collection) and “the desk” (analysis, theorizing) exists or is automatically meaningful. The concept of the analytical protocols links to the history of experimental settings as a site of interest in the social sciences and humanities (Rheinberger 1997; Latour 1999; Tilley 2011; Kowal, Radin & Reardon 2013; Davies et al. 2018; Wolfe 2018 in Ballestero & Winthereik 2021). The course will cover a broad range of topics such as multimodal approaches, multispecies ethnography, sensory modality, decolonization of methodology and modes of collaboration. The theoretical scope of the course is anchored in the anthropology of technology and Science and Technology Studies with a slight emphasis on application of “object-oriented” methods in STS (e.g. Maguire, Watts, Winthereik (eds), 2021). The course invites students to engage and reflect on both their empirical material as well as their individual analytical practice. We invite students to engage with questions such as: How are we confined by traditional ways of thinking about analysis as we approaching our own ethnographic material? How do experimental approaches to analysis inform the production of knowledge, the treatment of data, as well as the empirical sites we enter? How can we as researchers nurture a space of play opening up ways of experimental thinking? What new insights about our data and our object of study can we achieve by applying concrete protocols with method for experimentation? How to use experimental ethnographic analysis as impetus for research in collaboration with others?
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Use experimental ethnographic methods to analyzing their data material. - Pursue experimental thinking in conducting fieldwork. - Challenge their biases, thinking habits and analytical practices. - Identify analytical openings and possibilities and create circumstances for surprise and discovery. - Scrutinize their own analytical frameworks and take more creative and engaging routes in their thinking. - Switching between methods and modalities, blurring the distinctions between field work, data collection, analysis, and writing. - Take a step back from inherited concepts, theoretical interests and preconceived categorizations. - Collaborate in analysis.
42716:
Name English: STS Approaches to Energy Research
Danish Title: STS Approaches to Energy Research
General Course Objectives: Energy matters and conceptualizations have come to be a mainstay of diverse social scientific and humanities research. What theoretical affordances might the broad inter-discipline of science and technology studies (STS) provide for the study of energy? This overview course aims to show students how our variegated energy systems have come into being together with particular epistemologies, collective cultural identities, power asymmetries in knowledge and power, and particular ideas of how to shift the world towards a sustainable future.
Content: DAY 0 (1 week before course begins) Create groups and divide readings, write summaries of readings before course officially begins. DAY 1 (May 22, Monday) I THEORETICAL ORIENTATIONS (9am-2pm) II ENERGY AND COLONIZATION (2-5pm) DAY 2 (May 23, Tuesday) III ENERGY AND DEMOCRACY (9am-2pm) IV ENERGY FUTURES (2-5pm) DAY 3 (May 24, Wednesday) V THE GOOD ECONOMY AND THE PERMATIVE WORK AND EFFECT OF VALUATIONS (9am-12pm) VI MAPPING AND MODELING (2-5pm) DAY 4 (May 25, Thursday) VII CONCEPTUALIZING USERS (9am-12pm) VI ENERGY CONTROVERSIES AND ACTIVISM (12-3pm) DAY 5 (May 26, Friday) IX ENERGY KNOWLEDGE PRODUCERS AND INTERDISCPLINARITY (9am-12pm) X ENERGY RISK AND SECURITY (2-5pm)
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Categorise different theoretical approaches to the study of energy - Develop competencies in cross-cultural evaluation of the mutual constitution of energy and society in different parts of the world - Connect how colonialism—differently experienced around the world—have shaped global energy systems. - Evaluate how risk, uncertainty, and the politics of expertise are investigated within a coproductionist framework - Identify different conceptualizations of ‘users’ in energy systems - Identify the reasons for social movements against both ‘dirty’ and ‘clean’ energy systems - Develop competencies in identify research gaps, both in terms of empirics and theory. - Practice generative collaborative work, where peers engage in “co-creation” of research processes
42772:
Name English: PhD Spring School on Megaproject Management
Danish Title: PhD Spring School on Megaproject Management
General Course Objectives: The successful execution of megaprojects is at the core of making our green transition goals a reality. Executing those large infrastructure projects – from electricity to smart cities to transportation – has never been more challenging, nor more important. We are therefore experiencing a paradigm shift in large construction projects: Today, the expectations are no longer 'only' to deliver on time and on budget, but also against a (rightfully so) increasingly ambitious sustainability agenda. At the same time, while we have significant success with some megaprojects, overall our ability to deliver megaprojects requires significant attention and development. The overall objective of this course is to strengthen the education of PhD students specifically in the area of megaproject management, and create additional research and collaboration opportunities across academia, industry and policy stakeholders. As a participating PhD student, you will • Get access to a world-class megaproject management organization for an empirical, implementation-focused research engagement (e.g. a validation case study) • Train to articulate your findings and ideas for a practitioner audience. • Improve your empirical research skills through lectures and assignments. • Generate concepts and material for future publications. In exchange, we expect you to contribute by: • Submission of a "pitch "statement regarding the relevance of your research findings for application in megaproject management • Participation in two in-person meetings in Denmark of 2-3 days each • Active research engagement during the 4 months between the PhD School meetings. • Preparation of joint final deliverable with other participants (for example, a newspaper article or the development of a data warehouse)
Content: The PhD Spring School consists of a set of 5 activities for the PhD student. The Spring School is organized in collaboration with a megaproject management organizsation (in 2022, Femern A/S) that supplement the academic teaching modules and provide access to megaproject management subject matter experts and data for a research engagement. The 4 content elements of the PhD spring school are: 1) Preparation Module (20 hours): Articulation of a research hypothesis motivating an empirical research engagement with a megaproject management practitioner. 2) In-Person Module 1 (20 hours): Framing, Match-Making, Training Day: Matching of research interests with megaproject management practiioners. Presentation of industrial challenges. In-depth teaching module on megaproject management theory and academic research streams. 3) Project module (80 hours): Planning and execution of empirical research engagement between PhD students and megaproject practitioners 4) In-Person Module 2 (20 hours): Summary of findings, critical presentation and discussion amongst participants, organizers and megaproject managers. Academic in-depth lectures on megaproject management publishing.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Formulate a research hypothesis (or research question) in the context of existing megaproject management research. - Identify and articulate the theoretical foundation of your specific research activities in the context of megaproject management research. - Communicate your research idea to a practitioner audience. - Identify and apply suitable empirical research methods to satisfy both academic expectation as well as those of a megaproject management practitioner. - Plan and execute an empirical research engagement with a megaproject management practitioner. - Present and discuss your findings orally as well as through a journal paper draft. - Provide peer feedback to publication drafts of other course participants - Articulate research insights for megaproject practitioners in an actionable way
42S01:
Name English: Philosophical foundations of Sustainable Leadership
Danish Title: Philosophical foundations of Sustainable Leadership
General Course Objectives: The aim of this course is to build a common understanding of sustainable leadership, create a personal vision within sustainability, and frame the Immersive Learning Project and develop a Personal Leadership Development plan, both of which are carried out throughout the programme.
Content: This course lays out the philosophical foundations of sustainable leadership and sets the starting point for the programme Master in Sustainable Leadership. We begin with an overview of the main theories and approaches within leadership, such as situational leadership, and examine different leadership techniques and practices, including facilitation, mentorship, coaching, and mindfulness. We focus also on team building and profiling, and how to establish psychological safety and safe spaces. The second part of the course focuses on sustainability, in which we unpack sustainability definitions, trends, and interlinkages. By taking a holistic perspective, we study systemic thinking and planetary boundaries, and assess the challenges and failings of current paradigms. Finally, the third part of the course focuses on scientific principles and research methods, which support the design and execution of the Immersive Learning Project and Master’s Thesis of the programme. Participants will also create their Personal Leadership Development (PLD) plan.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Build a common understanding of sustainable leadership and a personal vision within sustainability - Compare different leadership frameworks - Develop your vision, values, and motivation for sustainable leadership - Establish a safe space for dialogue - Identify and interpret global trends in sustainability - Identify global needs and challenges around - Master the basic scientific principles and research methods - Identify a sustainability topic within a value chain and outline the Immersive Learning Project - Create a Personal leadership development (PLD) plan
42S02:
Name English: Leadership in Sustainability Strategy
Danish Title: Leadership in Sustainability Strategy
General Course Objectives: The objective of this course is to analyze the drivers and challenges facing strategic level sustainability commitments.
Content: This course focuses on sustainability strategy and value creation. We unpack sustainability goal setting and road mapping, the key strategic drivers behind sustainability such as net-zero targets and circular economy and examine how they impact value chains. Assessing risk and resilience are key to evaluating system level impact and change, and this course provides the tools for that. Apart from the strategic tools, we focus on incentive alignment and motivating behavioral change, both internally and externally. We practice identifying, mapping, and engaging with stakeholders in order to ensure legitimacy and longevity for the outlined sustainability strategy. We also examine the role of boards in goal setting.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Understand what motivates and drives sustainability strategy decisions - Analyze corporate sustainability strategies and impact critically - Apply risk and resilience into sustainability strategy - Determine how to align strategic growth and sustainability incentives - Design sustainable growth strategies through goal setting and road mapping - Identify, assess, and engage with key strategic stakeholders - Apply motivation techniques with team members - Practice facilitation, mentoring, and coaching
42S03:
Name English: Complex Problem Framing across Value Chains
Danish Title: Complex Problem Framing across Value Chains
General Course Objectives: The objective of this course is to break down complex sustainability challenges and design solutions to these challenges.
Content: In order to create positive societal impact, it is essential to understand and address complex systems in which sustainability challenges sit, as well as the trade-offs that are associated with sustainability. This course tackles this challenge and unpacks complex problem framing in sustainability solutions across a value chain. By adopting the approaches of human-centered design, design thinking, and inclusive innovation, participants will practice analyzing and synthesizing complex problems into manageable problems that account for the problems’ root causes and surrounding ecosystems and actors. The learnings of the course will be directly applied to the problem framing of the Immersive Learning Project. The Personal Development Plan is closely integrated with this course, as participants will practice facilitating complex, non-linear processes as well as mentorship and coaching techniques through peer feedback throughout the phases of the course.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Understand basic concepts related to complex problem framing, such as root cause analysis, and system mapping - Synthesize complex problems into manageable problems - Map and analyze the systems and stakeholders surrounding problems - Align critical problems and motivations across agendas and actors - Navigate complexity in practice - Design, prototype, and test solution concepts - Apply appropriate facilitation leadership styles in connection with complex problems - Provide and receive peer feedback in coaching
42S04:
Name English: Sustainability Oriented Organizations
Danish Title: Sustainability Oriented Organizations
General Course Objectives: The objective of this course is to harness organizational forms that are best positioned to cater to positive societal impact.
Content: This course addresses the question: What organizational form is best suitable for aligning for sustainable societal impact? We begin at the macro level, by addressing global governance mechanism and international agreements, and critically assess voluntary codes of conduct and sector specific initiatives. We unpack collaborative governance by designing and implementing a cross-sector partnership, which can be directly applied to the Immersive Learning Projects. In addition to organizational form, we zoom in on organizational culture and on strategic, operational, and tactical organizational layers to analyze the role of the leader in organizational sustainable transformation. We will practice facilitating across different mindsets and value systems, which is a typical hurdle in creating successful cross-sector partnerships.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Identify and analyze the forms that sustainability can take within organizations - Identify and compare organizational forms of sustainability culture - Apply leadership styles to organizational forms and cultures - Evaluate conditions for effectiveness of different organizational forms - Create opportunities for new forms and cultures for sustainable organizationsIdentify, assess, and engage with key strategic stakeholders - Identify, assess, and create suitable cross-sector partnerships related to sustainability - Master the main international Multi-Stakeholder Initiatives related to sustainability - Master non-profit management and understand how it differs from for-profit management
46015:
Name English: Digital energy societies
Danish Title: Digitale energisamfund
General Course Objectives: The course aims at providing the students with a general introduction to the role of energy in the society and the possibilities offered by digitization in connection to sustainability in energy systems.
Content: The students will work with the transition to sustainable energy societies with emphasis on the role of digitization. During the course the students are presented with definitions of sustainability and knowledge of the structure of energy systems. We will work with electricity as an energy-carrier and the challenges associated with the ambition of a sustainable energy system with a high degree of electrification. Here the students will learn how data about energy consumption and CO2 emission can assist in visualizing and solving some of these problems. We demonstrate how energy technologies can contribute to the realization of the UN Sustainable Development Goals and investigate in a broader sense the role of energy in a society, when the students themselves prepare an energy plan. The course is divided in two parts: - First part is composed of a range of lectures and associated hand-in assignments. - Second part is organized as a project work.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - give account for fundamental principles and technologies within energy and sustainability - design and dimension an energy solution and discuss it in relation to sustainability - demonstrate how sustainability of energy systems is supported by digital technology - perform fundamental processing and representation of data using Python - make use of the digital platforms provided by DTU, the laboratory facilities of DTU Wind and act according to good practice in a lab-environment. - organize and execute group-based project work - communicate technical subjects, theories and results in writing as well as in speech - evaluate and give constructive feedback to peers
46020:
Name English: Design project: Energy conversion and storage
Danish Title: Designprojekt: Energikonvertering og lagring
General Course Objectives: Kursets overordnede mål er at give de studerende en dybtgående forståelse af basale elektriske og termodynamiske principper og den fascinerende sammenhæng imellem dem. Efter en introduktion til elektriske og termiske grundbegreber forventes det at de studerende selv udvikler løsninger til designopgaver, som afprøves under laboratorieforhold. Elektriske kredsløb, termiske modeller, tab og energitæthed er nøgleord i kurset. I forbindelse med designopgaven og varmepumpeøvelsen arbejdes med elektrisk og termisk energi, hvorved der gives en forståelse, som danner grundlag for det videre arbejde med andre former for energikonvertering og lagring senere i studiet. Da en del af kurset er projektbaseret, lægges der også vægt på gruppearbejde og rapportskrivning.
Content: Der belyses de vigtigste principper indenfor elektrotermisk energikonvertering og lagring ved selvstændigt, kreativt arbejde i laboratoriet, understøttet af et introduktionsforløb om grundlæggende elektriske sammenhænge og varmetransmission. Gennemgående elementer er elektriske og termodynamiske grundprincipper, elektriske og termiske modeller, energitæthed, tab, optimeret konvertering og lagring, kreative løsninger og kritisk stillingtagen til resultater og løsninger. I første del af kurset behandles elektrofysiske principper, resistivitet, Ohms lov, Kirchhoffs love, Thevenin/Norton og superposition, som trænes ved grupperegning og laboratorieforsøg. Et batteri undersøges m.h.t. afladning og energiindhold. Derefter gennemgås de vigtigste principper for varmetransmission og analogien med elektriske systemer. Analyse af en varmepumpe. Principperne for en varmepumpe og realiseringen i den aktuelle udgave beskrives. Pumpens effektivitet analyseres eksperimentelt og de forskellige elementers indflydelse på virkningsgraden undersøges Kernen i resten af kurset er projektarbejde i laboratoriet om design, konstruktion, afprøvning og optimering af et termisk energilager. Heri indgår resistiv opvarmning, forskellige materialer til lagring af varmen, isolering og anvendelse af et monitoreringssystem til fjernaflæsning. Resultater fra det eksperimentelle arbejde holdes op mod passende teoretiske modeller af den valgte løsning. Afvigelser diskuteres.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Forklare begreb som effekt, energi, virkningsgrad og energitæthed - Gøre rede for de vigtigste principper indenfor varmetransmission - Anvende de vigtigste elektriske principper som Ohms og Kirchhoffs love - Analysere elektriske kilder ved brug af Thevenin- og Norton-ækvivalentet - Forstå analogien mellem 2 forskellige fysiske systemer, termisk og elektrisk - Designe og konstruere et termisk energilager - Vurdere løsningsmuligheder og vælge den mest optimale ud fra en række givne kriterier - Tilpasse og anvende testsystemer til analyse af energikonverterende og -lagrende enheder - Beskrive de elektriske/​termodynamiske principper anvendt i en varmepumpe - Arbejde i laboratoriet og anvende grundlæggende elektriske og termiske måleprincipper - Arbejde aktivt i en projektgruppe og skrive en dækkende og velstruktureret rapport
46025:
Name English: Introduction to renewable energy technologies
Danish Title: Introduktion til bæredygtige energiteknologier
General Course Objectives: Renewable Energy technologies are interdisciplinary fields. The ultimate goal is to develop systems with the capability of producing, transporting, delivering and storing energy in reliable, economic and environmental friendly ways. The overall goal of the course is to introduce the students to the fundamental aspects of three different energy technologies, namely wind energy, solar (photovoltaic) energy and electrochemical energy storage. The students will be qualified to estimate the performance of the energy technologies as well as analyzing the possibilities and limitations of these three energy technologies and be familiar with the commercial aspects of the technologies.
Content: The following three energy technologies are investigated: - Wind energy - Solar photovoltaic energy - Electrochemical energy storage (batteries) Each technology is presented and examined in terms of the physical principles, the technological realizations, state-of-the-art, performance and economical aspects, such as Levelized cost-of-energy (LCoE). The students will perform group work, where they dimension a hybrid power plant for supplying electricity to a small town on a monthly time scale. A simple demand model is formulated for the small town using the monthly temperature variation and a heat-pump is assumed to provide heating and cooling for the houses of the town. Secondly the citizens are assumed to have an electric car and a constant base load.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Describe the principles of elecricity production based on wind turbines - Estimate the energy production from wind turbine farms - Describe the principles of electricity production based on solar cells - Estimate the energy production from photovoltaic systems - Explain the fundamentals of energy storage technologies - Select appropriate types of batteries in hybrid battery and wind/PV systems - Formulate a simple energy demand model of a small city and compare with renewable production potential - Estimate Levelized Cost-of-Energy (LCOE) of solar PV and wind turbine electricity production
46030:
Name English: Electrical energy systems
Danish Title: Elektriske energisystemer
General Course Objectives: The main goal of the course is to enable the students to understand the basic relations in electrical energy systems and to perform calculations i simplified subsystems being found in grids with energy producing, transmitting and converting units like wind power, cables, converters and electric vehicles. The students achieve competences, which are necessary for further work with electrical energy systems, independent of the later specialisation in either digital solutions, energy techologies or energy systems. Theory is transferred to practical applications in a newly established learning environment, where the most important relations can be tested, while the students learn to work in laboratories and use relevant measuring and test equipment.
Content: • AC voltages and currents, complex representation • Impedances and AC circuits • Complex power • Transport of electrical energy from producer to consumer • Distribution systems and 3-phase grids • Diodes and transistors in power electronic systems • Converter structures and modelling approaches • Electric vehicles, battery design and charging principles
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Describe electrical energy systems - Calculate current, voltage, power and energy in simple electric AC circuits - Apply complex calculation methods to AC systems - Describe principles behind energy conversion between mechanical and electrical energy - Apply principles to analyze smart charging of electric vehicles - Consider the influence of various loads on system performance - Analyse simple circuits with diodes - Apply experimental methods to illustrate simple electrical relations
46035:
Name English: Energy management with embedded systems
Danish Title: Energistyring med indlejrede systemer
General Course Objectives: Smart Houses are introduced as the vision of a future energy optimized households, which are based on renewable energy sources and intelligent apparatus. Examples of Smart Houses technologies are household appliances that react intelligently to varying system conditions, automatic mechanisms for coordination of resources, and advanced information exchange systems. The objective of this course is to gain hands-on experience with energy management technologies used in such systems, by designing, implementing and testing a Smart House application on a microcontroller based, embedded system. The learnings from the course can also be applied to smart grids and intelligent energy systems.
Content: Most of the time, the students will work in the laboratory in project teams. Introductory lectures are given on: - Energy management systems (EMS) for smart houses and related ICT technology - Specific demand response in smart houses’ applications (projects) - A 32-bit ARM microcontroller(Arduino MKR1000/1010) system and its peripherals (A/D and D/A converters, Timer, I/O, PWM, Interrupter, and LCD display, etc.) including their corresponding registers' programming. - The integrated development environment Arduino Embedded Workbench - Communication systems in smart energy systems - User-centered interface design
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - understand the basic concepts of energy management systems in Smart Houses - analyze the requirements of intelligent household systems - design an application that uses inputs and outputs to interact with a physical device - design a user interface for local control and monitoring - design a communication interface for remote control and monitoring - implement the application on a microcontroller based, embedded system - design a test procedure that utilizes laboratory facilities to validate the function of the application - perform tests in the laboratory - document the entire process and the developed application
46040:
Name English: Introduction to energy analytics
Danish Title: Introduktion til energianalyse
General Course Objectives: The main aim of the course is to unveil the opportunities at the interface of digitization of the energy sector, by going through some introductory concepts in energy analytics, machine learning and optimization.
Content: The combination of increasing data availability in energy systems and the liberalization of energy markets brings a number of opportunities and challenges in the operation of energy systems. The course mainly concentrates on the case of electricity and related use cases. A compact introduction to electricity markets and prices will be given, as this will serve as the guiding application of the methods taught in this course. Various techniques for analyzing relevant datasets and solving a set of related problems will be introduced, such as regression, forecasting, machine learning and optimization. Emphasis will be placed on a number of analytics and optimization problems, e.g., the optimal scheduling of storage to maximize profits in a market, and the forecasting of electricity prices. Focus will also be placed on learning to setup rigorous optimization problems, on comparing different techniques (e.g., ARIMA models vs machine learning) and on training and properly evaluating the models. Moreover, students will employ the Python programming language to process data, execute analytics, and implement optimization methods. An important goal of the course is to combine the developed models and techniques (e.g., optimization and forecasting) for solving larger energy analytics problems using real data.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Describe a number of decision problems of electricity consumers and prosumers as optimization problems - Implement, use and evaluate regression and machine learning techniques with a focus on forecasting - Develop data analytics and optimization programs in Python - Combine various data analytics techniques into larger and more complicated problems - Design tools for optimizing the profits of electricity market participants - Develop and compare tools for forecasting electricity prices - Organize and execute group-based project work - Effectively present project work in written form
46045:
Name English: Design and Implementation of Coordinated Distributed Energy Systems
Danish Title: Design og implementering af koordineret styring for distribuerede energisystemer
General Course Objectives: Variable renewable energy resources, electrified consumers and energy storage together make up the building blocks of a fully renewabe energy system. But how do these technologies work together to balance the energy system? Effective cooperation requires control algorithms and communication to coordinate and balance power and energy levels continuously, forming a cyber-physical distributed energy system. Distributed energy systems can be formed for different goals, such as e.g. microgrids, which increase, energy community, or hybrid power plant. This course introduces the methods required to implement such a distributed system, enabling students to develop and test their own solutions, which include remote sensing and control, combined with fault tolerant communication to build a coordinated energy system. The main focus of this course is on a hands-on experience in designing and implementing a distributed energy system solution, applying control structures, distributed system fault tolerance and communication patterns, monitoring its operation, and testing its actual performance. The course main tools include Python programming, use of communication patterns, as well as Linux command line operations, remote operation via ssh and code collaboration tools. Use of AI tools is permitted and encouraged during the course for programming purposes, but not to replace a the student' overview of the concept design, testing strategies and test result interpretation. The final project is implemented on the distributed energy system "SYSLAB", located at Risø Campus. Keywords: distributed systems, sensor networks, IoT, communication, control, fault tolerance.
Content: Week 1: Introduction to smart energy systems control problems, and distributed control systems; solution concept design; differences between simulated and actual distributed control system. Introduction to physical laboratory facilities, lab safety and remote control of SYSLAB units; implementing communication in a distributed system; implementing controllers. Week 2: Coordination and fault tolerance strategies. Implementation of a control system on a simulated testbed, testing for reproducible outcomes. Deployment and evaluation of distributed controllers. Week 3: Control solution development, implementation and experiment execution in SYSLAB (Risø campus). Reporting and presentation of results.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain how distributed energy systems use coordination and communication to achieve their goals. - Recognize and clearly illustrate the communication, control and coordination aspects of a distributed energy application. - List, explain and apply typical communication patterns applied in distributed systems. - Explain and apply typical control structures and fault-tolerance strategies applied in distributed control systems. - Describe requirements and specify a concept for a distributed energy system solution, including control, coordination and communication aspects and its experimental validation. - Select and apply relevant control and communication patterns in a distributed control software. - Implement and deploy a distributed control software in a laboratory setting. - Specify a test for a distributed control software based on examining application requirements, including relevant performance metrics and test protocoll. - Implement and execute a specified test, document the test results and interpret the test results in terms of the distributed control system functioning and test requirements. - Collaborate efficiently in a team to develop solutions involving programming and communicating about code and about the use of AI to support development.
46050:
Name English: Innovative energy solutions
Danish Title: Innovative energiløsninger
General Course Objectives: The overall course objective is to enable the students to design, implement and evaluate an innovation proces aimed at the green, digital and interconnected energy system of the future in collaboration with internal and external actors.
