Name English: Module 3: Start-up Acceleration
Danish Title: Modul 3: Start-up Acceleration
General Course Objectives: This class is an advanced course in Entrepreneurial Management. The purpose of this course is to explore new venture creation by an active start-up. The course will offer a thorough theoretical and practical understanding of new venture creation combined with hands-on experience of practical techniques and methods for analysing and evaluating business opportunities, crafting growth-oriented strategies and developing creative approaches to commercialisation. A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to:
Content: Supervised group work on the students' start-ups with a special focus on building the product/service.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - understand the challenges of new venture creation in a comprehensive, integrative way - identify the early stages of the entrepreneurial process by working on a business project proposal - develop and test pretotypes/prototypes and a minimal viable product (MVP) - calculate the size and potential of different markets to select a beached market - Select a go-to market strategy taking the competitive dynamics and macro factors into account - project profiting losses for the business idea for 24 months after launch date - analyse, evaluate and modify new venture opportunities - develop an entrepreneurial mindset
41204:
Name English: Fundamental structural mechanics
Danish Title: Grundlæggende bygningsmekanik
General Course Objectives: The goal of the course is to give a basic understanding of how structures work, and provide knowledge of methods for analysis and design of simple structures. The course provides the basis for courses in structural design and more advanced theory of structural elements. Simple numerical tools are introduced to determine reactions, section forces and deformations. The main theme of the course is bars and beams and their role in statically determinate truss and frame structures. Central elements of the course are: determination of reactions and internal forces and moments in statically determinate structures for given loads, as well as the differential equation for beams, instability of columns and calculation of deformations by the principle of virtual work.
Content: The course is coherently comprised of lectures and subsequent exercise sessions. The exercises serve as examples and for practicing analytical and numerical methods. The overall content is covered in the following parts: 1. Loads and reactions by forces and moments. 2. Reactions and bar forces in truss structures. 3. Reactions and section forces in beams and frames. 4. Deformations and deflections of beams and frames. 5. Theory for columns and their dimensioning. Examples of structural analysis make use of simple numerical programs, while design with optimal use of material is included in connection with the determination of load carrying capacity, deformations and column instability.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Represent loads by forces and moments and determine reactions by equilibrium equations. - Determine reactions and member forces in statically determinate trusses. - Determine section forces in statically determinate beams and frames by equilibrium conditions and differential equations. - Use simple numerical tools to determine reactions, section forces and deformations in planar trusses, beams and frames - Explain the mechanisms of deformation of beams and the corresponding differential equation. - Determine simple cross-section parameters and normal stresses for a homogeneous beam. - Use the principle of virtual work to determine displacements in trusses, beams and frames. - Determine the stability load for simple columns and the critical load for columns with imperfections.
41263:
Name English: Experimental and numerical methods for ship resistance and propulsion
Danish Title: Eksperimentel og numerisk bestemmelse af skibsmodstand og fremdrivning
General Course Objectives: To train the participants to predict the hydrodynamic resistance of a ship using model tests, empirical calculation methods, and numerical simulations, and to use these predictions to specify an optimal bulbous bow and a highly-efficient propulsion system for the ship.
Content: Experimental and computational methods to predict resistance and propulsion in calm water. Froude scaling. Resistance model tests (ITTC-1978) with optimization of a bulbous bow. Power prognosis on the basis of the model tests, and calculation of the optimum combination of main engine and propeller (B-series). It is emphasised that the students must take an active part in the planning, preparation, testing, and analysis of the model tests.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - describe the assumptions associated with theoretical models and calculation methods associated with the resistance and propulsion of ships - explain the theory behind model testing for resistance and propulsion (Froude scaling) - organize and execute a series of ship model tests - perform calculations that transform data from model to full scale by ITTC-1978 or a similar procedure - calculate and assess the flow, including the generated wave system, around the ship with commercial software - describe the function of ship propellers, and explain the use of propeller diagrams (for instance the B-series propellers) - apply propeller diagrams to identify an optimum propeller - explain the interaction between ship, propeller, and main engine - specify the propulsive main engine that performs best with the ship and its propeller - collect experimental and numerical results in a high-quality technical report
41639:
Name English: Holistic Design of Engineering Systems
Danish Title: Helhedsdesign af Engineering Systems
General Course Objectives: This course applies engineering systems design principles to the design and re-design of socio-technical systems. The course emphasises systems thinking, systems analysis, systems architecture and systems design to address technical, social, organisational, and policy requirements; in connection also to UN's sustainable development goals. The socio-technical systems in focus are manifold and may range for example from hospital wards and medical devices to student festivals and sustainability technologies. As part of the course, the students will re-design a socio-technical engineering system, and create a physical prototype as part of the solution.
Content: Project work focuses on the development of a socio-technical engineering system. This includes technical, service, organisational, process and policy aspects and overall system integration. The project should cover the following aspects: - system-oriented analysis of the current state - definition of multi-dimensional requirements from a technical, service, organisational and policy perspective and analysis & discussion of requirement conflicts - interdisciplinary design and product development processes initiated according to a client's objectives, using the clients knowledge and competencies - exploration of design alternatives based on advanced domain knowledge - creation of a socio-technical design solution, including a physical prototype - simulation or pilot implementation of proposed design solution - customization of design process and reflection on your role as a designer
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Analyse socio-technical engineering systems and select relevant perspectives - Define and model socio-technical engineering systems - Articulate multi-dimensional requirements of engineering systems - Perform analyses to identify requirement conflicts and define possible design solutions - Synthesise design ideas and concepts - Analyse and re-design existing systems in order to optimise and improve selected attributes - Explain the practical, complex execution of system-level design processes and the students own role within these processes - Create and communicate design solutions, including a physical prototype - Argue for the application of the design solution within context - Provide reflected criticism of others' design processes and results - Critically evaluate, select and use AI tools to increase productivity of engineering design processes - Carry out a team design project and define own team role
41735:
Name English: Experimental methods in 3D printing (additive manufacturing)
Danish Title: Eksperimentelle metoder i 3D print (additiv fremstilling)
General Course Objectives: The course gives the student in-depth knowledge and practical experience with industry leading Additive Manufacturing (AM) technologies by working on cutting-edge projects in small groups. Project work comprises all stages of a project, including planning and performing relevant laboratory investigations as well as interpretation of experimental results.
Content: The students will gain hands-on experience using one of the several possible AM technologies. The different types of AM technologies available are 1. Mask-projection vatphotopolymerization using polymers 2. Mask-projection vatphotopolymerization using slurries infused with metals and/or ceramics 3. Metal Laser Powder Bed Fusion 4. Polymer Laser Powder Bed Fusion 5. Binder Jetting using metals and ceramics 6. Extrusion-based Additive Manufacturing The students will go through the entire manufacturing process chain including design, simulation, slicing, build preparation, AM, post-process cleaning and finishing, post-process heat and surface treatments followed by materials characterization. Each group will focus on one or several aspects of a specific AM process to perform experiment-based research to further the stated goals of the project.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Describe various industrial AM technologies and their associated sub-systems - Evaluate the applicability of various AM technologies for production of complex geometrical components - Explain the common applications of each type of AM technology across various industries - Formulate the tasks necessary to fulfil a project focused on a specific AM technology - Perform a literature review and interpret the latest findings within state-of-the-art for a specific AM technology - Explain the process-structure-property relationships for a specific AM technology - Explain the influence of material composition and properties on the manufacturability of said material in a specific AM technology - Propose a plan to utilize a specific AM technology within a research project
41862:
Name English: Production Technology 2
Danish Title: Produktionsteknologi 2
General Course Objectives: The course is a continuation of Productiontechnology 1, and has the overall objective to give the students an overview of industrial manufacturing processes with a special attention on the interaction between design, material selection, precision, quality, process optimisation and process modelling. The students will be introduced to Industry 4.0, particularly control and optimisation of manufacturing processes using data acquisition, statistical methods and mathematical models. The students are introduced to how manufacturing processes are optimised througn structured experiments coupled with fundamental mathematical modelling.
Content: Preparation of production of a component, preparation of the production equipment and production of small batches in the laboratory. Introduction to Industry 4.0, including acquisition of process data and use of simple mathematical models to describe the processes. Application of simple mathematical models to calculate pressure, temperature, velocity and process times in manufacturing processes. Acquisition of process data from manufacturing processes with the aim of analysing the processes.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Describe the fundamental principles for Industry 4.0 - Describe the most important control principles used in manufacturing processes - Use fundamental mathematical models to describe the manufacturing processes casting, forming, machining and assembly (including welding) - Use online data acquisition for surveillance of manufacturing processes - Use fundamental statistical methods to analyse process data acquired from a manufacturing process - Propose when and how quality control should be performed and which methods can be used for quality control - Optimise a manufacturing process using on experiments, mathematical models and statistical methods - Set up production of a component in the workshop and afterwards analyse production process
41863:
Name English: Mechanical dimensioning
Danish Title: Mekanisk dimensionering
General Course Objectives: Expanding the understanding of the fundamental concepts and methods of strength of materials achieved in 62806 Mechanical Design 2, in order to enable the student to analyze and calculate how a given structure ie. machine components, pressure vessels, shrinkage joints, structures, frames, etc. deform and when plastic deformation or fatigue occurs. The content of the course constitute a necessary prerequisite for the use and understanding of the finite element method (FEM), and not least, the ability to provide qualified assessment and interpretation of results obtained through FEM calculations.
Content: The course is taught in Danish. Three-dimensional stresses and strains. Principal stresses / strains and the associated principal coordinate systems. Hooke's generalized law. Plane stress and plane strain. Deformation of thick-walled pipes and circular discs. Plastic deformation mechanisms and yield hypotheses. Dimensioning against fatigue fractures. As part of the course, the student is introduced to multidimensional elastic stress and deformation analysis. Dimensioning is introduced against permanent deformation (plasticity) as well as fatigue fractures.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Determine the stress and strain state in a loaded continuum using Hooke's generalized law as well as any strain gauge measurements. - Perform analyses of principal stresses and strains and corresponding principal directions for general 3D-states. - Identify special stress states as for instance uniaxial, plane, cylindrical or hydrostatic - Calculate stresses based on strains and conversely, as a result of mechanical and thermal loading, for e.g. thin-walled pressure vessels. - Analyze the stress and strain state in circular in-plane loaded plates and thick walled pipes. - Utilize von Mises' and Tresca's yield hypotheses to dimension against plastic deformation in structures, including safety factors. - Dimension against fatigue and establishing reduced Haigh/Goodman diagrams - Determine safety factors while taking plastic deformation and fatigue into account, i.e. enabling the minimization of material consumption to ensure sustainability in accordance with the UN World Goals. - Describe the mechanical properties of time-independent materials under static uniaxial tensile loading.
41903:
Name English: Introduction to Civil Engineering
Danish Title: Introduktion til Byggeteknologi
General Course Objectives: In the course, an introduction to the civil engineers work is provided by allowing students to: - Develop disciplines such as problem-solving, group works, documentation, and presentation. - Be introduced to study methods such as lectures, self-study, group work, and project work. - Gain skills in design and experimenting, building materials, building energy, and structures. - Analyze simple functional relationships, allocate areas, propose structural and climate screen designs, and dimension basic technical systems. - Produce optimized and integrated project designs in drawing form, based on simple estimations. - Become familiar with basic relations and term in buildings and in Danish building practice. - Gain an understanding of the content of the design and project phases and the involvement of engineers in them.
Content: The course is an introduction to the building technology engineering study. In mini-projects within load-bearing constructions, materials and energy, problem-solving techniques and the use of various digital tools are practised. In a larger project during the 3-week period, building components and design, design and construction processes, building layout incl. land use, design of load-bearing construction system and climate screen. Estimated dimensioning of building parts and design and dimensioning of simple heating systems, use of digital models, production of drawings and a project presentation are carried out. The course also includes an introduction to study techniques, project work and stays abroad, just as the student conducts a self‑evaluation of their own learning and study practice and identifies personal development goals.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Apply basic building engineering principles through work with a design, including sketching, shaping, construction, and testing. - Identify and analyse simple building engineering problems. - Calculate reactions, stresses, and deflections for simple structural components. - Apply simple calculation principles for building energy conditions - Identify building materials and describe their basic properties, areas of application, and relevance in simple constructions - Evaluate material choices in relation to design solutions - Carry out simple experiments, including planning tests, recording data, and making a basic interpretation of results for use in models. - Use digital tools for sketching and geometric representation in typical design tasks. - Use simple digital calculation or simulation tools for basic analyses. - Describe and work according to fundamental engineering design processes, including idea development, iteration, documentation, and presentation - Participate in study and project work in a structured manner, including planning, distributing, and coordinating tasks in small groups - Reflect on personal learning, study practice, and engineering identity, including describing one’s prerequisites, motivation, areas for development, and long‑term goals
41925:
Name English: Introduction to Building Information Modeling (BIM)
Danish Title: Introduktion til Bygningsinformationsmodellering (BIM)
General Course Objectives: The purpose of the course is to build a basic understanding of processing and digital visual communication of information during the building design process. Civil engineering centred introduction to communication through sketching, modeling and using digital tools. That the participants develop their spatial perception of buildings and gain an understanding of the visual dialogue between key parties in building projects. The course introduces essential analogue and digital working methods and builds a basic understanding of Building Information Modeling (BIM).
Content: The course introduces the drawing material and the model basis as a prerequisite for communication. During the course, analog and digital aids are used to present the idea and function of buildings. Problem-solving techniques and the use of various digital tools are practiced through practical examples. The course introduces a systematic naming and classification of objects. The Building Information Modeling (BIM) concept is included as a central element, where topics cover layer structures, objects, types and best practice for the production of model-linked drawing material. Principle solutions and digital tools for drawing production and building modeling are worked on to create a basis for documentation, data extraction/bills of materials, simulation and project presentation. Group and individual exercises are carried out during the course.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Accumulate knowledge independently and in groups - Arrange and execute simple project assignments - Apply analog techniques (hand sketching, and possibly model building) to produce early design stage building concepts - Apply digital tools for application in a smaller building project - Apply basic methods for application of documents and drawings - Convert model representations in 3D to 2D and vice versa - Apply building models to exchange digital information - Apply basic BIM concepts an BIM techniques
41941:
Name English: Construction and architecture
Danish Title: Byggeteknik og arkitektur
General Course Objectives: The aim of the course is to provide an introductory knowledge of building technology and architecture for architectural engineers. Once you have followed the course, you will be able to record and analyze simpler buildings, explain their architectural concepts and relationships to the development of the history of architecture and technology. You will be able to explain the constructive design and construction engineering of simpler buildings, including explaining their static and climate engineering modes of operation.
Content: The course introduces basic knowledge of construction technology and architecture through lectures, excursions and exercises. The teaching includes sketching- and note techniques, building registration, building analysis with a focus on architecture, construction, thermal envelope, materials and sustainability. An understanding of the systems of buildings as well as the architectural concepts of buildings is built up, and features of the historical prerequisites of building technology and architecture are also reviewed. The course practises individual work, group work, presentationas well as report writing and presentation according to recognized formats. The course includes knowledge obtained in the other 1st-semester courses.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the function and expression of buildings - Explain the systems of buildings and how they work - Analyze buildings based on building registration - Explain static principles for simpler buildings and present them graphically - Explain the design of the thermal envelope and present it graphically - Explain architectural concepts and represent them graphically - Explain important architectural trends, name the most important architectural works and architects from the 20th century - Reflect on own work and own learning
41942:
Name English: Architectural Engineering Project 1, intro
Danish Title: Bygningsdesign Projekt 1, Intro
General Course Objectives: The course introduces practice-oriented design methods for architectural engineers and gives you the opportunity to test your acquired knowledge by designing (proposing, optimizing and documenting) a smaller, wood-based building. When you have followed the course, you can participate in an elementary building design process and - on the basis of a defined problem - develop relevant solutions, select the best solutions and communicate the results using drawings, models, presentations and reports.
Content: Design theory (Double Diamond, first diamond). Proposal making, alternative solutions, evaluation, optimization. Find/use architectural and engineering references. Projecting. Sketching, drawing, model building. Presentation technique, report writing.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Design a single building through a recognized design process (Double Diamond, first diamond) - Design constructions, thermal envelope and technical systems (heating and ventilation) in smaller buildings. - Suggest and test alternative solutions - Apply various visual tools in the design process, including analog and digital sketching and physical model building - Include references from real architectural and engineering projects in the work - Create relevant project communication through sketches, drawings and models - Present project results orally and written - Create project results in groups
41943:
Name English: Indoor Climatic Design
Danish Title: Indeklimadesign
General Course Objectives: The course gives you an introduction to the connection between architecture, daylight, acoustics and indoor climate through knowledge of phenomenology theory within architecture and knowledge of the engineering disciplines of daylight, acoustics and air quality (quality and quantity). After completing the course, you will be able to engage in dialogue with users and architects about indoor climate quality in relation to acoustics, daylight and ventilation in buildings; use simple methods to measure, model and calculate the most important parameters within the above and use these results in design processes in the initial phases of a building project.
Content: Introduction to the phenomenology theory of architecture. The relationship between light and sound as experienced, measured and calculated/modelled phenomena. Basic daylight engineering and acoustic concepts. Measurement of light and sound. Knowledge of daylight and modelling/calculation of quantity and quality of daylight in buildings. Knowledge of room acoustics and modeling/calculation of reverberation time. Knowledge of sound-absorbing materials and calculation of necessary absorbers to achieve appropriate acoustics in rooms with simple geometry. Analytical problem solving, group work, communication (report writing and presentation).
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the content of the phenomenology theory in relation to architecture - Explain the basic concepts and most important parameters within daylighting and acoustics (hereinafter referred to as "indoor climate") in rooms - Describe indoor climate experiences in rooms based on observations - Carry out simple measurements of important parameters for the quality and quantity of indoor climate in rooms - Determine daylight conditions and reverberation time in rooms using physical and digital models and calculation. - Perform simpler building simulation of indoor climate in relation to daylight, air quality and energy consumption using digital simulation tools - Design and place light openings, acoustic absorbers and reflectors in rooms to optimize the indoor climate - Evaluate and discuss consistency and deviation between experienced, measured and calculated indoor climate results - Give an account of selected, relevant reference works with particularly good indoor climate properties within the history of architecture
41944:
Name English: Architectural Engineering Design Project 2, indoor climatic design
Danish Title: Bygningsdesign Projekt 2, Indeklimadesign
General Course Objectives: The course gives you the opportunity to test your knowledge gained in the 1-2nd semester by developing the design of a complex building which has special daylighting and acoustic needs, e.g. a cultural center with an exhibition space and a concert hall. When you have followed the course, you can participate in an integrated building design process and - on the basis of ao open problem, develop relevant solutions, select the best solutions and communicate the results using drawings, modelling, presentations and reports. The course develops design and project skills, which have been acquired in course 41943.
Content: Integrated Design with a particular focus on the interaction of daylight and acoustics with an architectural, functional and durable building concept. Design Theory (Double Diamond). Proposals, alternative solutions, evaluation, optimization, planning. Communication of results through drawings, physical/BIM models, presentations and reports. Documentation of design decisions within daylighting, acoustics and indoor climate. Project planning and group work with individual responsibility. Reflection on own learning and the group's results (process report).
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Design an advanced building with regard to indoor climate technology, focusing on architecture, function, construction, acoustics, daylight and indoor climate through a planned and recognized design process (Double Diamond) - Analyze problems and context for an actual indoor-climatic oriented design project - Propose and test alternative solutions - Select significant parameters for optimization of solutions - Use various (subject-)relevant tools in the design process, including analogue and digital sketching, (digital-) modeling, building simulation and BIM - Incorporate and process references from real architectural and engineering projects in the work - Create effective project communication orally, graphically and in writing - Create project results in groups with self-defined division of labor
41945:
Name English: Design of Structures
Danish Title: Konstruktionsdesign
General Course Objectives: The course gives you an overview of different structural design principles and the corresponding static calculations. When you have completed the course, you will have gained an understanding of the force distribution in specific types of structures, such as beams, columns, frames, trusses, cables, arches, and cupolas, when they are subjected to ordinary loads. You can also check the capacity of particular load-carrying and stabilising structural elements. Furthermore, you will be able to design a larger construction with a holistic approach accounting for the material consumption and the function.
Content: Introduction to different structural types and their static behaviour. The course content includes calculation principles, structural shaping, choice of materials and more aestetic considerations when designing a larger construction. The students work with the course topics via several exercises where they: - Calculate load carrying capacity of components and joined structures of specific materials. - Learn how vertical and horizontal loads are transmitted to the foundation via the load-carrying and stabilising system. - Design their own building shapes and choose materials from demands to structural size and material consumption. The course includes time for a mid-way peer assessment, which is not graded, and purely to increase the level of deep learning.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the structural design principles of modern architecture - Describe the loads and load combinations used in building design in Denmark - Explain the behaviour and requirements of more complex building systems - Analyze buildings with different typologies - Create a construction with reduced material consumption - Calculate the capacity of the load carrying structure of complex builidings - Explain the relation between materials and statics - Assess a structural design with a holistic approach, including aesthetics, function, material choice, buildability, etc.
41946:
Name English: Architectural Engineering Design Project 3, Structural Design
Danish Title: Bygningsdesign Projekt 3, Konstruktionsdesign
General Course Objectives: The course provides you with the opportunity to apply the knowledge gained in the 1st-3rd semesters by working on the design of a sustainably designed complex building, which presents specific structural challenges such as a high-rise building or a structure with large spans. Upon completion of the course, you will be able to actively participate in an integrated building design process. You will be equipped to identify and develop relevant solutions based on a given problem, select the best solutions, and effectively communicate the results through drawings, models, presentations, and reports. This course builds upon the design and project skills acquired in course 41945, while incorporating design processes from course 41941 with a specific focus on structural aspects.
Content: Integrated Design with a particular emphasis on the interaction of structures within an architectural, functional, and sustainable building concept. Design Theory (Double Diamond): Proposing, exploring alternatives, evaluating, optimizing, and planning. Communicating results through drawings, physical/BIM models, presentations, and reports. Project planning and group work with individual responsibilities. Reflecting on personal learning and the group's outcomes (process report)
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Design a structural advanced building through a planned design process - Analyze problems and context for an actual structural-oriented design project - Propose and test alternative solutions - Select significant parameters for optimization - Use various (subject-)relevant tools in the design process, including analogue/digital sketching, (digital-) modeling, BIM and structural analysis - Incorporate and process references from real architectural and engineering projects in the work - Create effective project communication orally, graphically and in writing - Create project results in groups with self-defined division of labor - Reflect on own learning, the group's processes and results in the project work
41947:
Name English: Renovation and transformation design
Danish Title: Renoverings- og transformationsdesign
General Course Objectives: The course gives you the opportunity to plan the renovation and transformation of existing buildings in order to extend the life of buildings and thus strengthen sustainable development. Once you have followed the course, you can assess the condition of existing buildings in order to repair damage and improve usability.
Content: The course will present various typical Danish building traditions of different eras, including the strengths and weaknesses that characterize these. The student will be introduced to the civil engineer's traditional contribution to transformation and renovation processes, e.g. through knowledge of applied materials and structures. This is to be able to analyze an existing building, both in terms of typical damage and strengths and thus potentials for conversion and transformation. This will also include issues regarding different types of hazardous substances that have been used over time. Based on this, various options for renovation are analysed, both overall and at building component level. When assessing opportunities for renovation and transformation, the focus will be on the optimal use of resources; key topics will therefore be: - Service life and lifetime extension, not only technically but also functionally and aesthetically - Reuse of elements in construction - Contribution to CO2 reduction and Life Cycle Assessment (LCA)/Life Cycle Costing (LCC) calculations - Energy savings - Residual carrying capacity
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Describe the engineer's role in building renovation - Assess and outline options for conversion and transformation of buildings for other uses - Combine solutions with sustainability considerations, including LCA/LCC calculations in the assessment of different renovation and transformation options - Analyze the condition of an existing building in terms of damage and potentials - Explain typical Danish building structures from different eras as well as their strengths and weaknesses - Select relevant renovation methodology in different types of renovation tasks - Produce solutions for renovating typical building parts in the building envelope - Address current issues regarding hazardous substances in existing buildings such as PCBs, mercury, lead, mould etc.
41948:
Name English: Architectural Engineering Design Project 4, Building transformation design
Danish Title: Bygningsdesign Projekt 4, Bygnings-transformationsdesign
General Course Objectives: The course gives you the opportunity to test your acquired knowledge and skills on the education and more specifically from course 41947 by carrying out a sustainability-oriented building transformation project. The project is based on a real case - an existing building that has served its purpose. Through the analysis, evaluation and proposal of the project work, it is documented that the building has the potential to be used for a new purpose in the future and thus fulfill this new purpose with a smaller climate footprint as a result than a new building would entail. When you have followed the course, you as an architectural engineer can participate in an integrated building design process within sustainable building transformation - and thus contribute to creating sustainable solutions in relation to usability, durability and beauty within the built environment.
Content: Practice integrated design and interdisciplinary design based on the phase model within construction cf. Danske Ark's and FRI's service description. Building registration, conceptualisation, proposal, alternative solutions, optimization of function, architectural expression, use of materials, energy consumption and indoor climate quality, planning, receiving and giving feedback, communication of results through physical/BIM models, prototypes, presentations, video formats and reports. Documentation of design decisions within construction, material selection, energy, indoor climate and LCA. Project planning, group work with individual responsibilities and cooperation with external parties.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Carry out an integrated and interdisciplinary design process, in which the individual student contributes to project solutions with their own specialization within e.g. construction, energy or indoor climate. - Propose and document a sustainable building transformation based on a real case - Select, register and collect relevant building data from a real building - Evaluate a building's transformation potential in relation to form, condition, function, cultural value and environmental impact - Create sustainable, optimized design solutions with the focus on maintaining and expanding existing building values - Select and use optimal data and tools in the design process - Create project results in groups and in interaction with external partners - Create effective and in-depth project communication to various stakeholders
41952:
Name English: Timber Structures and execution
Danish Title: Trækonstruktioner og udførelse
General Course Objectives: 1. To give the students basic knowledge of static calculations of timber structures, including the influence of anisotropy and natural growth defects of wood. 2. Be able to design the static system of long-span timber buildings, based on beams-columns structural elements. 3. To build knowledge and skills in the design of basic structural elements and connections that are related to practical use. 4. Students acquire knowledge and skills in planning and maintaining structures with emphasis on long-span timber constructions.
Content: The course consists of lectures, seminars and preparation of a project assignment. 1. Mechanical properties of wood including strength, deformation and moisture conditions, rot, waterproofing and fire conditions. 2. Setting up the statical calculation models, including relevant load combinations. 3. Construction elements based on wood: structural timber, laminated wood, plywood, chipboard and fiberboard 4. Fasteners and joints: Glue, Dowels, Bolts, Nails, Screws and metal plates. 5. Calculation of multiple fasteners connections. 6. Calculation of strength and deformation of structural elements and structures of timber (ULS), including massive and composite beams and columns and stressed skin elements. 7. Stability problems, including folding of flanges and webs, and lateral torsional buckling. 8. Calculations in the serviceability limit state (SLS). 9. Stiffening elements of wood based materials. 10. Cross-laminated Timber (CLT) 11. Fire resistance of wood 12. Special construction methods for timber structures
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Describe the assumptions behind the calculation methods used in Eurocode 5, Design of timber Structures. - Evaluate the application of different wood-based construction elements. - Make simple, qualitative assessments concerning choice of structural systems and more detailed calculations of typical constructions in practice. - Analyze simple timber structures from a practical perspective and determine appropriate structural elements of long-span timber buildings. - Design beams, columns and built-up elements in timber constructions based on Eurocode 5. - Design mechanical fasteners and simple connections in timber constructions based on Eurocode 5. - Determine deformations in structural elements and simple timber structures. - Evaluate the fire resistance of simple timber elements in accordance with Eurocode 5. - Describe different construction methods and propose the most relevant method for long-span timber structures. - Communicate and argue for solutions both in writing and orally. - Conduct and present calculations in a structured and readable form.
41B1A:
Name English: Sustainable Building Design
Danish Title: Bæredygtigt Bygningsdesign
General Course Objectives: The aim of the course is to • introduce the students to analytical methods in relation to sustainability • introduce the students to the basic parameters for the design of sustainable construction • special focus on the parameters that are not normally included in usual calculations of sustainability • special focus on the importance of errors and construction damages in relation to sustainability • special focus on the importance of waste of materials in relation to sustainability • special focus on functionality and the use of space in relation to sustainability Based on the students' cases, sustainability is analyzed and treated in a broad sense and from a general holistic view
Content: - Parameters for sustainable building design - The importance of especially the factors that are not included in calculations and certifications - Materials - Failure, waste, robustness - Space/area use and building geometry - Functionality and implementation in practice
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Identify potentials for sustainability in a given project. - Explain and analyze the complexities of sustainability. - Analyze and identify possible greenwashing. - Work with building design based on basic parameters for sustainability. - Analyze the sustainable elements with a view to identifying schisms and barriers in the combination of different measures. - Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of different solutions. - Differentiate between different elements for sustainability (climate, social, biodiversity etc.), prioritize between these and integrate them into an overall solution. - Assess alternatives to make a specific project more sustainable.
41B1C:
Name English: Sustainable Building Worldwide
Danish Title: Bæredygtigt Verdensbyggeri
General Course Objectives: The aim of the course is to introduce the students to an international approach to sustainable construction, seen in the light of the following: • an analytical method in relation to sustainability • the basic parameters for the design of sustainable construction • special focus on the parameters that are not normally included in usual calculations of sustainability • special focus on the importance of errors and damages in relation to sustainability • special focus on the importance of material waste in relation to sustainability • special focus on functionality and area utilization in relation to sustainability
Content: Based on a study tour, the study objectives are analyzed and processed from the perspective of sustainability in a broad sense and from a general holistic view. The students must also expand their international network on sustainable construction through the study tour.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain and analyze the complexity of different approaches to sustainability. - Explain and analyze methods and solutions used in the study objects. - Analyze the objects of study in relation to both the local and the international context. - Discuss advantages and disadvantages of the different methods and solutions. - Identify possible greenwashing. - Identify potentials for learning regarding sustainability from other projects and approaches to the concept. - Analyze the sustainable elements with a view to identifying schisms and barriers in the combination of different initiatives. - Distinguish between different elements for sustainability (climate, social, biodiversity, etc.), prioritize between these and integrate them into an overall solution.
41B2A:
Name English: Digital Methods for Sustainable Construction
Danish Title: Digitale Metoder til Bæredygtigt Byggeri
General Course Objectives: The purpose of the course is for the student to acquire knowledge, skills and competences to use digitally supported working methods in connection with the implementation of sustainability in construction. The course focuses on the possibility of using semantically machine-readable data across software platforms.
Content: Contain: - A review of the principles of FAIR data, along with several examples of open and standard data formats that adhere to these principles. - Information on methods for data transfer or sharing, accompanied by various technologies for data collection. - The fundamental distinctions between commercial, open-source, or self-developed applications, emphasizing data integration and updates. - Examples of data sources, including public registers, environmental databases, and EPD (Environmental Product Declaration). - Approaches to evaluating digitization strategies concerning sustainable construction.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Apply the principles of FAIR data (findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability). - Explain the difference between proprietary, open, and standard data formats and being able to distinguish between information and data. - Explain various methods for digital information sharing. - Explain the necessity of machine-readable data in automated transfer. - Describe selected data standards for environmental product declarations (EPD). - Describe characteristics of commercial, open-source, or custom-developed applications. - Assess and addres risks associated with automatic data transfer. - Describe typical digital tools for sustainable construction in a Danish context.
41B2B:
Name English: Sustainability as a concept
Danish Title: Bæredygtighed som begreb
General Course Objectives: The aim of the course is to give the students an introduction to sustainability as a concept, including the different definitions and approaches to sustainability. The course also deals with the complexity of sustainability and the interaction between different dimensions of sustainability. The focus is on giving the students a general understanding of this, as well as applying this competence in relation to the construction industry, with the aim that it can contribute to creating a more sustainable society. The students will be introduced to national and international sustainability initiatives to promote more sutainable construction.
Content: The students are introduced to sustainability as a theoretical concept and to the different definitions and approaches to sustainability - for example the triple bottom line of environmental, social and economic sustainability and the concept "Doughnut economics". An overview is given of the complexity of sustainability and the complexity of building sustainably. In the same way, interaction between the environment and people is also looked at. The students will be introduced to concepts such as the UN's Global Goals and absolute sustainability, as well as how these relate to the built environment. The students will learn about new national and international initiatives to promote more sustainable construction, including DGNB, the Reduction Roadmap, the EU's Taxonomy and Science-Based Targets. The students will apply their acquired knowledge in relation to concrete cases from construction practice.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Analyze how society's production and consumption contribute to environmental impacts on an overall level - Distinguish between different definitions of sustainability and their main focus as well as differences between definitions. - Compare different approaches to setting environmental boundaries and analyze what influences boundary setting; including concepts such as 'planetary limits' and absolute sustainability. - Describe initiatives such as the EU's Taxonomy and deduce how this can be used in specific cases - Combine different initiatives from practice and analyze their relevance in relation to concrete cases; eg Reduction Roadmap, DGNB Planet and Science-Based Targets. - Explain doughnut economics with a focus on people and the environment in a global and local perspective. - Apply these objectives in relation to concrete cases, and discuss synergies and trade-offs between different sustainability dimensions - Consider concrete solutions in relation to concrete cases, and discuss their positive and negative effects on various sustainability dimensions
41B2C:
Name English: Life cycle assessments and life cycle costing
Danish Title: Livscyklusvurderinger og totaløkonomi
General Course Objectives: The aim of the course is to give the student an introduction to methods for a holistic assessment of sustainability of construction projects, components and materials based on environmental, social and economic criteria. The student will be able to make calculations and assessments based on environmental life cycle assessments in an LCA calculation (Life Cycle Assessment), social life cycle assessments in an SLCA (Social Life Cycle Assessment) and total economic assessments in an LCC calculation (Life Cycle Costing). The student will be able to discuss and assess the quantitative and qualitative results of the three different methods in relation to each other and relate them to practice through a specific case.
Content: The course covers the following topics: - - The resource and environmental problems faced by industrialized countries, including the role of construction in this. - The life cycle approach as a concept for a holistic assessment of impacts and effects on environmental, social and economic sustainability. - The underlying principles for LCA, SLCA and LCC calculations and assessments. - Methods and tools for life cycle assessment (LCA), social assessment (SLCA) and total economic assessment (LCC) for evaluating the environmental, social and economic impacts and consequences of construction projects - Collection, processing and quality assurance of quantitative and qualitative data for LCA, SLCA and LCC on construction, as included in e.g. building codes and in sustainability certification. Based on the above mentioned, the students will be able to carry out calculations based on specific cases, as well as analyse, compare and assess the uncertainty and reliability of calculation results. Based on this, the students will consider and discuss alternative solutions.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the relevance of using different types of life cycle assessments (LCA, SLCA and LCC) in different contexts. - Explain principles for and main differences between relevant standards and methods for different types of life cycle assessments (LCA, SLCA and LCC). - Apply LCA methods and tools to determine the environmental impacts and consequences of a building project, including determining the relevant functional unit. - Apply SLCA methods and tools to assess the social impacts and effects of a building project, including determining relevant qualitative criteria and indicators. - Apply LCC methods and tools to determine the total economic impacts and effects of a building project, including setting up relevant investment alternatives. - Discuss, analyze and assess the LCA results, including the sources of the largest environmental impacts in the construction life cycle. - Discuss, analyze and evaluate SLCA assessments, including the methodological challenges of quantifying positive and negative social impacts. - Discuss, analyze and assess the LCC results, including establishing a prioritized list of investment alternatives. - Discuss, analyze and assess the reliability and uncertainty of LCA, SLCA and LCC results over the life cycle of the building, including methodological limitations and level of maturity. - Integrate and present the three different analyses for a holistic assessment of the overall environmental, social and economic impacts and consequences of a building project. - Design concrete proposals for optimization of the environmental, social and economic impacts and consequences of a building project, based on a specific case.
42016:
Name English: Business Economics and Finance
Danish Title: Forretningsøkonomi og finansiering
General Course Objectives: The course offers concepts and tools in economics and finance to support strategic managerial decision-making. The course connects corporate finance and economic theory to strategic management. It emphasizes theory and practice, with real-life examples, to sharpen analytical skills, teach the fundamentals of corporate finance necessary for strategic financial decisions, and integrate the Structure–Conduct–Performance (SCP) paradigm and Porter’s competitive framework. and provide intuition for strategic competition under different market structures. Students will experience solving decision-making problems using the tools covered in the course. The importance of theory in the decision-making process, the key issues in pricing in different market structures, and product differentiation choices will be introduced. The effects of strategic decisions and government regulation on firm performance and social welfare will be discussed. To give students an understanding of… • How to use capital budgeting techniques to assess strategic investments • How risk and return shape financial performance • How demand and supply forces work under different market structures • How market structure, firm conduct, and performance are linked • How to assess competitive intensity • How oligopolistic markets differ from perfectly competitive markets and a monopoly • How to think strategically when there is mutual interdependence between market players • How pricing, output, and location strategies affect firm performance and welfare in different markets
Content: I. Course introduction II. Strategic Investment Decision-Making a. Intro, basic concepts, and definitions b. Valuation c. Fundamentals of capital budgeting d. Risk and return III. Structure, conduct, performance a. Basic Market Structure (Demand and Supply, elasticities, and consumer and producer surpluses) b. How to measure market structure: concentration measures, product heterogeneity, entry/exit barriers, information c. Understanding firm conduct: pricing-output decisions with market power (more detail in game theory), R&D, advertising, collusion (cartels: OPEC) d. How to measure firm and market performance: profit, different performance measures, efficiency, welfare IV. From SCP to Competitive Strategy a. Mapping SCP to Porter’s Five Forces • Rivalry among existing firms • Threat of entry • Threat of substitutes • Bargaining power of buyers • Bargaining power of suppliers b. Industry attractiveness vs firm performance c. Cost leadership vs differentiation d. Strategic positioning within industry structure V. Step into other players’ shoes (strategic interactions) a. Simultaneous move (Normal form) games: Dominant strategy, iterated elimination of dominated strategies, Nash equilibrium (brief intro to best response functions) Examples: prisoner’s dilemma (PD), pollution abatement, coordination, technology adoption, game of chicken, strict competition. b. Sequential move (Extensive form) games: Backward induction, subgame perfect equilibrium, strategies to deal with empty threats and promises (Examples: Chain-store, centipede, bargaining) c. Repeated games (finite and infinite): discounting, tit-for-tat, and grim trigger strategies (Examples: repeated PD, can collaboration be saved?) VI. Markets and pricing strategies a. Perfect Competition: a benchmark market structure b. Monopoly: highest market power, natural gas, oil, and electricity as natural monopolies c. Monopolistic Competition: product differentiation creates monopoly power d. Price Discrimination i. 1st degree (perfect) discrimination ii. 2nd degree (quantity) discrimination: à la carte vs buffet iii. 3rd degree (group) discrimination: student/senior discounts VII. Strategy in oligopolistic games a. Cournot: duopoly, N-player, symmetric, asymmetric, welfare (Example: Airbus vs Boeing) b. Bertrand: pricing in homogeneous/​heterogeneous product markets, welfare (Example: Pizza Hut & Dominos) c. Stackelberg: symmetric/asymmetric costs, welfare (Example: Coke vs Pepsi) d. Spatial and attribute space location choice: Hotelling’s linear city, Salop’s circle (Examples: gas stations, ice cream flavors)
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Apply comparative statics to understand how market equilibrium changes - Understand and use capital budgeting techniques - Use elasticity estimates for managerial decisions - Describe the relation between assets’ risk and return - Estimate and interpret the market risk of a financial asset - Understand and quantify key determinants of market structure, performance, and conduct. - Assess competitive intensity using SCP and Porter’s Five Forces - Strategically determine optimal location, quantity, and price choices - Find optimal pricing and output levels in different markets using game theory - Evaluate the link between competition, regulation, and welfare. - Formulate strategic recommendations based on economic analysis of markets
42146:
Name English: Energy Economics: Energy Consumption
Danish Title: Energy Economics: Energy Consumption
General Course Objectives: The energy transition is taking place rapidly in the face of urgent needs for climate change mitigation, supply security, and decarbonization. Energy consumption is a critical issue for energy transition and society, as it impacts a wide range of aspects, including economic growth, climate change, decarbonization, environmental sustainability, supply security and human health. Energy is essential for a variety of functions, including running homes and the operation of industries, and transportation. The efficient use of energy and the adoption of sustainable energy sources are crucial for reducing the adverse effects of energy consumption and promoting sustainable development. Therefore, there is a need for educated human resources that do research and develop policies in this area. The Energy Economics PhD summer schools will take a role in teaching how to use economic theory, energy modeling, and computational tools for research to address these contemporary global challenges. The course will provide a platform for students to present their research topics, discuss their ideas with scholars and receive feedback. Students will receive help from and discuss their ideas with senior researchers and other Ph.D. students who are accepted to the course.
Content: Energy Economics and Policy Energy Demand Energy and Economic Growth Basic Econometric Methods Qualitative Methods Energy Justice Energy Poverty Time Series and Panel Data Analyses Electrification of Energy Consumption (Heating) Electrification of Energy Consumption (Transportation)
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - learn how economics knowledge can be used to analyze and model energy consumption. - demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of quantitative and qualitative methods and how these can be used to investigate energy consumption and evaluate policies. - understand the important aspects of energy consumption in the determination of economic growth. - understand how energy consumption is related to energy justice and energy poverty. - demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of electrification of energy consumption in the heating and transportation sector. - work with scholars to build models for energy consumption. - practice to developed empirical models from theoretical models. - do comprehensive analyses by using energy data and quantitative methods
42147:
Name English: DTU’s Advanced Operations Research PhD Summer School
Danish Title: Avanceret operationsanalyse til optimering af beslutninger - Sommerskole
General Course Objectives: To describe, understand and apply methods and techniques related to this years' advanced topic in Operations Research, in order to create new knowledge using these methods and techniques in a new context related to their own field of research.
Content: Operations Research is specialized in solving complex decision problems, resulting in advising what optimal decisions to take. This summer school unites DTU and external experts in an effort to share their knowledge within their fields with future experts (e.g. PhD students), on an advanced level. The aim of the course is to introduce these future experts to the year's Advanced Operations Research Topic (AORT), make them familiar with this domain, give them hands-on exercises to familiarize themselves with the area and prepare them to understand the latest development in the state-of-the-art, with the aim that they could take this knowledge and create new knowledge within their own research topic through synergies with the AORT. In addition, the course aims at community building. Therefore, half a day is reserved for focus on community building among the participants.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Summarize the main research problems related to the year’s Advanced Operations Research Topic (AORT) - Describe some of the main solution approaches to tackle this year’s AORT - Argue for using one solution approach over another for a specific problem, based on the strengths and weaknesses of the different approaches belonging to this year's AORT - Solve challenges related to the AORT using scripting software like Julia or Python - Argue for the benefits and disbenefits of applying different techniques related to the AORT for a specific problem context - Develop ideas for new (small) extensions of this year's AORT, either in the form of changes to the tools or new applications - Appraise these ideas in a toy-problem setting, through implementation and evaluation of results - Report the obtained results structured, comprehensively, briefly, clearly, in a critically evaluating/concluding way, and of course also in accordance with good practice for a written presentation within the discipline
42404:
Name English: Maritime Logistics and Management
Danish Title: Maritim logistik og ledelse
General Course Objectives: The main objective of the course is to provide an advanced overview of the maritime industry, its sectors, actors and concepts in maritime logistics and management. The students will learn the important role of the maritime industry in the global economy and societies. The course will also enable students to identify and analyse key aspects of maritime trade, seaport development, and international policy frameworks. The course content and activities will highlight the international and dynamic aspects in maritime logistics and management, including their future outlook and impact.
Content: The course covers • Different aspects of maritime sectors including port, shipping, marine engineering, maritime services, international policy frameworks • The actors involved and their interrelationships • An overview of ships, maritime cargoes, shipping markets, and maritime transport modes • An overview of seaports, terminals, and their development • How are maritime logistics and supply chains managed efficiently and how to make decisions to enhance competitiveness • Emerging developments in autonomous shipping, digitalisation and AI in shipping • New developments in maritime decarbonisation and emission reduction, including an overview of technologies and market-based measures • Concepts of cluster and hub in the context of the maritime industry The course uses real-life case studies for illustration, application and facilitating student discussions.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain and compare the sectors, actors and their interrelationships in the maritime industry - Identify and explain the major types of ships, maritime cargoes, and shipping markets - Identify and explain the major types of maritime transport modes - Analyse the role of maritime industry and trade in the global economy and societies - Examine the key concepts in seaports and terminals - Illustrate international policy frameworks and the involved regulatory bodies in maritime sectors - Assess and apply key concepts in maritime logistics, supply chains, and analyse how to make decisions to enhance competitiveness - Analyse and discuss the new developments in autonomous shipping, digitalisation and AI in shipping - Analyse and discuss the complexities, dynamics, and outlook in maritime logistics and management, then propose strategies - Analyse and discuss the new developments in maritime decarbonisation and emission reduction - Assess and apply the concepts of cluster and hub in the context of the maritime industry
42620:
Name English: Science, Technology and Society (Polytechnical Foundation)
Danish Title: Videnskab, Teknologi og Samfund (polyteknisk grundlag)
General Course Objectives: The purpose of this course is to equip students with perspectives and tools to be able to understand and critically analyse how technological innovation and technology intensive projects impact society and the environment. They will be able to identify and address trade-offs and dilemmas with respect to environmental and social sustainability and recommend responsible strategies for the attainment of sustainability.
Content: The sustainability challenge and the role of technology and engineering. Lifecycle assessment and sustainable development goals. Methods for mapping public controversies about technology. Analysis of the social and democratic sustainability of technological projects.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Establish the significance of SDGs in relation to engineering projects and discover how they can be used in practice and analysis - Know and understand prevailing definitions of sustainability and the history of the concept of sustainability - Understand the importance of adopting a life cycle/systems perspective and considering a comprehensive range of impacts within each of the three sustainability dimensions - environment, society and economy - Identify how social values are embedded in engineering projects and how technology can become a matter of public concern - Describe the role of ethics in engineering work within one’s own engineering field and in collaboration with other fields and stakeholders - Describe and evaluate the primary social processes of designing, implementing, adopting, and contesting innovation - Apply social scientific methods for analyzing arguments and actors in public controversies about technology - Discuss key dimensions of responsible research and innovation and apply them to evaluate engineering projects, especially anticipation, reflexivity, inclusion, and responsiveness - Recommend responsible strategies to foster democratic and environmental sustainability of engineering projects
42622:
Name English: Science, Technology and Society (Polytechnical Foundation)
Danish Title: Videnskab, Teknologi og Samfund (polyteknisk grundlag)
General Course Objectives: The purpose of this course is to equip students with perspectives and tools to be able to understand and critically analyse how technological innovation and technology intensive projects impact society and the environment. They will be able to identify and address trade-offs and dilemmas with respect to environmental and social sustainability and recommend responsible strategies for the attainment of sustainability.
Content: The sustainability challenge and the role of technology and engineering. Lifecycle assessment and sustainable development goals. Methods for mapping public controversies about technology. Analysis of the social and democratic sustainability of technological projects.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Establish the significance of SDGs in relation to engineering projects and discover how they can be used in practice and analysis. - Know and understand prevailing definitions of sustainability and the history of the concept of sustainability. - Understand the importance of adopting a life cycle/systems perspective and considering a comprehensive range of impacts within each of the three sustainability dimensions - environment, society and economy. - Identify how social values are embedded in engineering projects and how technology can become a matter of public concern. - Describe the role of ethics in engineering work within one’s own engineering field and in collaboration with other fields and stakeholders. - Describe and evaluate the primary social processes of designing, implementing, adopting, and contesting innovation. - Apply social scientific methods for analyzing arguments and actors in public controversies about technology. - Discuss key dimensions of responsible research and innovation and apply them to evaluate engineering projects, especially anticipation, reflexivity, inclusion, and responsiveness. - Recommend responsible strategies to foster democratic and environmental sustainability of engineering projects.
42701:
Name English: Behavioural economics and the environment
Danish Title: Adfærdsøkonomi og miljø
General Course Objectives: This course will provide students with an understanding of how to use insights from behavioural economics and experimental methods to investigate environmental problems. The emphasis is on conducting tests of behavioural economic theory and testing policies related to environmental problems using an experimental approach and being able to critically evaluate studies using these approaches. In the first part of the course, experimental methods are discussed including causality, and different types of experiments (lab, lab-in-the-field and field experiments). The second part of the course provides an overview of the main behavioural economic theories and links them to environmental problems. The final part focuses on the design and analysis of experiments and how to use experiments for policy support. A course project will support the lectures and will provide an in-depth and practical understanding of the content of the course.
Content: 1. Behavioural economic theory 2. Experimental methods 3. Experimental design and analysis of experiments 4. Behavioural economics and experiments applied to environment problems 5. Behavioural economics, experiments, and policymaking
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - demonstrate knowledge of the main topics in behavioural economics - understand the recent developments in behavioural economics - demonstrate an understanding of how behavioural economics can be used to analyse environmental problems - demonstrate an understanding of different experimental methods - demonstrate an understanding of how different experimental methods can be used to investigate behavioural economic theories and evaluate policies - critically appraise studies employing behavioural economics and experimental methods when investigating environmental problems - conduct a lab, a lab-in-the-field and a field experiment - analyse the results of lab, lab-in-the-field and field experiments
42787:
Name English: Exploring the State-of-the-Art in quantitative transport science
Danish Title: Udforsk state-of-art indenfor quantitativ transport forskning
General Course Objectives: Gaining knowledge in recent research results in the transport research area. Get familiar with recent methods and tools in publishing. Learn to present technical material to an audience, learn to present critique as an opponent, learn to communicate, learn to judge papers fast and slow.
Content: After the seminar students are expected to participate in a scientific discussion critically reviewing the approach taken and suggesting areas of related and future research as well as topics that could be included in the course. The expected is 140 hours. Much of this is used for preparing lectures, reading papers and advancing academic work of the students that are presented at the course.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - structure the writing of scientific papers - use the most recent AI tools to improve scientific productivity in a manner that do not violate research integrity and ethics - read, analyze, understand and assess seminal and recent research papers from different areas - get a widening knowledge regarding methods and applications - present technical papers for an audience such that the material is easily comprehendable - be able to act as critical opponents - read papers fast and slow - improve his/her innovative mindset? - learn good practice with respect to scientific referencing - develop ideas for future research in transport research - improve his/her way of exchanging ideas - use the DTU library
42893:
Name English: Psychology for engineers
Danish Title: Psykologi for ingeniører
General Course Objectives: The course will equip students with basic knowledge about selected psychological concepts, theories, and methods of key importance for understanding human behaviour in engineering contexts. In addition, the course will teach the students how to utilize this knowledge for the design and evaluation of products, interfaces, and behavioural interventions promoting health, safety or pro-environmental behaviour.
Content: The course is divided into two blocks: The first block is based on cognitive psychology and human factors research. Here, students learn about core abilities and limitations of human information processing and perception and will apply this knowledge to identify how easy or difficult a product or interface is to use in a usability test. The second block is based on selected theories and concepts of social and environmental psychology. Here, students learn about social perception, attitudes and norms and their effect on behaviour and more general theories of behaviour and behaviour change. Based on this knowledge, they will sketch a behaviour change intervention and learn how to evaluate its effect based on a short theory-based survey.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Describe the core abilities and limitations of human information processing and perception (e.g. visual processing, depth perception, limits of short-term information storage) - Apply knowledge about human information processing to identify and analyze problematic human-machine interfaces (e.g. in display design or ergonomics) - Identify key cognitive, social and environmental factors that influence human behaviour - Describe selected psychological decision theories and theories of behaviour change - Apply a psychological theory to a guide a behaviour change intervention - Differentiate between different experimental and non-experimental designs - Explain the advantages and limitations of different study designs - Collaborate effectively in randomly assigned student groups by establishing and adhering to a set of mutually agreed-upon rules
42B92:
Name English: Cybersecurity
Danish Title: Cybersecurity
General Course Objectives: This elective course aims at equipping participants with the knowledge to comprehend the changing cyber threat landscape. By understanding the key cyber threats and related attacks, leaders can effectively assess and mitigate risks, develop informed strategies together with cybersecurity professionals, and thus take well-informed decisions to protect their organizations. While technical cybersecurity expertise is not required and expected at the management level, a comprehensive understanding of cybersecurity is essential for having meaningful and constructive dialogues with the organization’s cybersecurity personnel, and thus appropriately managing cyber risks. By prioritizing cybersecurity, organizations can establish a culture of resilience and enhance their long-term success in the increasingly digitized world.
Content: In an increasingly interconnected world, where digital technologies are integral to every aspect of our life and of business operations, the need for effective cybersecurity has become paramount. Indeed, as companies increasingly rely on digital systems for their products and infrastructures, they inherently become more vulnerable to cyber-attacks. Cyber threats are constantly evolving, becoming more sophisticated and persistent over time. Nowadays, cyber threats are among the most critical business risks facing corporations, including financial loss, reputational damage, legal liabilities, and the compromise of sensitive data. It's therefore essential to understand that any organization leveraging digital technologies faces cyber risks. The question is no longer whether a cyber-attack will occur or not, but when it will and how effectively respond to that. This elective course aims at equipping participants with the knowledge to comprehend the changing cyber threat landscape. By understanding the key cyber threats and related attacks, leaders can effectively assess and mitigate risks, develop informed strategies together with cybersecurity professionals, and thus take well-informed decisions to protect their organizations. While technical cybersecurity expertise is not required and expected at the management level, a comprehensive understanding of cybersecurity is essential for having meaningful and constructive dialogues with the organization’s cybersecurity personnel, and thus appropriately managing cyber risks. By prioritizing cybersecurity, organizations can establish a culture of resilience and enhance their long-term success in the increasingly digitized world.
