Quantitative models are central for assessing resource status, evaluating management options, and supporting evidence-based decision-making. Single-stock assessment models are the foundation of fisheries management advice globally. Management decisions rely on robust, well-documented assessments of stock status to provide catch advice and evaluate outcomes of management strategies. In part 1 of the course, students gain hands-on experience with two internationally recognized single-stock assessment models and learn to validate and interpret results according to best practices. Effective fisheries management must also address complexity of real-world systems beyond single-stock approaches. In course part 2, students explore biological and technical interactions in multi-species and mixed fisheries dynamics with multiple target and bycatch species exploited simultaneously by different fisheries. Tools are introduced accounting for species and fisheries interactions, fleet behavior, and data limitations. Part 3 of the course considers fisheries systems holistically through ecosystem-based and integrated approaches. Students engage with models incorporating ecological, economic and social dimensions, i.e. fisheries bio-economic and broader ecosystem models being spatial explicit. The course introduces methods for analysing current system status, projecting future dynamics, and conducting Management Strategy Evaluation (MSE) of different options. Students obtain skills to analyse stock, fisheries, and ecosystem dynamics, evaluate management scenarios, assess uncertainty and risks, and analyse the ecological, technical, and socio-economic complexities in fisheries systems.
Content: The course introduces principles and practice in modern fisheries management, with focus on quantitative evaluation methods and their role in scientific management advice. It begins with an overview of international fisheries and ecosystem-based management systems including their foundations, institutional frameworks, data sources, advisory processes, governance structures, and decision-making under multiple ecological and socio-economic objectives and risks. The remaining course is structured into the following three main parts: Part 1: Single-species management advice Hands-on training in application of two advanced single-stock assessment models used by the ICES advisory framework: a stochastic surplus production model (SPiCT) and a stochastic age-structured stochastic model (SAM). Students learn to estimate stock size, fishing mortality, and stock status relative to maximum sustainable yield (MSY) reference points using time series of catch and survey data. Model diagnostics, uncertainty quantification, and best practices for validating assessments are key in the training, and will conclude with an application of MSE also used in the next course parts. Part 2: Multi-species and mixed fisheries management advice Introduction to biological interactions between stocks involving a stochastic multi-species assessment model (SMS) and broader MSY reference point ranges accounting for trade-offs in exploitation of several species in the same fisheries. It also introduce simple and advanced methods (TEMAS, FCUBE) integrating the complexity of technical interactions in mixed fisheries and multi-fleet dynamics. Students will define and analyse interactions between target and bycatch species fishing mortality by fleet using data on effort, selectivity, and behavior also covering recreational fisheries. Part 3: Holistic fisheries system and ecosystem management advice Practical training in spatially explicit bio-economic and vessel-based MSE tools (e.g. VMS-Logbook-Tools, DISPLACE) combining logbook and VMS (satellite tracking) data for tactic management advice for several fisheries. These simulation models assess impacts of maritime spatial planning scenarios, e.g. windfarm closures, on fishing fleets, target stocks, and the seabed according to ecological and economic sustainability. Further, students evaluate output from advanced ecosystem-models integrating biological interactions, environmental forcing (e.g., climate change, eutrophication), and fisheries dynamics enabling strategic long-term management advice. This allows to explore broader ecological and socio-economic implications of management strategies before implementation. Students work with both simple and advanced models in data-rich and data-poor contexts, developing the ability to critically evaluate trade-offs, risks, and sustainability of alternative management strategies.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Describe the development and increasing complexity of fisheries and ecosystem-based management, including advisory processes, quantitative methods, and institutional frameworks. - Implement single-species stock assessment models used in ICES advisory processes to evaluate stock status, population dynamics, and associated uncertainty. - Analyse biological interactions, including species-specific natural mortality, adapting quantitative multi-species models. - Apply quantitative mixed fisheries models to analyse technical interactions, including fleet- and stock-specific fishing patterns across target and by-catch species. - Evaluate spatially explicit bio-economic and vessel-based management strategies to model the impacts of maritime spatial planning on fleets, fish stocks, and seabed habitats. - Interpret the results from advanced ecosystem models to support strategic fisheries advice, including the integrated impacts of fishing, environmental drivers, and species interactions, and socio-economic dimensions on resource dynamics. - Predict future stock dynamics and fishery yields under alternative harvest control rules and management scenarios according MSY-based targets using Management Strategy Evaluation (MSE) across single-species, multi-species, mixed fisheries and ecosystem contexts. - PhD Course: Design a novel harvest control rule and evaluate its performance by means of Management Strategy Evaluation (MSE).
25627:
Name English: Quantitative Modelling of Natural resources
Danish Title: Kvantitativ modellering af naturressourcer
General Course Objectives: This advanced statistics course aims to enable the students to draw inference from models which are not covered by linear model routines in standard statistical software packages. Such non-standard models are very common in natural resource modelling an dcould e.g. contain: non-trival non-linearities, complex covariance structures, complicated couplings between fixed and random effects, or different sources of observations needing different likelihood types. in additionthey could contain large amounts of data. By the end of the course the students should be able to formulate (on paper and in code) non-standard models, estimate model parameters from these, quantify uncertainties, and test model hypothesis.
Content: This advanced statistics course deals with non-standard models, which are models that are not possible to analyze via pre-written code in standard statistical software packages. The analysis of non-standard require the analysts to explicity write efficient code for the likelihood, which function of the problem and optimize the likelihood, which require use of modern techniques for automatic calculation of derivatives. These tools will be taught and studied. In addition to the technical side of things a lot of emphasis will be put on model-formulation, on drawing correct conclusions from the models and on validating that appropriate models are being applied. Among the types of models that wll be studied are: Non-linear regression models, general random-effects models (including state-space models), multivariate models, and models informed by multiple different data sources.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Identify observational situations that cannot be analyzed via standard statistical software packages. - Carry out analysis for non-standard statistical models with non-trivial non-linearities and multiple data sources. - Describe non-standard models precisely in text and formulas. - Carry out inference efficiently in models including random and fixed effects. - Utilize efficient representations of the multivariate Gaussian to implement spatio-temporal (and similar high-dimensional) models . - Propagate uncertainties from observations to estimates and derived quantities of interest. - Conduct proper statistical model validation of statistical models with non-normal and non-independent observations. - Formulate the result of a statistical analysis (estimates, uncertainties, and hypothesis testing) in a style suitable for a scientific publication.
25628:
Name English: Fisheries Ecology and Advice
Danish Title: Fiskeriøkologi og rådgivning
General Course Objectives: This course provides students with a comprehensive understanding of modern fisheries management, emphasizing both single-stock approaches and ecosystem effects. Students will learn to interpret ICES catch advice and perform basic stock assessments and fishing pressure projections using the R programming environment. Using scientific literature and hands-on modeling exercises, students will also learn to critically evaluate management advice considering biodiversity conservation challenges and formulate their own evidence-based recommendations for sustainable fisheries.
Content: Fisheries support many millions of livelihoods, provide food security, and contribute to national economies as well as coastal societies, but fisheries can also impact ecosystems negatively. For instance, fishing activities may disrupt food webs, damage the sea floor, or be responsible for the unintended captures of threatened marine animals. During the past decades, important effort has been made to develop the science and fisheries policies. In this course, we will study how fisheries scientists assess the size of fish stocks to produce stock-by-stock catch advice and how ecosystem considerations currently is moving up on the fisheries management agenda. We will look at concrete examples of fisheries management measures, including quota limits, time/area closures and actual Marine Protected Areas (MPA). The lectures will have a global perspective but will focus more closely on the North-East Atlantic and EU waters. The R programming language, being one of the most often used in ecology and fisheries science, will be used for the analytical parts of the course. The course program consists of (1) four modules covering the global perspective on fisheries, stock-by-stock assessments, and the ICES advice system, (2) four modules with analytical exercises in R, (3) four modules on the ecosystem approach to fisheries management, including a short legislative background and the tools available to managers to ensure fisheries sustainability and biodiversity conservation, and (4)Report assignment, in which students will apply the concepts and tools learned throughout the course to develop a management recommendation for a marine fish stock of their own choice. The students should find relevant scientific literature and data and select model approaches, and the result should be an evidence-based advice that considers stock dynamics, the fishery, and broader ecosystem or climate-related factors.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain and compare the basic principles and practical applications of single-stock and ecosystem-based approaches to fisheries management. - Interpret and summarize the main content presented in ICES advice sheets. - Adapt and implement R scripts to estimate stock size, calculate biological reference points, and simulate short-term catch scenarios. - Reproduce the ICES advice for a given fish stock by locating relevant data and implementing the necessary modeling code. - Compare Virtual Population Analysis with a statistical stock assessment model or propose alternative forecasting approaches accounting for additional drivers beyond the biomass of the spawning stock. - Identify and synthesize current challenges at the intersection between fisheries management and biodiversity conservation - Propose and defend practical strategies for implementing ecosystem-based fisheries management in a real-world fisheries context, addressing ecological, practical, and policy-related factors. - Critically evaluate and apply scientific literature within the scope of the course to support evidence-based arguments related to fisheries management and sustainability.
26128:
Name English: Chemistry and applications of inorganic materials
Danish Title: Uorganiske materialers kemi og anvendelser
General Course Objectives: Apply fundamental chemical principles to describe important inorganic materials and their applications in industrial and sustainable chemical processes.
Content: The course explores the real-world applications of inorganic chemistry across industry, energy systems, and environmental science. Focusing on large-scale processes and emerging technologies, students will examine the chemistry behind industrial manufacturing, advanced materials, energy storage and conversion, and the role of inorganic compounds in the environment. The key topics include metal resources, catalysis, batteries, fuel cells, green chemistry principles, sustainability, water purification, and emission control. Through a blend of lectures, problem-solving sessions, and group work with case studies, students will gain the skills to apply inorganic chemistry principles to address global challenges and sustainable development.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the general production and recycling of metals - Account for the role of catalysts in key industrial processes - Discuss the structure of advanced inorganic materials in energy storage and conversion systems, such as batteries, fuel cells, and solar energy technologies. - Describe the impact of inorganic pollutants in the environment and potential remediation strategies in water purification and emission control - Account for the 12 principles of green chemistry - Calculate the E-factor to assess the sustainability of a chemical process - Apply fundamental inorganic theory in the analysis of industrial processes and environmental challenges - Work in teams and effectively communicate science and technology in a pitch format
26241:
Name English: Applied Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics
Danish Title: Anvendt farmakokinetik og farmakodynamik
General Course Objectives: Understand the principles of PharmacoKinetics-PharmacoDynamics (PK-PD) relationships and their significance in drug development.
Content: This course covers a range of topics relevant to both clinical settings and early drug development. In clinical settings, the course explores therapeutic regimens, dose-time-effect relationships, therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM), dose adjustments, managing missed doses, and dosing for special patient groups such as children and elderly patients. For early drug development, the course delves into PharmacoKinetics-PharmacoDynamics (PK-PD) relationships, effects at receptor and ion channel levels, and effect measurements like changes in biomarkers, endogenous hormones, or enzymes. Additionally, the course addresses many aspects of pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic variability, including population PK-PD modeling methods, simulation of PK-PD relationships, and analysis methods for PK/PD. Regulatory affairs and approval processes for PK/PD are also considered. Practical sessions include computer sessions for PK/PD modeling using commercial programs.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Understand the pharmacokinetic concepts and the links between pharmacokinetics (PK), pharmacodynamics (PD) and physiological factors - Master calculations of pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of drug candidates taking different types of formulations into account - Demonstrate an understanding of PK and PD both at the individual and population levels - Obtain knowledge on variability in patient populations - Obtain knowledge on PK/PD for biologics - Obtain knowledge on PK/PD in human physiological context - Obtain insight and hands-on experience with pharmacokinetic and pharmadynamic data analysis - Obtain experience with commercial modelling software for data analysis - Explain the basic principles and use behind different types of bioanalytical techniques
27021:
Name English: Bioengineering - online  (Polytechnical Foundation)
Danish Title: Bioengineering - online (Polyteknisk grundlag)
General Course Objectives: The recent technological advances have created the foundation for engineering biological systems in order to address a wide variety of societal challenges and provide sustainable solutions for the health, food, environment and energy sectors. This course is intended to provide all BSc students with an introduction to biological principles and an understanding of the key fundamental technologies underlying cross-disciplinary applications of biology across engineering areas.
Content: This course will introduce fundamental principles of biology and biotechnology that relate to a wide variety of disciplines. The course will introduce the chemical basis for life and its relation to biochemistry and enzymes. DNA is introduced as the universal information-carrying molecule of life, and the students' are introduced to how biology converts sequence information through the processes of replication, transcription and translation into chemical functionality. Course content will consist of lectures, discussions, exercises and group work. Content will be structured in three blocks: - Block I will introduce the fundamental principles and applications of molecular biology, the phenomenon of evolution, some basic notions of ecology and the important role that large data sets play in modern biology (weeks 1-6). Lectures of Block 1 will be streamed and recorded and exercises will have online TA-support. - In block II (weeks 7-10), participants will be able to choose between different tracks, that have different focus. Each track will be co-organised by at least 2 different departments. The broad focus areas of the tracks available for the in-person course 27020 are biosensing (track BED), biomimetics and biomaterials (track MIM), bioengineering for the green transition (track BFG), and simulations and control of biological systems (track SIM). At least one of these 4 tracks will be made available for this course (27021). - Block III will consist of a group project incorporating themes from Blocks 1 and 2. The project will be carried out in interdisciplinary groups of 6 students and evaluated at a poster presentation session on the last day of the course (12-18h).
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the requirements and fundamental physical properties of life - Explain the functions and roles of proteins and how they can be engineered and improved. - Explain the central dogma of molecular biology and the conversion of digital information into analog biomolecular functions - Describe evolution on the basis of the central dogma and knowledge on cellular reproduction - Explain the main principles of ecology and biological communities with specific emphasis on bacterial communities. - Describe the specific role of data, and data science in biology and bioengineering. - Describe different examples of how biology inspires engineering. - Describe different examples of how biological systems can be engineered. - Design and quantify a bioengineering solution to a real world problem.
27030:
Name English: Biomedical cell and tissue biology
Danish Title: Biomedicinsk celle- og vævsbiologi
General Course Objectives: This course provides the student with a fundamental understanding of the biology of human cells. The course will focus on the molecular principles underlying cell structure and organization, cell division and maintenance, and cellular responses to stresses, how these functions are interconnected and regulated via control of metabolism, signal transduction, etc., and how dysregulation of these processes can lead to disease states in cells. The student will, through virtual microscopy, also gain an understanding of how cells and extracellular material are organised to give rise to different tissues and how tissues and cells can be visualised with histological methods.
Content: Structure and function of mammalian/human cell organelles and membranes. Molecular pathways and mechanisms connecting them to cellular phenotypes, e.g., signaling, metabolism, etc. Hallmarks of cancer cells and their development. Characteristics and organization of different tissues. The course focuses on the molecular understanding of cell function and regulation.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the structure and organisation of a human cell and describe the structure and function of intracellular organelles and the cytoskeleton - Describe the structure and function of cell membranes as well as the mechanisms of transmembrane transport - Explain intracellular protein trafficking and the secretory pathway - Describe the structure and function of cellular receptors and explain the molecular principles of cell communication and intracellular signalling - Explain the cell cycle, cell growth, and cell death and the regulation of these processes - Describe the basis of cancer development and the general characteristics of cancer cells - Describe the organisation of cells and extracellular matrix in different tissues, including epithelium, muscle, connective tissue, and nervous tissue - Describe the structure and function of specialised cells in epithelium, muscle, connective tissue, and nervous tissue - Use virtual microscopy on histologically stained tissue sections to identify cells, structures, and the tissue type for epithelium, muscle, connective tissue, and nervous tissue - Describe basic pathological cell and tissue changes - Combine and apply the knowledge of cell and tissue biology to analyse problems and data, and to suggest and explain hypotheses
27063:
Name English: Protein purification
Danish Title: Oprensning af proteiner
General Course Objectives: Theoretical and practical introduction to techniques for purification of proteins in milligram quantities.
Content: The chromatographic principles and basic theoretical background of ion-exchange, hydrophobic interaction and affinity chromatography, as well as gel filtration. Chromatographic systems design, including pumps, columns, and detector systems. Purification strategies and their optimization. Selection and combination of purification methods. Column materials chemical and physical properties. Handling of proteins, as well as an introduction to other methods used in protein purification on a laboratory scale, for example, SDS-PAGE, ultrafiltration and freeze drying. The above is illustrated through experimental exercises / projects.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the chromatographic principles and the basic theory of ion exchange, hydrophobic interaction and affinity chromatography - Explain the chromatographic principles and the basic theory of gel filtration. - Explain the basic design of chromatographic equipment. - Outline strategies for the purification of proteins, including selection and combination the purification methods - Discuss strategies for improved separation of chromatographic methods. - Use of chromatographic equipment. - Outline the chemical and physical properties of common column materials - Explain pre-purification steps including cell-lysis, homogenization and centrifugation.
27436:
Name English: Innovations in biopharmaceutical drug development
Danish Title: Innovation i lægemiddeludviklingsprocessen
General Course Objectives: To give the students an overview and understanding of the multi-disciplinary nature of biopharmaceutical drug discovery and development, emphasizing the integration of various fields such as Industrial Biotechnology, Biochemistry, Protein Engineering, Pharmacology, Preclinical and Clinical Investigations, Manufacturing, Regulatory Affairs (e.g. GXP), Patent issues, etc.
Content: The course gives an overview of the key stages of biopharmaceutical drug discovery and development. Through a mix of lectures and exercises, students will gain an understanding of the various facets of biopharmaceutical development in the industry. Case stories are presented in collaboration with Danish pharmaceutical companies, offering real-life examples to enhance the learning experience.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Describe key innovations in drug development, including vaccines, cell and gene therapies, antibody treatments, mammalian cell-based production of biopharmaceuticals, and advanced drug delivery systems such as micromotors and nanocarriers. - Recognize the potential and applications of various innovative technologies, enabling them to identify areas for further specialized study. - Outline the overall drug development process of a biopharmaceutical, from initial discovery through preclinical and clinical phases. - Explain general assay technologies and their roles and use in drug discovery and development of biologics - Analyze when different analytical methodologies are used to assess the purity of the final drug product. - Analyze which analytical methodologies can be used to assess the stability and aggregation of the final drug product. - Describe the procedures and regulatory requirements involved in the different phases of biopharmaceuticals, preclinical and clinical trials. - Design a top-level up- and down-stream process for manufacturing a biopharmaceutical based on its properties. - Demonstrate a general knowledge of patent issues and the role of different regulatory authorities at various stages during the drug development process.
28145:
Name English: Introduction to Chemical Reaction Engineering
Danish Title: Introduktion til reaktionsteknik
General Course Objectives: To give the student basic knowledge of the coupling between chemical kinetics and the design of chemical reactors. The student will be able to design and optimize chemical reactors. It is further the purpose to give knowledge of the most important reactors for homogeneous and heterogeneous reactors and their use in the industry.
Content: The course treats: Gas- and liquid phase reactions in ideal reactors, including reactor chains and recirculation reactors. Catalytic reactions in combination with physical transport inside catalyst pellets. Multiple reactions and choice of reactor type and process conditions for optimal production. Coupling of the energy and mass balance for reactors.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the difference between rate expressions for elementary reactions and non-elementary reactions, and write down the rate expression for elementary reactions - Explain the principles of the ideal reactor models: plug flow reactor, continuously stirred tank reactor, ideally stirred batch reactor - Set up and solve mathematical models for the ideal reactors under isothermal conditions for a single reaction, for multiple reactions - Set up and solve mole balances for other reacting systems than the three ideal reactor types - Set up the energy balance for reacting systems for single reactions - Calculate the equilibrium conversions for multiple reactions for isothermal and non-isothermal reactions - Explain how multiple steady states occur in stirred reactors - Design reactors for optimum and safe operation - Set up and solve mathematical models for diffusion and reaction in porous catalyst pellets and calculate the effectiveness factor for a 1st order reaction - Design optimal reactor konfiguration for reactor chains
28155:
Name English: Introduction to Process Control
Danish Title: Introduktion til procesregulering
General Course Objectives: The overall aim is to provide the students an understanding of: - process dynamics - the operation and application of simple feedforward and feedback control - how measurements and actuators can be connected in a process plant The course should thus provide the student the ability to design, implement and simulate single input - single output (SISO) control systems for chemical and biotechnical processes to achieve a more consistent operation.
Content: basic modelling principles - model linearisation - Laplace transform - transfer functions - state space models - process dynamics - feedback control - PID controller (design and tuning) - frequency response analysis - feedforward control - ratio control - cascade control
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Knowledge of basic process instrumentation - Linearise a non-linear system of differential equations - Solve linear differential equations using Laplace transforms - Convert a system of differential equations to transfer function and state-space notation - Represent a system as a block diagram - Design and tune a feedback controller - Design and tune a feedforward controller - Evaluate the stability of a system - Simulate a system with feedback/feedforward control
28725:
Name English: Bioprocess Unit Operations and GMP Exercises
Danish Title: Bioprocessenhedens operationer og GMP-øvelser
General Course Objectives: To bridge the gap between theoretical knowledge and practical application in the realm of (bio)chemical unit operations and good manufacturing practice (GMP) used in the chemical, biochemical and pharmaceutical industry. By engaging in experiments conducted on semitechnical and technical scales, students gain valuable insights into real-world operations and usage of GMP. Application of theoretical concepts on own generated data as well application of GMP guidelines shows their applicability, validity and limitations.
Content: This practical course includes 4 unit operation exercises and 3 Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) exercises which are performed in groups of 3 students. The unit operation exercises cover a full biomanufacturing process: Upstream fermentation exercise for all groups (2 full days) as well as 3 selected unit operations (1 day each) from the following downstream unit operations: Centrifugation, Homogenization, Rotary Drum Vacuum filtration, Ultrafiltration, Ultrafiltration with vibrating membrane, Protein purification with Ion Exchange Chromatography. The three GMP exercises include: I) a hygienic evaluation of one of the above used units. II) a cleaning in place (CIP) and sterilization in place (SIP) exercise, and III) an audit exercise with the aim of auditing a fictional biomanufacturing company using the previously used processing equipment according to EudraLex Vol 4 6 reports have to be handed in, which includes 4 reports from the unit operation exercises, were one includes the executed hygienic evaluation. The CIP/ SIP report contains results from the CIP exercise as well as the Sterilization in place (SIP) from the fermentation exercise. Finally, an audit report based on the audit roleplay with the fictional pharma producer has to be made. Overall, the course contains 6 mandatory physical exercise days, 4 days with classroom activities (e.g. introduction to exercises, audit roleplay). The rest of the time is reserved for exercise preparation and report writing.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain principles and main components of relevant unit operations for biomanufacturing - Recognize technical components on real life plants. - Evaluate cleanability and hygienic design of these components - Operate a pilot scale experimental setup, incl. data acquisition, control manipulation, and sampling. - Maintain good operating condition by monitoring critical process parameters - Analyze results and apply theory on practical experimental problems. - Formulate conclusions concerning the quality of the experimental data and applicability of the theory - Analyze a process operation’s conformity to GMP standards.
28755:
Name English: Process adaptation in Fermentation Based Biomanufacturing
Danish Title: Procesadaptering i Fermenteringsbaseret Bioproduktion
General Course Objectives: In a linear economy, resources are converted into products, and the products will eventually end up as waste. In a circular economy, products and materials are recirculated and waste is eliminated as much as possible. A circular economy combined with renewable energy should yield a more sustainable system. In a sustainability context, fermentation processes have the ability to convert renewable resources to useful products. Therefore, fermentation can be considered as one of the cornerstones of a greener and more circular economy. The main purpose of this course is to introduce students to the methods and tools that are available when transferring a cell from a lab or research environment to pilot and full scale. The student following this course should therefore acquire a better understanding of the interactions between the cells and the hardware (the reactor), and will learn how to aim for optimal conditions for the cells to grow in large scale. Topics such as in situ product removal (ISPR), solid state and gas fermentation, scale up/scale down of a fermentation process will also be highlighted as part of the course. Special attention will also be paid to acquiring essential digitalization and data handling skills. The lectures will be given by experienced DTU teachers, combined with guest teachers from industry. The course includes a visit to a large-scale fermentation facility.
Content: Elements included in this course are: • reactor designs (the hardware) and reactor operating modes • mass balances related to the different operating modes • suspended growth systems vs. immobilized growth systems (biofilms) • miniaturized reactor systems (high throughput fermentation) • scale-up and scale-down of a process • on-line sensors (both traditional and novel systems) and biosensors • basic bioreactor control concepts • on-line process control • introduction to computational fluid dynamics and compartment models • data (types of data, on-line versus off-line), proper handling of data • different ways to use the available data (estimate parameters in a mechanistic model, extract process knowledge) • basic concepts of artificial intelligence applied to fermentation data • solvent recovery • in situ product removal • biofuels and biorefineries • processes for converting waste into resources • industrial symbiosis principles
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Set up a mass balance for different bioreactor operating modes - Simulate different reactor operating modes and interpret the simulation results - Describe the effect of introducing basic process control on a process in a bioreactor - Describe the essential challenges related to solid state fermentations and fermentation processes using gaseous substrates - Select a suitable set of on-line measurements for a cultivation process, as well as distinguish between pros and cons of specific basic and advanced sensor devices - Describe the effect of scale on the performance of a microorganism, as well as pros and cons of different methods to mathematically describe or simulate effects of scale - Develop process based strategies to optimize product formation in a fermentation process - Distinguish between different downstream unit operations and evaluate the pros and cons of introducing in situ product removal (ISPR) on a specific process - Identify and evaluate opportunities for process retrofitting towards reduced environmental impact - Identify opportunities for industrial symbiosis; - Design and implement a basic strategy for collection and handling of data on a fermentation process - Distinguish between basic AI / machine learning tools for fermentation data processing;
28777:
Name English: Project management in applied industrial symbiose
Danish Title: Projektledelse i anvendt industriel symbiose
General Course Objectives: To plan, manage and execute a group project related to industrial symbiosis and technological innovation
Content: The participants are introduced to industrial symbiosis and in particular Kalundborg symbiosis who will provide project ideas for this course. Based on these ideas, the participants will analyze the proposed idea and the data foundation in order to select a specific project and scope it based in the relevant information, participants competences and the time constraint by the end of the first week. During the first period of the course, lectures in project management, and order relevant technical topics will be planed. During the week 2-5 the groups will execute and manage their projects with supervision from the course instructors and relevant corporate stakeholders. In the final week, the groups will disseminate the results in oral presentations and in a technical report with recommendations concerning future exploitation by the stakeholders.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the role of key project management tools - Design the scope and plan for project based on a openly defined idea - Perform and self manage a project in a group of students - Analyze and collect the relevant data and literature - Perform quantitative analysis to support you results - Describe key uncertainties affecting project results - Analyze techno-economic feasibility of the project idea - Suggest recommendation for future exploitation - Disseminate project results in an oral presentation and in a technical report
30410:
Name English: Antenna and microwave techniques
Danish Title: Antenne- og mikrobølgeteknik
General Course Objectives: The course aims to make the student understand the theories, methods, physical mode of operation, and the technical construction of the passive microwave components and antennas used in wireless systems.
Content: Short review of microwave systems for wireless communication, radar and radiometer applications. Repetition of transmission line theory. Analysis and synthesis of planar transmission lines and waveguides. Microwave network analysis for waveguiding systems. Impedance transformation and matching. Microwave resonators, power dividers and directional couplers. Antenna fundamentals and simple radiation systems incl simple antenna arrays. Wire and loop antennas. Broadband antennas (dipoles). Patch antennas.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - analyze and design transmission lines (rectangular waveguide, coaxial cables, microstrip, and stripline) and demonstrate knowledge of TEM, TE and TM waves - use S-, Z-, Y-, ABCD parameters for the analysis of microwave networks - design impedance matching circuits (discrete components, single and double stub, and quarter-wave transformer) - analyze and design microwave resonators (lumped element equivalents, TEM transmission line resonators, and cavities) and demonstrate knowledge of resonator coupling mechanisms - design power dividers and directional couplers and analyze symmetrical microwave networks using the even-odd mode excitation technique - understand antenna fundamentals and simple radiating systems incl. simple antenna arrays - analyze and design wire and loop antennas - analyze and design broadband dipoles (and other selected antennas) and associated matching techniques - analyze and design patch antennas using analytic approaches and commercial electromagnetic simulation software
34063:
Name English: Epitaxy: Principles and Applications
Danish Title: Epitaksi: Principper og Anvendelser
General Course Objectives: This course provides a foundational understanding of epitaxial growth processes and techniques and their role in semiconductor technology. The course is designed for both those looking to work directly in the field of epitaxial growth and those who will potentially collaborate with epitaxial foundries, equipping them with the knowledge to assess growth processes, understand growth limitations, interpret characterization data, and communicate effectively with fabrication facilities.
Content: This course provides an in-depth introduction to crystal growth, a fundamental pillar of modern semiconductor technology. Students will explore key epitaxial techniques, including molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) and metal-organic vapor phase epitaxy (MOVPE), while gaining insight into thermodynamics, growth kinetics, defect formation, and engineering of bandgap and strain. Topics also include the growth of low-dimensional nanostructures—such as quantum dots, quantum wells, and nanowires—along with selective epitaxy and the monolithic integration of III-V compound semiconductors on silicon. Through lectures, discussions of research papers, and case studies, the students will develop the skills to understand and analyze epitaxial processes, assess their impact on device performance, and communicate effectively with epitaxial research groups and fabrication facilities. The course is designed for both students pursuing careers in epitaxy and those collaborating with epitaxial groups and foundries in research or industry. By completing the course, the students will be equipped to critically assess epitaxial research, understand fabrication constraints, and design growth strategies for various applications in electronics and photonics.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Describe the fundamental principles of epitaxial growth and its role in semiconductor technology. - Compare key epitaxial techniques and evaluate their advantages and limitations. - Analyze the impact of defects, strain, and band bending on device performance. - Select appropriate epitaxial growth methods based on material requirements and application needs. - Evaluate limitations and constraints of epitaxial growth, considering the material system and application. - Critically analyze and evaluate research papers on epitaxial growth and identify key findings. - Identify appropriate characterization methods to evaluate different parameters of epitaxial materials. - Design an epitaxial growth process considering material properties, defects, and performance requirements.
34374:
Name English: IoT Hardware and PCB Design
Danish Title: IoT Hardware og PCB Design
General Course Objectives: The course provides students with hands-on experience in designing, developing, and preparing IoT hardware systems for production. Through project-based learning, students follow the full hardware development process, from concept and schematic design to PCB layout, and component selection. Key topics include power supply architecture, microcontroller integration, and designing interfaces for GPS and LoRa modules. Students will generate manufacturing files and learn practical workflows for building cost-efficient, low-power IoT devices ready for prototyping and production.
Content: The course introduces IoT hardware principles, covering fundamental concepts, architectures, and practical hardware considerations. It includes schematic design and printed circuit board (PCB) layout using professional CAD software Altium Designer. The course addresses critical aspects of IoT hardware development, including selection and integration of power management modules (e.g., LDO, buck converters, and battery management ICs), STM32 microcontrollers, and wireless communication modules (GPS and LoRa), focusing particularly on RF circuit design and impedance matching. Students gain practical experience in preparing PCB designs for fabrication, including creating essential manufacturing documentation (BOM, Gerber files). Students will engage in hands-on project work in groups, taking a concept through the entire IoT hardware development process. Practical exercises and tutorials are included to support project development. Evaluation is based on exercises completed during the course and a final technical report documenting the hardware design and development process. Students are expected to have basic knowledge of electronic circuits. No specific textbooks are required; course materials will be provided.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Describe the structure and fundamental components of IoT hardware systems. - Identify and select appropriate electronic components based on datasheets and application requirements. - Explain printed circuit board (PCB) anatomy, including layers, traces, vias, and pads. - Design schematic diagrams and PCB layouts using professional CAD software (e.g., Altium). - Evaluate and select suitable power supply architectures based on energy efficiency and application needs. - Integrate battery management ICs and battery protection circuits into IoT hardware designs. - Implement microcontrollers within custom PCB designs, considering peripheral requirements and low-power operation. - Implement hardware interfaces for GPS and LoRa modules, including impedance matching and RF considerations. - Generate and validate manufacturing documentation, including Bill of Materials (BOM) and Gerber files. - Document hardware design decisions clearly in professional technical reports. - Apply an end-to-end IoT hardware development workflow from initial concept through PCB production.
34603:
Name English: Electric circuits with alternating currents
Danish Title: Elektriske vekselstrøm kredsløb
General Course Objectives: Understanding and application of analog signals, components and their composition in alternating current circuits as well as their usage in applications
Content: Electric signals in alternating current circuitries in time and frequency domain, passive components in alternating current contexts, analog electrical circuits, transfer functions, and their applications (e.g. passive and active filters, amplifiers, motor drives, oscillator, power supplies)
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Reproduce different notations and parameters of alternating currents, voltage and power - Explain basic Fourier series - Calculate decibel and apply bode plot - Explain basic physical principles behind passive components (resistors, inductors and capacitors) - Determine properties of passive circuits, such as impedances and power - Apply basic LaPlace transformations and determine and analyse transfer functions - Analyse active alternating current circuitries - Link basic theoretical knowledge to practical applications - Demonstrate knowledge about technical terms also in English - Compare different simulation and measurement tools - Design solutions for realistic engineering problems under realistic working conditions for practicing engineers - Co-creation of all exercises and self-reflection on own learning and wellbeing in an engineering environment
34636:
Name English: Integrated analog electronics 1
Danish Title: Integreret analog elektronik 1
General Course Objectives: To enable the student to analyze and use analog amplifier circuits with the main emphasis on integrated circuits in CMOS technology.
Content: Amplifier stages, opamps, feedback
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Knowledge of large-signal and small-signal models for MOS transistors and being able to use these models in circuit calculations. - Analyze single-transistor amplifier stages realized with MOS transistors - Analyze differential stages realized with MOS transistors - Use multistage amplifiers realized with MOS transistors - Analyze circuits with negative feedback - Design a simple two-stage operational amplifier realized with MOS transistors - Analyse simple circuits for generating bias currents and voltages - Simulate CMOS integrated circuits using LTspice - Understand Danish as well as English electro-technical terminology - Be able to explain challenges in connection with practical implementation of MOSFET-circuits.
34765:
Name English: Digital Control
Danish Title: Digital Regulering
General Course Objectives: Students will develop an understanding of the relationship between continuous-time and discrete-time systems, learning fundamentals of digital control design for dynamic systems. The course covers Z-transform, various discretization methods and their effects. Students will also learn to select appropriate sampling periods, evaluate quantization effects, and implement, test, and debug digital controllers to assess their performance.
Content: This course covers key aspects of digital control of linear systems and fundamental theoretical concepts like difference equations and the Z-transform. It explores different discretization methods, their distinctions, and how they should be applied. The course also addresses sampling period selection and its impact on system performance. Additionally, it delves into the design of discrete-time controllers, including the conversion of continuous-time controllers into digital form and the practical implementation of digital controllers on computers. The course includes 10 lectures and 3 sessions for final project. The practical project will include programming in C++ (Arduino style).
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Compare continuous-time and discrete-time control approaches, understanding when digital control is advantageous. - Analyze digital control systems using discrete-time models. - Apply Z-transform techniques for system analysis. - Compare and apply different discretization methods (e.g., zero-order hold, bilinear transform) and their effects. - Design and analyze digital controllers using discrete-time equivalents of classical controllers (e.g., digital PID). - Select appropriate sampling periods based on system considerations. - Evaluate the influence of quantization. - Implement, test, and debug digital controllers and assess their performance.
41239:
Name English: Numerical Methods in Structural Mechanics
Danish Title: Numeriske metoder i konstruktionsmekanik
General Course Objectives: To enable the participants to understand and apply computational models for statically determinate and indeterminate elastic beam, frame, membrane and plated structures, including discretization of continuous models for finite element analysis. Furthermore, to make the participants able to operate a commercial Finite Element Method program for analysis of plane and spatial structures.
Content: The course concerns statically indeterminate elastic structures and analysis methods such as the Deformation/Stiffness Method and the Finite Element Method for plane and spatial structures, as well as application and training in the use of a commercial Finite Element Method (FEM) program within the civil engineering and naval architecture fields. The course has the following content: - The Deformation/Stiffness method for trusses and frames. - Distributed loads and equivalent nodal loads for bars and beams. - Element stiffness matrix for plane beam elements, 2D and 3D beam elements. - Transformation of elements in the plane. - Boundary conditions and symmetry conditions. - The Finite Element Method (FEM) - Basic plane and solid continuum element types (formulations, advantages and disadvantages). - Iso-parametric plane and spatial elements. - Equivalent nodal loads for plane and solid continuum elements. - Gaussian integration. - Stress determination and mesh distribution.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Apply the Deformation/Stiffness Method to solve simple beam, truss and frame problems by hand calculations. - Explain the assemblage of the global stiffness matrix and load vector for plane trusses and frames including accounting for boundary conditions. - Explain the equivalence between the Deformation/Stiffness Method and the Finite Element Method. - Use a mathematics program to analyze statically indeterminent truss and frame structures using the Deformation/Stiffness method. - Account for the interpolation functions for simple bar, beam and plane elements. - Account for the transformation of element stiffness matrices. - Account for the solution of the global finite element system. - Use a commercial finite element program to solve truss, frame, membrane and plate problems. - Perform convergence analysis for a finite element analyses. - Analyze and evaluate deformations and stress distributions in a commercial finite element program. - Critically evaluate the importance of the choice of element types, size and boundary conditions in finite element analysis. - Perform finite element analysis of selected applied structural design problems.
41348:
Name English: Internal combustion engines - theory for the application of conventional and renewable fuels
Danish Title: Forbrændingsmotorer - teori for anvendelse af konventionelle og bæredygtige brændstoffer
General Course Objectives: The goal of the course is to give the student knowledge of internal combustion engines and the ability to use the relevant calculation techniques for the construction and development of engines. Special emphazise will be put into explaining differences for engines applying conventional and renewable fuels.
Content: Parameters used to rate the performance of the engine in terms of specific power, efficiency and emissions are discussed. The link between engine performance and the need of a vehicle is exemplified. The fundamentals of combustion is followed by thermodynamic cycles utilizing the heat extracted from the combustion. Ideal Otto and Diesel cycles are followed by a realistic example. The resulting output torque is derived together with a discussion on engine mechanical balance. The fluid flow in the cylinder and the turbulence generated is discussed before combustion in Spark Ignition, SI, engine is explained in some detail. The uncontrolled combustion, knock, is also explained. Engine out emissions from SI engines are explained before the introduction of exhaust aftertreatment systems. The combustion with Compression Ignition (Diesel) is explained. Exhaust emissions and aftertreatment of the CI engine is introduced. The gas exchange system of two and four stroke engines is introduced. The usage of mechanical compressors and turbos is also explained. There will be experiments with a diesel engine in a test cell to evaluate the performance, efficiency and emissions. A basic engine simulation software will also be developed by the students.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Calculate basic parameters that are important to characterize the operation of an engine and analyze the effect of varying them on the performance and fuel economy - Calculate the needed engine size of a road vehicle reaching a given top speed and the effect of engine layout on vehicle fuel consumption per distance. - Determine stoichiometric ratio for regular and advanced fuels and evaluate the heating value of such mixtures. - Extract the engine specific emissions based on exhaust concentration measurements. - Assess the differences in specific performance (IMEP) and efficiency of ideal thermodynamic cycles like the Otto-cycle, Diesel-Cycle, Seiliger (pressure limited) cycle and Rankine-cycle. - Elaborate on the interaction between in-cylinder flow and combustion. - Use simple models to describe the combustion processes with conventional and sustainable fuels in Spark Ignition and Compression ignition engines. - Explain the principle of exhaust aftertreatment systems used for SI and CI engines. - Discuss the use of major parameters that govern the gas exchange process in two- and four-stroke engines. - Develop a simple mode for tuning of inlet and exhaust systems for two and four-stroke engines to maximize volumetric efficiency. - Assess the synergy of engine and turbos for optimum performance and efficiency.
41419:
Name English: Advanced Industrial Thermal energy Storage
Danish Title: Avanceret industriel termisk energilagring
General Course Objectives: This course addresses advanced thermal energy storage (TES) systems, providing students with specialized knowledge in their design, operation, and integration into industrial relevant applications. Advanced TES technologies include latent heat thermal energy storage, thermo-chemical energy storage, and Pumped Thermal Energy Storage (PTES). A fundamental focus of the course is on the TES properties, systems design, and dynamic operation, which together bridge the gap between micro- and macro-scale phenomena, linking fundamental TES behavior to system performance and economic viability. Through in-depth analysis, investigation and discussion, students will explore these multi-scale interactions, gaining a comprehensive understanding of the latest advancements in TES.
Content: This course covers Advanced Thermal Energy Storage (TES), from materials and components to technologies, followed by applications and integration in industrial systems. Modelling techniques will be introduced and employed (e.g. Python, EES or equivalent) for quantitative analysis and optimization. Students will collaborate on group projects, firstly involving design and evaluation of selected advanced TES solutions, and secondly on assessing the techno-economic feasibility and integration of such solutions. These projects will foster practical understanding and experience in the evolving field of TES. The course will cover the following content: Materials, components and models for Advanced TES: a) Liquid storage media b) Solid storage c) Dual Storage Media d) Latent heat Energy Storage e) Thermo-chemical energy storage f) Dynamic modelling for design and optimization of advanced TES components Applications and integration of Advanced TES: a) Industrial Storage Applications b) TES Systems for Equivalent Storage of Electrical Energy c) Power to Heat & Advanced TES d) Monetizing Thermal Energy Storage: Sources of Values, Value Stacking e) Forecasting models for control and operation of Advanced TES
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Analyze the thermophysical properties of various TES materials, including liquid, solid, and dual storage media - Evaluate the performance of advanced sensible, latent heat and thermo-chemical storage systems for industrial applications. - Develop algebraic-differential models for the simulation and optimization of TES components - Design advanced TES systems considering material selection, heat transfer mechanisms, and dynamic operation - Compare the efficiency and feasibility of different TES technologies for industrial applications - Optimize TES integration in industrial energy systems to enhance stability and efficiency - Apply forecasting models for optimal TES operation to improve system performance - Recognize emerging applications of machine learning (ML) to advanced thermal energy storage systems - Identify economic opportunities in TES through value stacking and monetization strategies - Critically evaluate TES lifecycle aspects, including scalability and cost-effectiveness - Interpret real-world data to assess TES performance under dynamic conditions - Formulate strategies to overcome technical and economic challenges in TES deployment in industry
41469:
Name English: Solar resource assessment and forecasting
Danish Title: Resourcevurdering og forudsigelse af solenergi
General Course Objectives: Students learn to quantify, analyze, and forecast the solar resource through ground-based measurements, satellite-derived datasets, numerical weather models, and empirical radiation models.
Content: Students learn the fundamental principles of solar radiation, including its components, geometry, variability, and spectral effects. They gain hands-on experience in measuring and quality controlling solar irradiance as well as using reanalysis and satellite-derived datasets. The course also equips students with skills to model and forecast solar irradiance, enabling applications in photovoltaic and solar heating system performance assessment, energy trading, grid integration, and utilization of solar energy in buildings.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the basic principles of solar radiation including components - Calculate sun position and apply empirical radiation models - Conduct irradiance measurements using pyranometers - Identify and critically apply irradiance data from different sources - Perform quality control of solar irradiance data - Determine the long-term average solar resource for a given location - Create forecasts of the available solar resource for a solar energy project - Identify and describe factors contributing to the uncertainty of solar resource measurements and forecasts
41750:
Name English: Composites Manufacturing
Danish Title: Fremstilling af kompositter
General Course Objectives: The overall objective of the course is to give the students insights into composite manufacturing for structural applications. The course will compare different manufacturing techniques (compression moulding, filament winding, pultrusion, vacuum infusion, additive manufacturing, etc.) with respect to their usage within automotive, aerospace, and wind energy application. Establishing the process-material-structure-property links will be a focus for composites with carbon/glass fibre reinforcements and thermosetting polymer matrix materials. The course will dive deeper into the vacuum infusion process, with analytical and numerical modelling of resin flow and the curing behavior. Further, thermo-mechanical modelling of the pultrusion and ultrasonic welding process will be used to predict deformations in components. Manufacturing quality assessment methods relevant for composite components will be introduced, and their application to improve effective manufacturing strategies will be discussed. Finally, the topics of sustainability, automation, and digitisation of composite manufacturing processes will also be covered. The course with combine theoretical descriptions with concrete calculation exercises and simulations using advanced commercial software.
Content: Intro to fiber reinforced polymer composites manufacturing; Constituent materials including future materials and bio-based materials; Applications and the evaluation of different approaches; Polymer (matrix) characterization and curing kinetics; Rheology, flow mechanisms during infusion and vacuum infusion for large scale applications; Post-manufacturing analysis and quality (defect detection and analysis); Sustainability in composite manufacturing; Intro to thermal stresses, 1D thermo-elasticity and analytic solutions; Intro to 3D thermo-elasticity and orthotropic materials; Intro to pultrusion and thermomechanical analysis; Curing induced stresses, residual stresses and springback effects; Process induced defects and multi-scale simulations of resin flow.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Describe the key principles involved in the manufacturing of composites by primary processes (such as vacuum infusion and pultrusion) and secondary processes (such as ultrasonic welding). - Explain the challenges associated with composite manufacturing processes, particularly for the manufacturing of wind turbine blades - Explain the concepts behind the relevant characterization methods (like Differential Scanning Calorimetry and Dynamic Mechanical Analysis, permeability and rheometry) for estimating material properties that are relevant during manufacturing processes. - Evaluate the significance of permeability, viscosity, pressure, temperature and other factors in the design of resin infusion strategies through hand-calculations. - Investigate and model the curing kinetics of resin for composite manufacturing. - Explain the concepts of thermal strains, thermal stresses and how volumetric strains (thermal, chemical) play together with classical elasticity theory as well as classical laminate theory - Apply numerical methods and analytical methods to calculate thermal stresses in processes like pultrusion and resin transfer moulding - Explain the importance of thermally induced residual stresses for the subsequent mechanical performance of manufactured parts - Evaluate and discuss the potential of various composite manufacturing techniques based on materials quality, scale, production volume, cycle times, sustainability, performance, and cost
41972:
Name English: Plated Steel Structures
Danish Title: Stål-pladekonstruktioner
General Course Objectives: The course aim at provide students with advanced knowledge of the analysis and design of steel structures, enabling them to handle advanced larger steel structures. In addition, the aim is to enable students to analyze strength and stability of various types of technically important plate structures made of steel and other metallic construction materials on a mathematical-physical basis, and to use this analysis expertise to analyze and dimension plate elements in steel structures such as bridges, buildings, ships, offshore and other industrial structures.
Content: 1) Unstiffened and stiffened plates: Differential equations, stiffness properties of stiffened plate panels, stress determination, boundary conditions, solution methods (Navier and Rayleigh-Ritz methods). Plates with large deflections. 2) Stability of plates: Analytical buckling solutions, the energy method, stiffened plates and the influence of imperfections. 3) Ultimate strength and failure mechanisms: Yield line theory, ultimate strength in compression for metallic plates. 4) Analysis and design of welds for large advanced steel structures. 5) Bending and stability of combined plate fields such as plate girders, bridge and ship cross-sections, including the influence of stiffeners and yield and supercritical load capacity. 6) Bending and stability of large lattice and jacket structures consisting of assembled bar and beam elements. 7) Fatigue-affected steel structures and fracture mechanics determination of fatigue life. 8) Design principles and practical application of both analytical methods and FEM analyses for structures within typical applications of steel structures such as bridges, buildings, ships, offshore and industrial structures.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the underlying assumptions for advanced analysis models, including plate theory for both unstiffened and stiffened plates. - Perform qualitative assessments as well as more detailed analysis of large advanced steel structures. - Perform analysis and design of advanced steel structures from practice, including formulating relevant boundary conditions for plate fields in larger plate structures. - Perform theoretical stress and deformation analyses of unstiffened and stiffened thin-walled plate structures using Navier's, Levy's and Rayleigh-Ritz methods. - Perform analysis and design of plate girders, including determination of post-critical capacity. - Analyze and dimension welds for large advanced steel structures. - Perform theoretical stability analysis of rectangular unstiffened and stiffened plates. - Account for ultimate strength of rectangular, laterally loaded unstiffened and stiffened plate structures. - Use a commercial FEM program to analyze and design both unstiffened as well as stiffened plate structures consisting of steel or alternative metallic materials. - Determine the fatigue life of large advanced steel structures. - Compare analytical, numerical and experimentally achieved results for a given plate structure and evaluate the quality of the results. - Write a technical report containing analysis including the above mentioned points applied on a practical design example from a bridge, building, ship, offshore or industrial structure.
41B06:
Name English: Structural Fire Safety Design
Danish Title: Konstruktionsbrandteknik
General Course Objectives: The students will build knowledge and skills to verify design and calculate load-bearing structures affected by high temperature in the form of fully developed and standard fire.
Content: The course content is divided in 4 main parts, one general on the structural background and fire action (0.) and three related to the application of the fire action to the structural design of: 1. steel, 2. timber, 3. concrete. 0. BACKGROUND ON FIRE AND STRUCTURE (1st module) Structural background: force, moment, reactions and cross-sectional forces. External and internal equilibrium equations. Stress, strain, elasticity (Hook's law). Moment of inertia and modulus of resistance of the element cross-section. Fire background: Meaning of flashover assumption in structural fire safety. Ventilation- and fuel-controlled conditions. Fire characteristics (Fuel load, ventilation factor, and thermal inertia), DK parametric fire, standard fire. Fire rating and resistance classes. Safety coefficients for load and mechanical properties in fire condition. 1. STEEL ELEMENT DESIGN (1st and 2nd module) Thermal properties of steel. Section factor. Lumped heat capacity method for the heating temperature of uninsulated steel. Insulating materials for fire protection of steel elements. Heating temperature of insulated steel under the assumption of thin insulation. Degradation of strength and stiffness of hot-rolled steel. Elastic and plastic design. Calculation of load bearing capacity of unprotected and fire-protected steel elements (verification) for beams and columns. Calculation of the min insulation thickness to sustain the imposed mechanical loads in fire (design) for beams and columns. Thermal expansion of steel, eigen-stresses and reduction of the capacity of columns with hindered thermal expansion. 2. TIMBER ELEMENT DESIGN (2nd module) Timber as combustible material. Firestorms and city fires. Timber as construction material. Charring of wood: charring temp. and charring rates. Degradation of timber mechanical properties. Cross-section reduction method and strength reduction method. Calculation of the load bearing capacity of timber beams and columns for parametric and standard fire (verification). 3. CONCRETE ELEMENT DESIGN (3rd module) Thermal properties of concrete. Type of concrete failures and examples of collapse. Hot and cold condition. Concrete temp. for mono- and bi-directional heating. Symmetry lines and equivalent fully exposed section for temp. calculation at any given time and depth of any concrete cross-section. Degradation of mech. properties of concrete and reinforcing steel. Permanent damage and residual strength. Damage factors (zone method) and use of CONFIRE. Calculation of load bearing capacity (verification) of concrete beams and slabs in bending. Transient strain and axially loaded columns with no or little eccentricity.

Name English: Marketing
Danish Title: Marketing
General Course Objectives: To provide participants with insight into the common methods and tools used in the preparation and implementation of a company’s entire marketing effort.
Content: Marketing is often regarded as an important discipline in consumer-focused companies, yet with an emphasis on running marketing campaigns. This course expands the scope of marketing and provides participants with insight into the common methods and tools used in the preparation and implementation of a company’s entire marketing effort. We will approach marketing from a strategic point of view. The emphasis will be on leveraging marketing assets to drive long-term business success and competitive advantage. Instead of focusing solely on short-term results like individual sales or campaign metrics, the emphasis is on building enduring competitive advantages. To achieve this, marketers have three primary strategic levers: product, brand and customer assets. Product assets represent the organization’s ability to create and deliver offerings (i.e., products and services) that generate value for customers and the firm. When managed strategically, product assets become renewable sources of differentiation and long-term growth. Brand assets represent the value that a brand contributes to a business, beyond its physical or functional offerings. These assets encompass the reputation, recognition, and emotional connection that a brand establishes with its audience. Strong brand assets differentiate a company in crowded markets and influence how customers perceive, trust, and engage with its products or services. Customer assets represent the relationships and value a company derives from its customers over time. Customer assets are the foundation of a company’s financial health and growth. Without loyal, engaged customers, even the strongest brand will struggle to succeed. In today’s dynamic market environment, focusing on product, brand and customer assets allows marketers to strategically allocate resources for maximum impact. By investing in these levers, businesses can not only drive short-term outcomes but also establish a foundation for long-term success. To understand the marketing discipline and the importance of the role that marketing and marketing assets plays in a company, the course focuses on the following central marketing areas: • Positioning marketing as a strategic process • Analyzing the marketing environment • Building brand assets through brand strategy • Developing a marketing program with a variety of marketing actions • Building customer assets through customer experience and success management • Implementing marketing strategies that leverage brand and customer assets
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Understand and apply the principles of creating and managing marketing assets - Capture and interpret market and customer insights, using qualitative and quantitative methods - Integrate marketing strategy with overall business and financial objectives to create sustainable, long-term value. - Analyze and design marketing programs that strengthen product innovation, brand equity, and customer relationships - Develop, evaluate and optimize marketing strategies and actions within an asset-based marketing system - Demonstrate strategic and analytical thinking in translating marketing insights into actionable growth and renewal plans - Evaluate and manage product, brand, and customer assets as strategic resources to build sustainable competitive advantage - Design and implement integrated marketing strategies that align positioning, brand building, and customer experience across markets and contexts

General Course Objectives: Molten salts are a versatile class of ionic compounds in liquid form often at elevated temperatures. They exhibit unique properties such as extraordinary solubility of many organic and inorganic compounds, superior thermal and radiolytic stability, high electrical and heat conductivity, and extremely low vapor pressures. Molten salts are hence an excellent engineering fluid for generation, conversion, and storage of sustainable energies. The course introduces the fundamentals of molten salts, including structure, chemistry, electrochemistry, physical properties, and materials challenges. It provides a multidisciplinary platform for understanding molten salt–based sustainable energy technologies, spanning energy generation (e.g., nuclear reactors) and energy storage and conversion (e.g., thermal energy storage, fuel cells, batteries, carbon capture, and Power-to-X). By the end of the course, students will have a comprehensive understanding of molten salts and related energy technologies and will be equipped to contribute to research and innovation in this dynamic field.
Content: The course consists of three modules: (1) fundamentals of molten salts, (2) energy conversion and storage technologies involving molten salts, and (3) nuclear energy technologies based on molten salts as liquid fuels, coolants, and reprocessing media. The course will start by introduction of chemistry, electrochemistry, and materials science of molten salts. Relevant molten salt technologies will be presented with respect to design, operation, principles, challenges, and sustainable perspectives, including nuclear reactors, fuel cells, batteries, thermal storage, and novel power-to-x processes. The course content is crossdisciplinary, engineering orientated, and fitting wide backgrounds of students.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the physicochemical and thermochemical properties of molten salts - Analyze thermodynamic and phase equilibria of molten salt systems - Explain redox behavior and electrochemical stability of materials and their applications - Describe techniques for handling and characterizing molten salts and related materials - Evaluate mechanisms of material corrosion and degradation in molten salts - Assess impact of radiation on molten salt chemistry, particularly in nuclear applications - Examine roles of molten salts in reactors, fuel processing and other energy technologies - Discuss molten salt applications in heat storage, batteries, and metal recycling - Explore emerging research areas and technological advancements involving molten salts
