MA675:
Name English: Mechanics
Danish Title: Mekanik
General Course Objectives: The overall aim of the course is to provide the student with an understanding of the fundamental principles of mechanics. This includes plane statics for statically determinate systems, Newtons Laws, and conservation laws for energy and linear momentum.
Content: Forces and couples. Plane equilibrium equations. Dry friction. Truss and frame structures. Distributed loads. Motion with constant and varying acceleration. Newton's 2nd law for planar/circular motion. Kinetic and potential energy. Conservation of energy. Work of non-conservative forces.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Draw free-body diagrams for planar mechanical systems and system parts with a clear indication of external forces and couples. - State and solve the static equilibrium equations for planar mechanical systems. - Identify dry friction forces (Coulomb friction) on bodies in static equilibrium or in motion. - Find forces in plane truss elements using the method of sections and the method of joints. - Identify statically equivalent concentrated loads for linear load distributions including water loads. - Solve kinematic problems for particle motion with constant and varying acceleration. - State and solve Newton's 2nd law for planar and circular motion of particles. - Find the kinetic energy of particles. - Find the work of forces and potential energy of spring and gravity forces. - Apply work-energy relations to particles affected by conservative and non-conservative forces.
MA681:
Name English: Materials science
Danish Title: Materialelære
General Course Objectives: The course provides a broad and general knowledge of materials. The course aims to give an understanding of how different materials are and what these differences mean for the mechanical properties and applications of the materials. The course highlights the relationship between the microstructure of the materials and their mechanical properties and provides insight into ways to change them. Insight will be gained into methods to select the most suitable materials for a given application and to meet given requirements and demands for a particular component, including using a material data base.
Content: The course treats materials generally with main emphasis on metals; polymers, ceramics, and composites are presented complementary. Focus is on the relation between manufacturing and processing of materials, their resulting internal structure and their mechanical properties and performance. The course contains: - atomic bonds, crystal structures, lattice defects, amorphous and semi-crystalline materials - phase diagrams, interpretation of these and calculation of mass fractions, phase equilibria, phase transformations and heat treatment of steel - changes in the microstructure of materials due to mechanical and thermal load - mechanical properties, testing and methods of changing the strength of metals, polymers and ceramics - cracks, fatigue failure, and protection against - introduction to material database software - method of selection of materials as well as application of a material index
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - define materials classes (metals, polymers and ceramics ) - describe principal types of bonding for different materials classes - recognize unit cells and crystal lattices in metals and simple ceramics - distinguish between the main types of polymers, ceramics and composite materials - interpret binary phase diagrams - calculate amounts of phases present in binary alloys in equilibrium - differentiate between the elastic and plastic behavior of metals, ceramics and polymers - relate strengthening mechanisms in metals to their internal structure - suggest heat treatment of steel for obtaining specified properties - predict failure of metals (creep, fracture, fatigue) - select appropriate materials for products based on their properties using materials selection software
MA911:
Name English: Mathematical Analysis and Modelling
Danish Title: Matematisk Analyse og Modellering
General Course Objectives: To provide the students with the ability to apply fundamental mathematical concepts and modern computer tools solving classical problems of engineering. The scope and form of the course supports application of the modelling circle aiming at the treatment of relevant problems within the different study lines. To enhance the digital formation and "computational thinking" of the students, modern computational tools (currently Maple) are introduced continuously throughout the course as a CAS-tool as well as a numerical tool. The teaching is organised with increasing taxonomical levels leading up to the subsequent course, 01922, Linear Algebra and Modelling.
Content: Complex numbers, polynomials, differential equations of order one and two, Taylor's formula for functions of one variable, approximation and numerical solution.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Carry out calculations with complex numbers including the complex exponential function, both by hand and using a computer. - Use polynomials with real and complex roots. - Do calculations with polynomials, both by hand and using a computer. - Solve simple differential equation of first and second order, both by hand and using a computer. - Use Taylor polynomials to approximate functions in one variable and solutions to differential equations. - Apply mathematics to solve simple engineering problems. - Apply the symbolic software-tool Maple to solve and graphically display mathematical/engineering problems. - Understand the difference between exact, approximated and numerical solution to differential equations and be able to evaluate and understand simple error estimates.
02280:
Name English: Artificial Intelligence and Multi-Agent Systems
Danish Title: Kunstig intelligens og multiagent-systemer
General Course Objectives: This course introduces students to advanced techniques within artificial intelligence (AI), with particular focus on automated planning and multi-agent systems. The objective of the course is to become able to explain, analyse and implement advanced AI techniques, to explore and present the latest research literature in the area, as well as to combine and develop novel AI techniques in a large software system.
Content: The course primarily focuses on topics within automated planning and multi-agent systems, but will also address other areas of AI (e.g. problem-solving by searching, knowledge representation and reasoning with logical agents). The programming project concerns the design and implementation of advanced AI techniques in a simulated multiagent environment. The programming project is very open-ended and invites for the development of your own algorithms and multiagent architectures. The project is carried out in groups, and should result in a working system and a video in which you present the system and its underlying algorithms and ideas in the style of research presentations at AI conferences. In addition to the programming project there will be a number of smaller assignments during the course. These assignments will give the students experience in doing video presentations within the areas of the course curriculum, and will assist in building up to the final programming project.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - describe a number of the most prevalent techniques in artificial intelligence and multi-agent systems - both in overall terms and on a detailed technical level - compare and assess the appropriateness of various AI techniques within automated planning and multi-agent systems for solving a given concrete problem - combine different AI techniques in a theoretically sound and practically useful way - apply a given AI technique to a given concrete problem - clarify the general complications and pitfalls involved in practical uses of AI techniques within automated planning and multi-agent systems - independently search for, read, and critically analyse research literature relevant to a specific AI project within automated planning and multi-agent systems - implement advanced AI techniques within automated planning and multi-agent systems in a large software system - orally communicate the content of recent research publications within automated planning and multiagent systems in a clear and technically precise manner - design and implement novel AI algorithms and solutions through the combination or extension of existing techniques - orally present developed AI algorithms and experimental results in the style of a scientific conference contribution
02820:
Name English: Explainable AI and user experience
Danish Title: Forklarbar kunstig intelligens og UX
General Course Objectives: Understand modern XAI methods, apply/evaluate them, and effectively communicate the outcomes to users. A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to:
Content: - Different types of XAI methods: feature-attribution methods (LIME, SHAP, gradient-based methods, LRP); visualization of latent spaces (e.g., t-SNE, UMAP), representational alignment (e.g., CCA, CKA). - Evaluation of the explanations, both the quality (how well they explain the model), and from the user’s perspective (how well they communicate the information). - Human-centered design principles, discoverability, user interface design and heuristic evaluation. - Designing and evaluating the outcome of user experiments. - Data ethics and human alignment.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - explain the motivations behind XAI: societal, ethical, regulatory, and practical; - apply explainability tools for machine learning models (e.g., LIME, SHAP, LRP, CAV); - evaluate explanations quantitatively and qualitatively (fidelity, stability, plausibility, comprehensibility); - critically assess the limitations and potential misleading aspects of explainability methods; - compare multiple explanation methods for the same model and dataset, identifying differences in fidelity and usefulness; - communicate explanations effectively to non-technical audiences (e.g., business, policy, or medical stakeholders); - design, execute and evaluate an experiment to assess XAI and interactions with target users; - communicate their results through both writing, oral presentation and critical discussion.
10406:
Name English: Numerical Simulation of Magnetised Plasmas
Danish Title: Numerisk simulering af magnetiserede plasmaer
General Course Objectives: The objective of the course is to provide students with an applied understanding of how magnetised plasmas are modelled and simulated numerically, with particular emphasis on fusion-relevant systems. The course introduces the hierarchy of models from fluid to kinetic descriptions and demonstrates how geometry, turbulence, heating, and sources are represented in numerical simulations. Through simplified and reduced models, the students acquire the ability to implement, analyse, and critically assess numerical simulations. The course provides a foundation for advanced work in fusion plasma physics, plasma turbulence, and numerical modelling of complex plasma systems.
Content: Numerical modelling of magnetised plasmas. Plasma model hierarchy: fluid, drift-reduced, kinetic and gyrokinetic descriptions. Numerical discretisation of partial differential equations. Single-fluid and resistive magnetohydrodynamics. Drift-reduced and two-fluid models. Plasma turbulence and transport diagnostics. Tokamak geometry, magnetic coordinates, and geometry-aware numerical schemes. Kinetic models including Vlasov and Particle-in-Cell methods. Conceptual introduction to gyrokinetic modelling. External heating and particle sources with emphasis on Neutral Beam Injection. Verification, validation, and uncertainty assessment in plasma simulations
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the hierarchy of plasma models and their domains of validity - Formulate fluid and reduced kinetic equations suitable for numerical simulation - Apply numerical discretisation methods to advection-dominated plasma equations - Describe how tokamak geometry and magnetic coordinates enter numerical models - Simulate reduced models of plasma turbulence and transport - Model external heating and particle sources, such as Neutral Beam Injection, in simplified form - Be able to use Verification and Validation techniques - Assess numerical results critically, distinguishing physical effects from numerical artefacts - Select appropriate modelling approaches for given physics problems
10415:
Name English: Nuclear Reactor Technology
Danish Title: Atomkraftteknologi
General Course Objectives: The course aims to provide the student with an overview of different nuclear reactor designs and their characteristics. The course discusses the current and the next generations of nuclear energy systems but focuses on the design and operation of Light Water Reactors, the most common type of commercial nuclear reactors operated today. We cover nuclear heat production, nuclear thermal-hydraulics, and thermodynamic conversion to electricity. The course introduces the principles of nuclear reactor safety and covers the various steps of the nuclear fuel cycle.
Content: Survey of commercial reactor types and common design characteristics, conversion of thermal energy to electricity, control and operation of reactor, coupling of the nuclear and the conventional islands of a power plant, reactor transient analysis, nuclear safety design, technical and policy aspects of the fuel cycle covering uranium supply, fuel fabrication, reprocessing and waste disposal.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Describe the main types of nuclear reactors and nuclear fuels, including future systems. - Describe the systems and operation of a Light Water Reactor (steam supply system, safety system, instrumentation and control systems). - Analyze reactor core designs and reactor core management. - Evaluate the risk of Pellet-Clad interaction based on linear power calculations. - Evaluate reactivity balance terms. - Formulate, analyze, and solve simple thermal-hydraulics problems. - Perform heat transfer calculations. - Reflect on reactor material degradation under thermal stress and irradiation. - Explain the basic principles of nuclear reactor safety. - Describe the nuclear fuel cycle, including the front and back end.
10869:
Name English: Experimental Methods and Instruments in Physics
Danish Title: Eksperimentelle Metoder og Instrumenter i Fysik
General Course Objectives: In this course you will learn to measure physical quantities as well as to design experiments in physics. The goal of the course is not to demonstrate specific physical laws, but rather to provide you with experimental and engineering skills to build an experimental setup yourself and design an experiment that can illuminate a physical law, where certain physical quantities are varied while others are measured. In the course, you will primarily use electrical and optical experimental methods.
Content: You will be introduced to methods, measurement principles and equipment through lectures and compulsory exercises, but will then under supervision spend most of the time on designing and building an experimental setup where electrical or optical measurements must be included. Before the experimental work, you must get together with 2-3 fellow students and form a group. You and your group must then use your setup to plan and carry out an experiment. You must use the last part of the course to analyze your data and document your experiment in a short and concise report, which will form the basis for the assessment.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Know and comply with safety procedures for work in the laboratory. - Explain specifications of the used equipment and ensure that the equipment is used appropriately without being damaged. - Use methods for digital data acquisition, and ensure that data is stored according to a specified data management plan according to DTU's recommendations. - Plan an experiment and build an experimental setup for carrying out the experiment, including choosing methods to control certain physical quantities and methods to measure the derived effects on other physical quantities. - Use instrument specifications and statistical methods to assess measurement capability and uncertainties. - Identify and eliminate noise and error sources, and assess their relevance in relation to the observed deviations. - Use sensors and transducers for precise control of physical quantities, including programming and setting a PID (Proportional-Integral-Derivative) control to control a system. - Use both DC and AC measurement methods, and be able to record and analyze measurement data in both the time- and the frequency domain. - Be able to present raw data and analyzed data in informative graphs and tables with an indication of uncertainties. - Describe the used experimental methods, experimental conditions and used equipment in sufficient detail, so that the experiment can be repeated by peers - Document the experimental setup with sketches and images. - Summarize the work in a short and concise report, where the experiment and results are presented, and the report generally appears aesthetically appealing, i.e. well worked through and with a homogeneous layout.
10960:
Name English: Natural Science (Polytechnical Foundation - B.Eng.)
Danish Title: Naturvidenskab (Polyteknisk grundlag - diplom)
General Course Objectives: The course Natural Science introduces students to the fundamental principles underlying modern engineering, with a particular focus on energy, modeling, and the understanding of physical systems. Through an integrated approach combining mechanics, thermodynamics, electromagnetism, and elements of chemistry and biotechnology, students develop a coherent understanding of how energy is produced, converted, transported, and stored in technical systems. Students work with core concepts such as forces, motion, work, energy, and power, and use Newton’s laws and energy conservation as a foundation for analyzing physical systems. The course also introduces electrical and magnetic phenomena, as well as thermodynamic processes, including heat pumps, heat engines, and energy storage in chemical bonds. These fundamental principles are linked to modern technologies such as wind power, batteries, fuel cells, and Power-to-X. A key objective of the course is to develop students’ ability to approach scientific problems quantitatively and critically. Students learn to apply SI units, dimensional analysis, and Fermi estimation to assess orders of magnitude and model real-world systems. In addition, Python and generative artificial intelligence are used as tools for data analysis, computation, and problem solving. The course emphasizes both conceptual understanding and practical skills, enabling students to analyze and evaluate energy-related challenges within an engineering context.
Content: Introduction to basic concepts in natural science centered around energy, i.e., mechanical, thermodynamic, electromagnetic, and chemical energy.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Describe the function of energy production and storage systems such as hydropower, wind power, nuclear power, bioreactors, batteries, fuel cells, and Power-to-X. - Analyze energy flows and energy storage in technical systems and explain how energy is converted between mechanical, electrical, thermal, and chemical forms. - Apply SI base units and dimensions, and perform Fermi calculations to estimate orders of magnitude in scientific and engineering problems. - Apply core concepts in mechanics such as position, velocity, acceleration, forces, work, energy, and power. - Apply and analyze physical systems using Newton’s laws, the work–energy principle, and conservation of energy. - Explain magnetic fields and magnetic forces acting on charged particles. - Explain and analyze the conversion between electrical and mechanical energy in technical systems. - Apply the ideal gas law and explain and use the first and second laws of thermodynamics, including energy storage in chemical bonds. - Explain simple thermodynamic processes and the operation of heat pumps, heat engines, and refrigeration systems. - Explain energy relationships in chemical and biochemical reactions. - Use Python to analyze and solve physical problems, including the use of generative artificial intelligence.
10961:
Name English: Data (Polytechnical Foundation - B.Eng.)
Danish Title: Data (Polyteknisk grundlag - diplom)
General Course Objectives: The course Data introduces students to experimental work and data processing as central elements of the engineer’s toolkit. Although the course focuses on data, the experimental aspect is at its core: students learn to investigate physical problems through measurements, analyze their results, and critically assess the quality of both data and models. Through planning and conducting small-scale experiments, students gain experience in selecting measurement methods, identifying relevant variables, and controlling influencing factors. They work systematically with measurement uncertainties, including the distinction between random and systematic errors, as well as how uncertainties are quantified and propagated through calculations. At the same time, statistical methods and regression analysis are introduced as tools for describing and evaluating relationships in data. The course integrates programming in Python as a key tool for handling and analyzing data—from data import and structuring to visualization and modeling. Students learn to compare experimental results with theoretical models, assess the validity of these models, and apply data-driven methods to estimate physical parameters. Emphasis is placed on developing a critical and reflective approach to experimental work, where students not only acquire technical skills but also gain an understanding of data quality, methodological choices, and the limitations of models. The course thereby supports the ability to work systematically and investigatively with real-world problems in an engineering context.
Content: Introduction to data; generation, collection, filtering, and treatment. Estimating uncertainties and computing with numbers with uncertainties. Data analysis of experimental data. Planning and execution of smaller and larger experiments.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Apply and evaluate measurement uncertainties, including the use of uncertainty propagation and statistical methods for determining uncertainties. - Assess variation in repeated measurements and distinguish between random and systematic uncertainties. - Plan and carry out small-scale experiments, including selecting measurement methods, collecting data, and comparing results with theoretical models. - Design experiments to address specific physical questions, including identifying relevant variables and controlling influencing factors. - Use Python to import, structure, filter, transform, analyze, and visualize data. - Perform regression analysis and evaluate model quality, including residuals and validity range. - Assess agreement between models and data, taking uncertainties into account. - Apply symbolic and numerical methods to solve equations and simple differential equations in the context of data modeling. - Organize, represent, and communicate experimental data in tables, graphs, and short technical reports. - Reflect on data quality, measurement methods, and the limitations of models in experimental investigations. - Apply data-driven methods to estimate physical parameters from experimental measurements.
22170:
Name English: Value Creation in Pharma and Biotechnology
Danish Title: Værdiskabelse i farma- og bioteknologi
General Course Objectives: The course equips students with the competencies needed to translate scientific innovation into strategic and commercial value in industry. While the course is grounded in the pharma and biotechnology sector, it is open to all students who want to understand how business value can be created from scientific discoveries and inventions. Students learn to assess the strategic, market, intellectual property, and financial dimensions of a new discovery or idea, and to develop a structured plan for its implementation and commercialization. The course is particularly relevant for students considering a career at the intersection of science and business, whether being in a commercially-oriented role, as a start-up founder, or applying business thinking in research.
Content: Value Creation: stakeholder, shareholder and societal value impact of innovation, value creation versus value capture. Competitive strategy: industry structure analysis, Porter’s Five Forces, the technology S-curve, and first-mover versus late-mover advantages in pharma and biotech markets. Intellectual property rights: types of IP protection, patentability requirements in pharma and biotech, patent lifecycle, freedom to operate, and strategic choices between patenting and trade secrecy. Game theory: strategic interaction, Nash equilibrium, sequential games, patent races, pay-for-delay agreements, and coordination in IP-intensive industries. Pricing strategy: value-based pricing, willingness to pay, market segmentation, and pharma-specific pricing approaches, including sequential skimming and access pricing. Market sizing: TAM/SAM/SOM framework, epidemiology-based sizing, and revenue forecasting for pharmaceutical products. Financial valuation: net present value, discounted cash flow analysis, drug asset valuation, and an introduction to deal structures for commercialization, including licensing and spin-out. Group project: students work in groups to develop an implementation plan for a selected pharma or biotechnology innovation or discovery.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - analyze the competitive landscape of a pharma, biotech, or bioinformatics market using established strategic frameworks - assess whether a new discovery meets the criteria for patent protection and identify an appropriate IP strategy. - analyze strategic interactions in pharma, biotech, and bioinformatics markets using strategic game theory, including patent races, licensing negotiations, and market entry decisions. - estimate the commercial potential of a new discovery using market-sizing and revenue-forecasting methods. - evaluate the financial value of a drug asset or innovation project using discounted cash flow analysis. - compare and justify a commercialization pathway for a pharma, biotech, or bioinformatics innovation, considering, for example, licensing and spin-out as alternative routes. - develop a structured implementation plan that integrates scientific, strategic, and financial contributions into a coherent written deliverable. - collaborate effectively in a multidisciplinary group throughout the project development process. - use AI tools as a thinking partner to support strategic and commercial analysis, and critically evaluate AI-generated outputs before incorporating them into a business case or implementation plan.
22181:
Name English: Design Build for PK/PD Controlled Drug Testing: Infection-on-Chip
Danish Title: Design Build for PK/PD Kontrolleret Drug Testing: Infektion-on-Chip
General Course Objectives: This course provides students with foundational knowledge of bacterial infections and infectious diseases, as well as basic principles of pharmacokinetics (PK) and pharmacodynamics (PD) for antimicrobial therapy. In parallel, students will design and build a microfluidic device that supports bacterial biofilm production. The device will be used to study antimicrobial treatments using dosing regiments that approximates human PK/PD profiles. The prototype instrument will enable real-time data acquisition and treatment modeling.
Content: This course builds on the problem-based engineering and prototyping skills developed in the course Design-build in Life Science (22180) and focuses on applying them to PK/PD-controlled infection-on-chip experiments. Background knowledge on bacterial infection biology, PK/PD principles and microfluidic systems will be provided through lectures that deliver the theoretical foundation for the projects. Microfluidic chip technology allows mimicking physiological drug exposure and infection conditions. The prototype will be built around an infection-on-chip microfluidic chip, which allows controlled flow and transport conditions, enabling different drug delivery strategies. It will integrate pump control for drug mixing and treatment delivery, combined with sensor-based monitoring such as cameras and optical sensors to enable real-time monitoring of bacterial growth and eradication throughout the experiment. A microcontroller will be employed to acquire real-time data using basic scripting.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - explain biofilm formation and bacterial growth dynamics during infection. - describe essential PK and PD concepts and how they apply to antimicrobial efficacy. - design and build a microfluidic chip device simulating drug delivery. - grow bacterial cultures and apply antibiotic treatment in a microfluidic chip. - analyze experimental data obtained from the microfluidic device to quantify drug efficacy using PK/PD principles. - investigate scientific problems related to antibiotic efficacy during bacterial infection. - use Generative AI with effective prompting to evaluate and improve prototype designs. - present and critically analyze their design rationale, prototype implementation and experimental findings in an oral presentation.
22214:
Name English: Technologies in Translational Neuroscience
Danish Title: Teknologier i Translationel Neurovidenskab
General Course Objectives: The objective of the course is to give engineering students the neuroscience foundation needed to approach problems related to the nervous system. Through examples from current research, the course shows how relevant neurobiological and physiological knowledge is identified, which experimental parameters are important for a given question, and how methods used in neuroscience can be applied to generate meaningful data. The aim is not to provide full training in neuroscience, but to enable students to recognise what they need to know in order to define and approach an engineering problem in this field.
Content: The course introduces physiological and pathophysiological principles that motivate technological development in translational neuroscience. Headache and migraine are used as examples of research themes to illustrate how neurovascular and sensory mechanisms can be investigated with advanced experimental methods. Students work with research articles and case-based material to examine how neuroscience research defines mechanistic questions and how experimental approaches are selected to investigate them. Through these cases, students learn how to identify what is known about a given biological problem, which neurobiological mechanisms are relevant, and which physiological parameters must be measured in order to study them. Students are introduced to experimental methods currently used in translational neuroscience research, including electrophysiological recordings, approaches for measuring neuronal and neurovascular activity, and quantitative biochemical assays for neuropeptides and proteins. These methods are discussed in relation to the biological information they generate and the mechanistic questions they address. Clinical research paradigms conducted in hospital-based settings are included to illustrate how human experimental models are structured and how physiological and biochemical outputs are obtained. RNA-based modulation tools and rational peptide design strategies are introduced as examples of molecular approaches used to manipulate gene expression and receptor systems relevant to neuronal and neurovascular signalling. Genomic and registry based data systems are examined to illustrate how large scale datasets capturing genetic variation, gene regulation, and molecular profiles contribute to mechanistic understanding of disease related processes. During the course, students visit at least one research environment where experimental methods used in translational neuroscience are demonstrated in practice, allowing them to observe how measurement technologies and experimental workflows are implemented in active research.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Describe the neurobiological, physiological and molecular mechanisms that are relevant when approaching engineering problems related to the nervous system. - Identify key physiological parameters and biological processes that must be understood in order to define a measurable neuroscience problem. - Explain how electrophysiological systems and biochemical assays are used to quantify neuronal and neurovascular activity in experimental models. - Describe how controlled experimental paradigms in patients are structured to probe disease relevant mechanisms. - Explain how RNA based tools and rational peptide design strategies are applied to modulate and study biological responses in experimental systems. - Analyse how genomic data, and registry infrastructures generate large scale datasets that can inform mechanistic questions in neuroscience. - Evaluate scientific studies with focus on how appropriate technologies are selected, applied, and integrated to address specific biological questions. - Formulate an experimental approach in which relevant physiological knowledge, measurement technologies, and data analysis strategies are combined to address a defined problem in translational neuroscience. - Use generative artificial intelligence tools to obtain background knowledge in a neuroscience topic, critically evaluate the accuracy and limitations of the generated information against scientific literature and assess how such tools can support the rapid acquisition of prerequisite knowledge when approaching a new problem in neuroscience.
22240:
Name English: CRISPR engineering of mammalian cells
Danish Title: CRISPR modificering af mammale celler
General Course Objectives: The goal is to provide students with practical and theoretical knowledge and competencies in state-of-the-art mammalian cell engineering. The course integrates advanced CRISPR-Cas modalities, gene editing design and analysis, and phenotypic/genotypic validation to foster autonomous therapeutic problem-solving.
Content: The course is structured into three interconnected parts that build progressively from theory to hands-on application to autonomous design. In the first part of the course, students are introduced to the theoretical foundations of genetic engineering in mammalian cells. This covers nuclease systems and precision editing strategies, including gene knockout, homology-directed repair, base editing, and prime editing. Topics also include DNA repair pathways, off-target effects, transient gene regulation, and delivery systems for mammalian cells, with emphasis on their relevance in biotechnology and medicine. In the second part of the course, students gain hands-on experience with a mammalian cell editing workflow. Using a cultured cell model, students perform co-transfection experiments to generate targeted genomic changes and analyse the outcomes at both phenotypic and genotypic levels. This includes genomic DNA extraction, target amplification, flow cytometry, and interpretation of Sanger sequencing data using sequence deconvolution tools to quantify editing efficiency and repair outcomes. In the third part of the course, running in parallel with the taught modules and laboratory work, students undertake a semester-long Therapeutic Design Project. This problem-based learning initiative requires students to autonomously model a genetic intervention for a defined monogenic pathology, integrating domain-specific predictive machine learning models (e.g., inDelphi, AlphaFold) to forecast DNA repair outcomes and protein structural alterations. By the end of the course, students will be equipped to independently design, execute, and critically evaluate CRISPR-based genetic engineering strategies in mammalian cells, bridging the gap between laboratory experimentation and therapeutic application.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Evaluate and select appropriate precision genetic engineering modalities (e.g., high-fidelity Cas9, Base Editing, Prime Editing) for disease correction. - Design in silico guide RNAs and homology-directed repair (HDR) templates, mitigating off-target effects and PAM constraints. - Apply domain-specific machine learning algorithms (e.g., DeepSpCas9, inDelphi, AlphaFold) to predict DNA repair outcomes and protein structural alterations, critically evaluating the computational predictions. - Execute co-transfection protocols in mammalian cell cultures to induce targeted genomic alterations. - Quantify phenotypic shifts using flow cytometry and establish gating strategies. - Isolate genomic DNA, execute target amplification, and deconvolute Sanger sequencing chromatograms using algorithmic tools (ICE/TIDE/CRISPResso) to quantify editing frequencies. - Formulate tissue-specific delivery strategies (AAV, Lipid Nanoparticles) considering payload constraints and immunogenicity. - Navigate regulatory frameworks (EMA/FDA) for Advanced Therapy Medicinal Products (ATMPs). - Critically analyse discrepancies between in vitro laboratory proxies and theoretical therapeutic designs.
22286:
Name English: 3D printing of soft matter and living tissue (bioprinting)
Danish Title: 3D print af bløde materialer og levende væv (bioprint)
General Course Objectives: 3D printing technologies are opening new possibilities within biomedical engineering and research. Additive manufacturing methods are particularly well suited for shaping soft, water-rich, and dynamic materials that resemble human tissues. In addition, printing with living human cells - known as 3D bioprinting - enables the direct fabrication of engineered biological tissues. Together, these approaches are becoming integral across numerous areas of biomedical engineering, from preclinical research and stem cell–based therapies to advanced surgical applications. This course will introduce you to the fundamental principles of key 3D printing methods for biomedical engineering, focusing on soft and living matter. You will gain hands-on experience with selected 3D printing methods, and learn the strengths and weaknesses of: · Extrusion-based (bio)-printing, including direct-ink-write and embedded printing · Light-based printing, including stereolithography and two-photon polymerization
Content: In the first part of the course, we will introduce the theoretical foundation for extrusion-based and light-based 3D printing. This will cover chemical and physical principles, as well as compatibility with living cells. The second part will provide hands-on experience with key steps and 3D printing using light-based and extrusion-based 3D printing, based on structured exercises. In the third and last part of the course, students will formulate their own 3D printing ink and print codes toward replicating a specific tissue architecture. NB: Due to the practical nature of the course, participation in exercise sessions is mandatory
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Describe the basic working principles of extrusion-based 3D printing methodologies, including their chemical, physical, and rheological requirements. - Describe the basic working principles of light-based 3D printing methodologies, including their chemical, physical, and rheological requirements. - Discuss advantages and limitations of extrusion-based and light-based 3D printing methods - Analyze rheological data to evaluate the physical properties of print materials, before, during and after printing. - Formulate biomaterial inks for extrusion-based and light-based 3D printing. - Generate and modify print-files using CAD design software, slicers and generative AI. - Discuss the requirements for printing and culturing living cells and tissue. - Evaluate the feasibility of using 3D printing for replicating specific architectures in living human tissue.
22514:
Name English: Optical instrumentation design for biomedical engineers
Danish Title: Design af optiske instrumenter til biomedicinske ingeniører
General Course Objectives: Optical sensing has become a cornerstone of modern bioscience and medicine since light can probe biological systems non-invasively, with high sensitivity and high spatial and/or temporal resolution. Optical sensors use light-matter interactions to detect and quantify biological processes. The aim of this course is to support students to design optical sensors or instruments to measure quantities relevant to biosensing and healthcare applications. Each unit will be motivated by a real-world example. We will introduce design process frameworks such as the V-model and double diamond model, and discuss how user needs drive the innovation process. Students will apply concepts including the design and construction of an optical instrument, reading and analyzing data from their instrument, and interpreting the biological relevance of their results.
Content: The course covers a range of topics necessary for the successful design of instruments that use optical principles to measure physical quantities. In this hands-on course, you will complete three well-defined laboratory exercises in groups of 3-4 students to learn about how to develop and use optics-based instrumentation. Each exercise will be linked to an instrument currently in widespread use in biology or medicine. Where possible, external speakers will present the relevance of the experiments to their active research work. After each exercise, student will communicate their results in both written and oral reports. Some examples of lab exercises could be: 1.Build a pulse oximeter/PPG and use your device to measure your heart rate and blood oxygenation 2.Measure the size of objects using the diffraction pattern, as is done in flow cytometry 3.Build a simple spectrometer and measure the absorption spectrum of several solutions to identify their composition, as is used for blood analysis 4.Design and build a smartphone-based endoscope using an imaging fiber bundle and characterize its performance
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - use a design process framework such as the v-model or the double-diamond model to specify design requirements for an biomedical engineering project. - describe basic optics principles and light-tissue interactions, e.g., absorption, scattering, diffraction, and how these affect our ability to use optics for measurement of biologically relevant quantities. - design life science instruments which use optics principles to measure clinically- and biologically relevant physical quantities. - construct and align an optical instrument. - calculate optical attenuation through a sample. - measure the size of objects from a diffraction pattern. - analyze the biological relevance of measured quantities. - use generative AI to critically analyze the outcomes of an experiment. - apply statistical analysis such as error propagation to assess the reliability of their experimental results. - communicate scientific results in both a technical and a non-technical format.
22531:
Name English: Ionizing radiation protection and safety
Danish Title: Strålebeskyttelse og sikkerhed
General Course Objectives: After this course, the student will be able to make simple dose assessments for a range of exposure situations. This solid technical understanding is of particular importance when designing radiation protection measures for new activities involving ionizing radiation and for understanding regulatory requirements related to such activities.
Content: Ionizing radiation plays an important role in a wide variety of applications within nuclear energy production, health applications, space exploration, waste management, and science and industry in general. As exposure to ionization radiation can induce both cancer and acute effects in humans, it is important to have a good understanding of these risks. This knowledge is important for people working directly with ionizing radiation, for the general population that potentially may be exposed also, and for authorities that regulate this field or that provide emergency assistance in case of accidents. This course therefore establishes a fundamental understanding of the chain of physical, chemical, and biological processes involved, combined with the terminology and framework of current radiation protection regulations as recommended by the International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP).
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - apply the basic atomic and nuclear physics relevant for radiation protection computations involving electrons, protons, photons and neutrons. - explain the main radioactive decay modes and apply data from isotope databases relevant for radiation protection assessments. - analyze irradiation situations using key dosimetric concepts like activity, fluence, kerma, charged particle equilibrium, absorbed dose, equivalent dose, effective dose, and committed and collective dose quantities. - explain the key concepts of microdosimetry and perform simple computations using restricted stopping powers and linear energy transfer (LET) coefficients. - explain methods for ionization radiation detection and radiation protection measurements and how such instruments are calibrated to obtain metrological traceability. - describe key aspects of the radiation environments (natural and man-made) and radiation protection issues found in nature (including indoor radon), health (including nuclear medicine, radiotherapy and diagnostic radiology), nuclear energy production and research (including criticality), air travel, space and industry (including radiation processing). - compute doses to humans from given internal and external sources of ionizing radiation. - compute cancer risks for the workers and the general population from given doses of ionizing radiation. - explain how ionizing radiation can lead to ozone production and functional changes of plastics and semiconductors. - apply the key radiation protection concepts of justification, optimization and dose limits for planned exposure situations (e.g., nuclear facilities and medical uses), emergency exposure situations (e.g., accidents) and existing exposure situations (e.g. indoor radon) as recommended by the International Commission on Radiological Protection in ICRP publication 103. - analyze and communicate basic radiation protection requirements, vulnerability analyses, and risk assessments related to selected cases at a level where the student can engage in technical discussions with regulators, co-workers, and the general public. - demonstrate ability to critically assess the output of generative AI applications in radiation protection assessments.
23103:
Name English: Microbiological food safety in production chains
Danish Title: Mikrobiologisk fødevaresikkerhed i produktionskæder
General Course Objectives: The course will enable you to evaluate relevant microbiological hazards in food production chains. You will relate important microorganisms to their possible roles in spoilage and diseases that can be transmitted through the food chain to humans. Furthermore, you will use predictive microbiology tools to determine shelf life and develop safe products. As part of a group project assignment, you will conduct a hazard analysis and formulate a hazard control plan, which covers the raw materials, production methodologies and unit operations for a given food production chain.
Content: The course will provide in depth coverage of current and relevant food safety issues regarding microbiological hazards. The course presents relevant microbiological hazards in the entire food production chain from farm to fork. The course will enable you to evaluate relevant microbiological hazards in specific food production chains, to identify critical steps in the production line, and to construct a hazard control plan to control or mitigate these hazards. The course will introduce predictive microbiology approaches to assess the safe shelf life and predict effects of product redesigns. You will work with the topics through lectures, assignments, and group/project work.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Describe and analyze a food production chain with regards to potential issues of microbial food safety and spoilage - Identify relevant microbiological hazards for a given food production - Identify steps in the production chain that are critical with regard to microbiological hazards including current food safety legislation - Identify key elements of microbiological hazard analysis - Obtain relevant information from databases and literature on microbial responses in food - Apply predictive microbiology for safe shelf life determination, product development and control measure evaluation - For a given food product create a microbiological hazard analysis method in the food production chain - Explain the concept of food sampling schemes - Establish measures that will control the safety of the product (apply HACCP principles) - Assemble a concise written report that covers the design of a hazard control plan for a given food product
23104:
Name English: Chemical Food safety in production chains
Danish Title: Kemisk Fødevaresikkerhed i produktionskæder
General Course Objectives: The course will enable the student to evaluate relevant chemical hazards in food production chains.The student will relate important chemical hazards to their possible health risks in the food chain to humans. This will include calculation and evaluation of the occurrence of chemical hazards in foods using relevant data. Through a project assignment, the student will assemble a chemical risk assessment and write a report, which covers chemical hazards, the raw materials, production methodologies for a given food product.
Content: The course will cover current and relevant food safety issues with regards to chemical hazards. The course presents relevant chemical hazards in the entire food production chain from farm to fork and includes chemical aspects of the risk assessment. The course will enable the students to evaluate relevant chemical hazards in specific food production chains, to identify critical steps in the production and establish measures that will control the chemical safety of the food product, including management of allergenic foods. The student will work with the topics through lectures, assignments, and group/project work.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Describe and analyze a food production chain with regards to potential issues of chemical food safety - Identify relevant chemical hazards for a given food production system - Identify steps in the food production chain that are critical with regard to the chemical hazards including current food safety legislation - Identify key elements of chemical risk analysis - Apply chemical exposure assessment and risk characterization to a given product including alternative evaluations when the data is lacking - Explain food allergy and manage allergenic food in a given production - For a given food product create an assessment of chemical hazards in the food production chain from farm to fork - Identify and evaluate potential food fraud opportunities in the raw materials and the production chain - Establish measures that will control the chemcial safety of the food product - Assemble a concise written report that covers the formulation of a chemical risk assessment
23303:
Name English: Fundamentals of sustainable food packaging
Danish Title: Grundprincipper i fødevareemballage
General Course Objectives: This course provides an introduction to sustainable food packaging, covering fundamental principles of materials and food science, technologies, environmental and innovation assessment. Packaging decisions impact food quality, shelf life, and the environment, requiring a balance of food safety, environmental concerns, and technological needs. Students will learn to analyze packaging challenges, based on the above, and investigate solutions that could be used in future-proof packaging concepts with real-world relevance. The pedagogical approach prioritizes student-centered, problem-driven learning, ensuring that students contribute actively to the course's direction and depth. Through group projects and presentations, students will demonstrate their practical understanding and application of sustainable food packaging concepts.
Content: Through lectures, exercises, and group work, this 13-week course will cover fundamental principles of materials and food science, technologies, environmental and innovation assessment regarding sustainable food packaging. Students will work in groups, on problem-driven projects, to design future-proof packaging concepts that integrate core concepts learned over the course. The students will present the knowledge gained during the course in a poster and in a written group report.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Define key concepts related to sustainable food packaging, including materials science and technology, food safety, and environmental impact. - Explain how packaging decisions influence food quality, shelf life, and sustainability. - Apply principles of food science and materials technology to evaluate packaging solutions for different food categories. - Analyze packaging challenges by assessing trade-offs between food safety, environmental concerns, and technological feasibility - Evaluate existing packaging technologies and materials for their sustainability and real-world applicability. - Formulate innovative, future-proof packaging concepts that integrate environmental responsibility and consumer needs. - Collaborate with problem-driven group projects to develop practical solutions for sustainable packaging. - Present findings and proposed solutions effectively through oral and written (group report) presentations, demonstrating applied knowledge and critical thinking.
23721:
Name English: Hygienic design in the food industry
Danish Title: Hygiejnisk design i fødevareindustrien
General Course Objectives: Enable the students to evaluate and design processing facilities and equipment for food production and preparation, which meet legislative requirements as well as standards and guidelines for hygienic design.
Content: The objective of hygienic design of processing equipment and unit operations is to ensure high quality and safe food products, optimal processing times and total runtime of a process line. The course will deal with design of processing equipment and process lines from the hygienic design point of view with respect to material choices and structures based on existing laws, rules, norms and guidelines. The following are examples of topics which will be covered in the course: • Legislation and guidelines for hygienic design, • Good and inappropriate equipment designs in both open and closed processing systems, • Methods to characterize surface structures (topology) and to test equipment cleanability, • The impact of construction materials and structures on the hygienic quality, e.g., cleanability of surfaces (stainless steel, weldings, polymers and elastomers), • Corrosion types seen in the food industry and overview of material types most commonly used, • Efficiency of cleaning agents and cleaning methods including fluid flows, • Hygienic considerations in the construction of a food processing plant including site selection, product flow and hygiene in processing.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain and apply legislation, standards, guidelines incl. certifications concerning hygienic design and food contact materials in EU - Evaluate hygienic design aspects of construction materials, surface characteristics and equipment design details in regards to cleanability - Analyze hygienic design of processing equipment in open and closed systems - Apply criteria of hygienic design to identify cases where the relevant legislation has been violated - Examine hygienic design of processing plants, the rooms where processing takes place and placement of equipment - Develop conceptual re-designs of process equipment and processing lines based on information about construction materials, maintenance and cleaning procedures - Select suitable materials (stainless steel and polymers) and post treatments of materials to implement hygienic design - Identify potential corrosive environments in the food industry and recognize corrosion failures commonly seen in the food industry - Design proper cleaning and disinfection procedures for specific soils and process types and explain the effect of basic types of detergents and sanitizers - Apply procedures in employee personal hygiene and pest control
23750:
Name English: Beverage technology
Danish Title: Drikkevareteknologi
General Course Objectives: The main objective is that after the course, the students will be able to enter a beverage production plant, evaluate what is going on and be able to apply their knowledge to identify problems, concieve how to solve them and design new solutions, in order to improve brewing or beverage production.
Content: The course contains lectures from industry experts as well as researchers and experts from DTU and Copenhagen University. There will be calculation and other types of exercises, assignments, and the possibility for practical excercises and an excursion (see 'bemærkninger). There will be individual and group work. Specific real-life examples will be an integral part of the course. The course contains an introduction to the following subjects, brewhouse technology, fermentation technology, separation and filtration technology, beer processing technology, incl. pasteurisation, packaging technology, soft drinks technology, utilities technology, tank design, pipe systems and pumps. Some parts of the course will be taught in English since students need to be able to apply their knowledge in brewing and softrdrinks production which occurs in an international context.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Identify and describe the technological setup for manufacturing of beer in a classic brewery. - Identify and describe the technological setup for manufacturing of soft drinks. - Identify and describe the technological setup for packaging of carbonated drinks in bottles, cans and kegs. - Describe the requirements for utility services and water treatment in a brewery and/or soft drinks plant. - Conceive solutions to a given problem in a beer or soft drink plant. - Use original scientific literature regarding manufacturing of beer and soft drinks to propose solutions to a given problem. - Design and calculate a theoretical solution to a given problem in a beer or soft drink plant. - Work in a team to address overall objectives, and also to how to manage team dynamics. - Apply English in a professional engineering context related to beer and soft drinks production.
23934:
Name English: Biological chemistry
Danish Title: Biologisk kemi
General Course Objectives: The students should, based on the cell, acquire a basic understanding of biological processes. Consequently, the students will acquire knowledge about the cell structure, their biological functions, biochemical, molecular and biotechnological processes. With this background the students should be able to discuss present biotechnological problems.
Content: The cell as basic biological unit: structure, function, metabolism, growth, reproduction, heredity and biodiversity. The theory covers: structure of amino acids and proteins, nucleotides and nucleic acids, carbohydrates and lipids. Enzymes: structure, reactions, inhibition. Dynamic biochemistry: cata- and anabolism together with regulation of metabolism, redox processes and energy metabolism. Synthesis of macromolecules of information: DNA and RNA, protein. Regulation of activities in the cell e.g. synthesis of macromolecules, responses to external stimuli. Mutation and mutagenesis. Genetic processes in pro- and eukaryotes. Gene technology. Examples will be given where basic biological definitions are used in present and future biotechnology.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Describe the spatial, logistic, and structural organization of the living cell as well as the overall mechanisms and chemical structures behind its function. - Describe the overall structure, function and regulation of enzymes, and explain how several enzymes together can form a metabolic pathway. - Explain how carbohydrates can be broken down by living cells, and the chemical energy transformed into ATP bound energy during both respiration and fermentation. - Describe the antiparallel double helical structure of DNA; its replication and chromosomal organization in pro- and eukaryotes; as well as the bacterial cell division and eukaryotic meiosis and mitosis. - Explain the initiation, elongation, and termination processes during transcription and translation in pro- and eukaryotes. - Describe mechanisms for regulation of gene expression. - Explain the mechanisms for prokaryotic transfer of genetic material and how a virus reproduces itself by the use of the host reproductive system. - Describe the basal terms in Mendelian genetics. - Describe how recombinant DNA technology can be utilized to manipulate living cells.
23955:
Name English: Beer and beverage technology
Danish Title: Øl- og drikkevareteknologi
General Course Objectives: The main objective is that after the course, the students will be able to enter a beverage production plant, evaluate what is going on and be able to apply the CDIO engineering philosophy to identify problems, concieve how to solve them and design new solutions, in order to improve brewing or beverage production.
Content: The course contains lectures from industry experts as well as researchers and experts from DTU and Copenhagen University. There will be calculation and other types of exercises, assignments, and the possibility for practical excercises and an excursion (see 'bemærkninger). There will be individual and group work. Specific real-life examples will be an integral part of the course. The course contains an introduction to the following subjects, brewhouse technology, fermentation technology, separation and filtration technology, beer processing technology, incl. pasteurisation, packaging technology, soft drinks technology, utilities technology, tank design, pipe systems and pumps. Some parts of the course will be taught in English since students need to be able to apply their knowledge in brewing and softrdrinks production which occurs in an international context.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Identify and describe the technological setup for manufacturing of beer in a classic brewery. - Identify and describe the technological setup for manufacturing of soft drinks. - Identify and describe the technological setup for packaging of carbonated drinks in bottles, cans and kegs. - Describe the requirements for utility services and water treatment in a brewery and/or soft drinks plant. - Conceive solutions to a given problem in a beer or soft drink plant. - Use original scientific literature regarding manufacturing of beer and soft drinks to propose solutions to a given problem. - Design and calculate a theoretical solution to a given problem in a beer or soft drink plant. - Work in a team to address overall objectives, and also to how to manage team dynamics. - Apply English in a professional engineering context related to beer and soft drinks production.
23F17:
Name English: Introduction to life-cycle assessment of food
Danish Title: Introduktion til livscyklusanalyser af fødevarer
General Course Objectives: This online introductory course provides professionals in the food sector with the fundamental concepts and practical tools needed to assess the environmental sustainability of foods and food systems. Participants are introduced to screening-level life cycle assessment (LCA), key sustainability indicators relevant for industry and regulators, and widely used software and databases such as OpenLCA and Ecoinvent. The course emphasises hands on understanding of system boundaries, data requirements, interpretation of environmental indicators, and basic uncertainty considerations. Towards the end f the course, participants apply these concepts to examine trade offs between food sustainability and food safety, integrating their prior knowledge of quantitative risk assessment and disease burden metrics (e.g., DALYs). This equips participants to support evidence based decisions in product development, regulatory assessments, and food system strategy.
Content: Foundations of food sustainability assessment: What sustainability means in the food system (environmental, resource, planetary boundaries), system boundaries, functional units, allocation in food supply chains. Overview of impact categories relevant for food: Climate impact (GWP - CO₂ eq), land use and biodiversity proxies, water use, and nutrient emissions. Life Cycle Assessment in practice: Inventory data collection for food chains, using database inventories (Ecoinvent, Agri footprint), performing a simple LCA, identifying hotspots and interpreting results, and intro to uncertainty and scenario testing. Sustainability of food-system interventions: Assessing interventions such as recipe reformulation, packaging changes, shifts in ingredient sourcing, or processing innovations; understanding system effects (e.g., rebound, substitution, shifting burdens); evaluating sustainability “claims” in industry and policy contexts; communicating sustainability indicators to non-technical stakeholders. Integrating sustainability with food-safety risk assessment: Why food sustainability decisions must consider both environmental performance and food-safety risk; identifying typical trade offs (e.g., reduced processing -> lower climate impact but higher microbial risk); combining sustainability indicators with food-safety metrics (exposure, risk characterisation, DALYs); introduction to Multi Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA).
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain core concepts in quantitative sustainability assessment of foods, including environmental footprints, LCA principles, system boundaries, and key impact categories. - Conduct a screening level environmental assessment using available LCA tools and standard databases. - Interpret key indicators such as GWP (CO₂ eq), land use, water use, eutrophication, and biodiversity proxies, and understand sources of uncertainty. - Explain sources of uncertainty in LCA and how these can be quantified and potentially reduced. - Assess sustainability implications of common food sector decisions (e.g., reformulation, packaging changes, production system choices). - Analyse trade offs between sustainability and food safety risk, integrating sustainability indicators with pre existing risk or health assessment metrics (e.g., exposure estimates, DALYs) using decision support approaches. - Support evidence based decisions in product development, regulatory assessments, and food system strategy. - Evaluate sustainability “claims” in industrial and/or political contexts. - Communicate results clearly to stakeholders in industry and public agencies.

25840:
Name English: Mathematical Modelling of Living Systems Journal Club
Danish Title: Studiegruppe i matematisk modellering af levende systemer
General Course Objectives: The overall objective is to increase the knowledge of mathematical modelling work across DTU Aqua and strengthen the level of mathematical expertise in developing, analyzing, evaluating and implementing mathematical models of living systems.
