26250:
Name English: Machine learning-driven molecular science
Danish Title: Machine learning-driven molecular science
General Course Objectives: This course focuses on experimental design and analysis for the molecular sciences using modern machine learning. Molecular space is vast, and navigating it efficiently requires a blend of algorithmic and chemical thinking. This course introduces the architecture of modern lab-in-the-loop and automated laboratory systems, with a focus on probabilistic foundations. It provides a rigorous mathematical and computational view of the design-build-test-learn cycle underpinning molecular discovery in chemistry, chemical biology and bioengineering.
Content: The course introduces the core principles underlying modern learning systems for the molecular sciences. We describe methods to formalize, analyze and scale up each component of the design-build-test-learn cycle, and how these pieces can be combined into automated lab-in-the-loop systems. The course begins with probabilistic models of molecules and molecular data. We introduce methods to relate a molecule's chemical structure or sequence to its activity, including those based on structural similarity and on neural networks. We introduce probabilistic models of assays and synthesis, using exponential family distributions. Next we cover methods for learning and inference. We explain methods to fit models to data, and how to apply these methods using probabilistic programming languages. We introduce methods to evaluate models' quality, focusing especially on quantifying uncertainty that comes from noisy assays or limited experiments. Finally we study methods to design and plan experiments. We specify different scientific goals as objective functions for learning or optimization. We introduce methods for iteratively selecting candidates to test, and introduce bandit algorithms for trading off between exploration and exploitation. Throughout, we focus on obtaining both a deep conceptual understanding and hands on experience. We explain how diverse problems in the molecular sciences (e.g. lead optimization, protein design, high throughput screening) can be formalized, analyzed, and implemented using core machine learning principles. We explain how diverse modern machine learning tools (e.g. Bayesian optimization, generative modeling, agents) instantiate these core principles.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Build adaptive lab-in-the-loop machine learning systems. - Explain common methods of extracting features from molecules, including those based on structural similarity and neural networks. - Explain common featurization methods for molecules, including those based on structural similarity and neural embeddings. - Account for different types of experimental noise and uncertainty, managing assays that involve sparse count data or skewed error distributions. - Derive decision rules for selecting candidates, and explain mathematically the tradeoffs between exploration and exploitation. - Write probabilistic programs to fit models to data. - Design experiments based on learned models. - Test and evaluate lab-in-the-loop machine learning systems with stochastic simulations.
26470:
Name English: Organic Chemistry
Danish Title: Organisk kemi
General Course Objectives: The purpose of the course is to familiarize the students with organic chemistry to the extent that enables them to apply the concepts of organic chemistry to problems encountered in biochemistry. biological chemistry and environmental chemistry. To provide the necessary background for understanding the organic chemistry literature on a sound scientific background.
Content: The organic chemistry is taught with basis in modern mechanistic concepts. The students are trained in the IUPAC nomenclature. The functional groups in organic chemistry are treated systematically. The stereo chemistry is treated in detail. The students are introduced to the chemistry of carbocations and carbanions. The structure of carbohydrates, proteins and lipids are presented. The methods MS, NMR and IR, are presented and the students are introduced to the use of these methods in identification of organic compounds.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Name organic compounds using the IUPAC rules and determine structural formula based on systematic names and also on selected common names - Apply Lewis and Brøndsted acid/base concepts in organic chemistry - Describe the stereo chemistry of organic compounds and apply the nomenclatures R, S, E and Z - Explain optical activity of organic compounds and reaction products - Name the functional groups of organic chemistry and predict their reactions - Identify the reaction types: addition, elimination and substitution - Explain formation, stability and utilization of carbocations and carbanions - Be familiar with the structure of carbohydrates, amino acids, and lipids - Understand the use of MS, IR, UV, and 1H-NMR spectra to identify organic compounds - Apply the concept resonance to predict reaction intermediates and products - Understand the use of curved arrows to explain reaction mechanisms - Propose syntheses and reagents for organic reactions occuring in several steps
27029:
Name English: Life science automation and robotics
Danish Title: Life science automatisering og robotteknologi
General Course Objectives: The course introduces biotechnology students to the theoretical foundations of laboratory automation and equips them with the practical skills required to operate Opentron's OT-2 pipetting robot platform. Students will gain insight into how robotic systems can be used to perform biological laboratory experiments and how automation can improve reproducibility, increase sample throughput, and improve data quality. The course emphasizes interdisciplinary skills by integrating biotechnology, programming (Python), and systems thinking, ensuring that students can design, implement, and optimize automated experimental workflows. Upon completion of the course, students will be able to design, document, implement, and evaluate simple automated workflows that perform common life science experiments.
Content: The course introduces students to laboratory automation in the life sciences, with a strong emphasis on practical implementation and the use of pipetting robotics platforms. The teaching is structured as an integrated sequence of lectures, case-based work, laboratory implementation, and plenary reflection. The video lectures introduce the theoretical foundation of laboratory automation, including the operating principles of the Opentrons OT-2 platform, liquid-handling concepts (e.g., liquid classes), workflow standardization, and the fundamentals of Python programming for robotic control. Following the theoretical introduction, students are presented with a concrete case (e.g., serial dilutions, PCR, ELISA, DNA purification, or enzyme assays). Working in small groups, they analyze the experimental objective and develop a theoretical automation strategy, e.g., translating a manual laboratory protocol into a structured robotic workflow while considering constraints, flexibility, and optimization. The proposed solutions are then implemented and tested in the laboratory using the OT-2 platform. This hands-on phase allows students to confront both the technical and biological challenges of automating experimental workflows. Each module concludes with a plenary session in which results, challenges, and design choices are discussed, and key learning points are synthesized. The course culminates in an exam project in which students, working in small teams, design, implement, and test a new automated workflow for the OT-2 platform, integrating the theoretical and practical competencies developed throughout the course.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Describe the technical foundations, advantages, and limitations of automating laboratory-based life science experiments. - Operate the Opentron OT-2 pipetting robotics platforms using existing protocols and scripts. - Use Python programming to implement and adapt automated workflows in a laboratory context. - Translate manual laboratory experimental protocols into automated workflows, considering flexibility, constraints, and optimization. - Map and evaluate resource utilization for work- flows (e.g. pipette tips, reagents), and identify bottlenecks. - Optimize workflows to minimize time and resource consumption while ensuring reproducibility and data quality. - Evaluate existing workflows, modularize them into reusable unit operations. - Assess when automation is beneficial and identify strategies for addressing hard-to-automate steps. - Capture the data output from robotics experiments and perform basic analysis aimed at improving the workflow’s performance. - Document robotics workflows in compliance with the FAIR principles.
27032:
Name English: Introduction to cell factories
Danish Title: Introduktion til cellefabrikker
General Course Objectives: To provide the students with a basic insight into the different methods that are used to generate effective, industrially relevant cell factories based on gene technology: LCA, TEA and upscaling considerations (fermentation/process engineering/down-stream processing), genetic stability, ALE, genome-scale metabolic models, pangenomics, omics analysis, heterologous gene expression, genome modifications, DBTL cycle.
Content: The introduction to cell factories course contains the following elements that are covered during the lectures and the exercises: What is a cell factory and how do you choose a relevant cell factory chassis organism for your product of interest? How does the value and purpose of your product affect your chassis choice? LCA, technoeconomic and upscaling considerations. General characterizations (substrate/nutrient utilization, maintenance energy, etc.) of the cell of interest. How to assess genetic stability and perform adaptive laboratory evolution experiments. Basic introduction to genome scale metabolic modelling, omics analysis, and engineering tools. Products from central metabolism, side-products, or new to nature. Heterologous pathway expression, flux redistribution, and removal of side-production formation in the DBTL cycle.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain what a cell factory is and how one in general can construct an industrially relevant cell factory - Evaluate how product value affects the choice of starting strain - Describe how LCA, technoeconomic and scale-up considerations can be used to guide an industrially relevant cell factory project - Design experiments to evaluate genetic stability and do adaptive laboratory evolution - Describe how genome scale metabolic models can be used to optimize cell factories - Outline approaches for the use of different Omics-analysis to guide a cell factory project - Explain how high TRY values can be achieved through different metabolic manipulations methods - Explain how the DBTL cycle can be used
27064:
Name English: Biotechnological protein production
Danish Title: Bioteknologisk proteinproduktion
General Course Objectives: Introduction to heterologous protein production from gene design to purification and characterization. The course integrates molecular biology, host selection, cell engineering, and bioprocess principles relevant for biotechnology and pharmaceutical applications. The course provides students with a comprehensive understanding of recombinant protein production across molecular, cellular, and process scales. Students gain insight into how genetic design, host selection, cell engineering, and downstream processing are integrated in modern biotechnology. The course enables students to analyze and design protein production strategies relevant to pharmaceuticals, industrial enzyme, and sustainable biosolution applications.
Content: The course covers the principles of heterologous protein production including: gene design and vector construction; promoter and ribosome binding site selection; host systems such as bacteria, yeast, mammalian, insect, plant and cell-free platforms; cellular engineering strategies; upstream bioprocess development and scale-up principles; downstream processing including affinity, ion exchange and size exclusion chromatography; and analytical techniques for protein characterization.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the principles underlying recombinant protein production. - Analyze structural and physicochemical properties of proteins relevant for expression and purification. - Design an expression construct including promoter, ribosome binding site, and selection marker. - Compare different host systems and justify their suitability for specific proteins. - Propose strategies for improving protein expression through cellular engineering. - Describe key principles of bioreactor operation and scale-up. - Design a purification strategy based on protein properties. - Interpret analytical data from the purification and characterization of proteins. - Integrate upstream and downstream considerations into a coherent production strategy.
27066:
Name English: Industrial enzyme discovery: From bioinformatics to function
Danish Title: Industriel enzymopdagelse: Fra bioinformatik til funktion
General Course Objectives: This course provides students with an integrated introduction to protein family analysis, functional an-notation, and AI assisted enzyme discovery and engineering. Through a combination of lectures, hands-on problem-solving, and iterative project work, students learn how to navigate protein sequence space, identify functional boundaries, critically evaluate databases, communicate scientific findings, and understand state-of-the-art AI tools for exploring (and engineering) enzymes. Active participation in group work and hand-in of mandatory assignments are prerequisites for exam participation.
Content: The course is structured around one group-based project reports split into two halves. In the first half of the course, students analyse protein families, explore possible annotation errors, and produce sequence-based literature reviews based on a selected application case. In the second half, students extend their project with enzyme design, assay development, and/or design of workflow automation. Invited industrial speakers and case-based teaching ensure strong relevance to biotechnology and industrial enzyme development.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain how protein families are defined and how to classify enzymes using bioinformatics and AI. - Describe major data resources and discuss their reliability, strengths, and common pitfalls. - Explain core principles of assay development, including laboratory automation. - Interpret scientific literature for manual curation of enzyme function. - Identify functional boundaries within protein families using bioinformatics tools. - Understand selected AI based tools for enzyme engineering. - Analyze the quality of functional enzyme annotations. - Work in teams to analyze complex datasets and communicate results clearly. - Construct and interpret visual elements (e.g., dendrograms and other phylogenetic/​family-analysis tools). - Design and justify an integrated in silico workflow for enzyme discovery from sequence to function. - Create a concise and brief science-based report for discovering industrial enzymes.
27200:
Name English: Data-driven bioengineering
Danish Title: Datadrevet bioengineering
General Course Objectives: The course provides a structured foundation for understanding biological systems through data, models, and computation. It introduces students to systems-level biological reasoning across molecular, cellular, and organismal scales, and develops the ability to connect biological questions with computational representations, measurement technologies, and multi-omics analytical approaches. The course covers biological regulation, sequence and structure principles, experimental design, omics technologies, statistical reasoning, machine learning, and modern AI-based analytical tools. Emphasis is placed on recognizing common analytical principles across biological data types, understanding how technologies constrain inference, and critically evaluating models and computational outputs. The course is designed as a broad cognitive foundation, preparing students for advanced study in bioengineering, systems biology, computational biology, and data-driven biotechnology.
Content: The course is structured in three connected phases covering systems biology, biological data generation, and computational analysis. It begins with systems-level biological foundations, including biological scales, representation of biological systems, regulatory interactions, network logic, sequence and structure principles, post-translational modifications, and experimental design with statistical inference. Students are introduced to how biological questions can be represented computationally as sequences, graphs, matrices, and model inputs. The second part of the course focuses on major omics technologies and their analytical logic, including whole genome sequencing and 16S profiling, metagenomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics. Emphasis is placed on understanding what each technology measures, the structure of common biological data formats, technological limitations, and how measurement shapes downstream interpretation. The final part of the course introduces computational modeling and modern analytical tools, including basic machine learning concepts, hidden Markov models, support vector machines, neural networks, pathway and network analysis, knowledge bases, protein language models, and multiomics integration through latent representations and autoencoder-based concepts. Throughout the course, students work with biological datasets in guided exercises, apply computational tools, discuss limitations of models and technologies, and critically evaluate AI-supported analyses. A group project integrates multiple course themes and concludes with oral presentations.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Interpret biological processes, interactions, and organization across molecular, cellular, and systems scales. - Identify regulatory elements, network motifs, and connectivity principles underlying biological behavior. - Translate biological questions into suitable computational representations such as sequences, matrices, graphs, and embeddings. - Interpret common biological data structures and file formats used in omics analyses and explain what information they contain and omit. - Apply basic statistical and machine-learning methods to biological datasets and critically interpret their outputs. - Perform and interpret downstream analyses including enrichment, pathway, and network-based analysis of biological datasets. - Evaluate assumptions, limitations, and risks of statistical, algorithmic, and neural-network models used in biological inference. - Compare how different omics technologies enable and constrain biological interpretation, and extract biologically relevant conclusions from their outputs. - Integrate information across multiple biological data types to support systems-level biological reasoning. - Use AI tools critically and responsibly through prompt design, output validation, and assessment of analytical relevance.
27221:
Name English: Microbiome engineering
Danish Title: Mikrobiom engineering
General Course Objectives: The course aims to provide students with competences in microbiome engineering, including both the design of microbial communities and the targeted modification of natural microbiomes. These competences will enable students to describe the breadth of biotechnology applications based on microbiomes, to explain recent technological advances in molecular biology, synthetic biology, and systems biology relevant to microbiome engineering, and to design, control, and optimize microbial communities by introducing or removing specific members, as well as by applying environmental or genetic interventions for applications in health, agriculture, and biotechnology
Content: The course provides an in-depth introduction to microbiome engineering, covering both the design of synthetic microbial communities and the targeted modification of natural microbiomes. It addresses the ecological and molecular principles that govern microbiome structure, function, and stability, including microbial interactions, chemical signaling, and environmental influences. The course will cover experimental and computational methods for microbiome characterization, such as sequencing-based approaches, cultivation strategies, sensor technologies, and model systems (e.g. biofilms). In addition, the course explores recent advances in molecular biology, synthetic biology, and systems biology that enable microbiome manipulation. Emphasis is placed on strategies to control and optimize microbiomes through introduction or removal of community members, as well as environmental and genetic interventions, with applications in health, agriculture, and biotechnology. Overall, the course equips students with the theoretical and analytical foundation to understand, analyze, and engineer microbiomes.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Describe the structure, function, and dynamics of microbiomes across different environments (e.g. soil, plant, and host-associated systems). - Explain key concepts and strategies in microbiome engineering, including both the design of synthetic microbial communities and the targeted modification of natural microbiomes. - Discuss current and emerging applications of microbiome engineering in health, agriculture, and biotechnology - Explain recent technological advances in molecular biology, synthetic biology, and systems biology relevant to microbiome research and engineering. - Describe and evaluate methods for microbiome characterization, including sequencing-based approaches, cultivation strategies, and experimental model systems (e.g. biofilm models). - Analyze and interpret microbiome data using computational approaches and appropriate statistical frameworks. - Design strategies to manipulate microbiomes by introducing or removing specific members, and by applying environmental or genetic interventions. - Critically assess scientific literature within microbiome research and engineering, including experimental design, methodology, and data interpretation
27232:
Name English: Modeling cellular metabolism
Danish Title: Modellering af cellulær metabolisme
General Course Objectives: This course introduces students to the theory and practice of building mathematical models of cellular metabolism, with applications spanning both prokaryotic and mammalian systems. The principal modeling frameworks covered are stoichiometric and constraint-based approaches, implemented in Python. A central aim is to illustrate the diverse ways in which the models can be used. Through numerous examples and exercises, students will build and apply constraint‑based models to a range of biotechnological problems, such as microbial and mammalian strain design, analyzing drug effects on metabolic pathways, optimizing media formulations, and exploring microbial community interactions. The course also covers strategies for incorporating transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic datasets into metabolic models. By the end of the course, students will be able to construct and apply metabolic models, and will have developed the critical judgment to understand what biological questions these models can and cannot address.
Content: This course covers the construction and application of mathematical models of cellular metabolism based on stoichiometric and constraints-based approaches. The primary focus is on prokaryotic organisms, but the course will also include examples and homework assignments based on eukaryotic and mammalian systems to highlight the generality and the diverse practical applications of metabolic systems biology. The course will comprise lectures that introduce core concepts along with guided in‑class assignments that reinforce and extend the lecture material. Students will also complete homework assignments and a group project. The course material will include a textbook, scientific articles, multi‑omic datasets from public repositories, guest lectures, and supplementary videos. All computational work will be carried out in Python.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Understand the difference between a network and a state. - Reconstruct an organism’s metabolic network from its genome sequence. - Convert the metabolic reconstruction into a mathematical model suitable for computer simulation. - Simulate different functional states of the metabolic network. - Identify and troubleshoot issues when models do not simulate properly. - Analyze properties of different functional states using flux balance analysis and other tools. - Understand core concepts of how different -omics datasets are generated experimentally, especially genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and fluxomic data. - Integrate metabolic models with different -omics data and understand the advantages and limitations of each data type. - Apply metabolic models to different use cases, for example metabolic engineering/strain design, media optimization, identification of drug targets and off-targets, and interactions within microbial communities.
27450:
Name English: Development of microbial biofertilizers and other whole-cell biosolutions
Danish Title: Udvikling af mikrobiel biogødning og andre cellebaserede biosolutions
General Course Objectives: The objective of the course is to provide students with an integrated understanding of the scientific, technical, regulatory, and entrepreneurial aspects involved in developing microbial biofertilizers and whole-cell biosolutions, from early discovery to market-ready products, called the R&D Pipeline.
Content: The course introduces microbial biofertilizers and other cell-based biosolutions, and the underlying scientific, technological, and regulatory principles. The course covers the end-to-end development of microbial biosolutions, including discovery and characterization, bioprocess and manufacturing development, formulation, greenhouse and field testing, regulatory frameworks, and commercialization. Teaching is based on lectures, selected literature, and case-based exercises that provide students with a systematic understanding of the biosolutions development pipeline.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Use key words/terms specific to the area. - Explain the R&D pipeline for microbial biofertilizers (TRL1–7). - Explain the scientific, technical, and regulatory challenges in each phase. - Evaluate strategies for strain discovery. - Evaluate fermentation and upscaling challenges. - Assess formulation and stabilization approaches. - Integrate biological and engineering considerations into technology development planning. - Understand the EU regulatory and safety framework for biologicals. - Interpret experimental and field data. - Propose strategies for developing biosolutions.
27829:
Name English: Good Enough Software Engineering for Bioinformaticians
Danish Title: Good Enough Software Engineering for Bioinformaticians
General Course Objectives: This PhD-level course provides a language-independent foundation in software design, equipping students with the skills to structure code and data effectively for research-driven tool development. By focusing on core principles such as problem decomposition, data organization, usability, and testing, students learn to approach software challenges methodically, regardless of the programming language used. The course includes in a hands-on project, allowing participants to apply these concepts to real-world tasks in their own research.
Content: This course offers a practical, language-independent introduction to software design, tailored for PhD students who want to build robust, maintainable tools to support their research. Unlike traditional programming courses that focus on syntax and language-specific features, this course emphasises the underlying principles of software design that apply across all programming languages. Whether you're working in Python, R, Java, or any other language, the skills developed here will help you structure your code and data more effectively. The course is ideal for students who have basic programming experience but want to deepen their understanding of how to approach software development tasks methodically and thoughtfully. By focusing on design rather than implementation, students will learn how to think like software architects—making their future coding efforts more efficient, scalable, and user-friendly. # Course Structure: The course is divided into four core modules, each taught over one day: ## Problem Decomposition Learn how to break down complex tasks into manageable components. Exercises will challenge students to model everyday activities (e.g., grocery shopping) as structured problems, revealing hidden complexity and encouraging systematic thinking. ## Communication and Usability of Results Explore how to present data and results effectively to diverse audiences. Topics include designing outputs for human readability, machine parsing, and accessibility. Students will practice creating interfaces that prioritise clarity and usability. ## Data Structures Understand how to organise and store data in ways that support efficient access and manipulation. Through relatable exercises (e.g., modelling the contents of a kitchen or a backpack), students will learn how to design data structures that reflect real-world relationships. ## Software Design Dive into the principles of good software design, including requirements analysis, input validation, testing strategies, and basic concepts like programming by contract and invariance. Students will work with pseudo-code to identify flaws and design robust solutions. ## Final Project: Following the teaching component, students will collaborate in a half-day session to define the requirements for a final project. Over the next five days, they will apply course concepts to outline and partially implement a software tool relevant to their own research. The course concludes with a half-day of project presentations, where students share their design decisions and reflect on the development process.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Problem Decomposition Students will be able to break down complex tasks into manageable sub-problems and identify hidden complexity in seemingly simple challenges. - User-Centric Communication Students will learn to design outputs that are accessible and usable for diverse audiences, considering factors like domain knowledge, disabilities, and downstream tool compatibility. - Data Structure Design Students will be able to organise and store data effectively by selecting appropriate structures that reflect real-world relationships and support robust access. - Software Design Principles Students will gain awareness of key software design components such as requirements analysis, input validation, and testing strategies, and apply them to small-scale tools. - Testing and Validation Students will be able to construct meaningful tests for software components, including unit and regression tests, and understand the role of automated testing pipelines. - Programming by Contract and Invariance Students will understand foundational concepts like invariance and programming by contract, and apply them to ensure software reliability and maintainability. - Computational Complexity Awareness Students will be able to recognize computationally expensive implementations, identify common performance bottlenecks, and apply profiling techniques to optimise code. - Project Planning and Implementation Students will be able to outline and partially implement a software project using the methodologies learned, demonstrating their ability to apply design principles to real-world research tasks.
34064:
Name English: Waveguide optics
Danish Title: Bølgelederoptik
General Course Objectives: To establish a solid understanding of the physical and technological background for optical waveguides and components for the control of a broad spectrum of light, from the visible to THz frequencies. Optical circuits are expected to become of great importance for future engineers within areas such as telecommunication, sensors and computer architecture. Optical fibers already play a crucial role within long-distance signal transmission, and are increasingly used as sensors, in laser systems, and for signal processing. This course gives an elementary understanding of integrated optical waveguides, optical fibers, plasmonic waveguides, simple optical components based on these, and a discussion of elementary THz technology. The course constitutes a solid platform for further work (e.g. masters projects) within these fields.
Content: Starting from Maxwell's equations, the fundamental principles for localization and manipulation of light are established. Dielectric waveguides, their geometries and mutual coupling, will be discussed. Furthermore, plasmonic waveguides and metallic waveguides for THz radiation are introduced. The course gives an introduction to the building blocks of optical circuits, such as passive waveguides, Bragg gratings and couplers. Microstructured optical fibers and their bandgap effects are also introduced. The course contains excursions to danish companies, thus giving a good impression of the ongoing activities within the field.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Formulate equations describing guided modes in straight and weakly bent optical waveguides, based on dielectric materials and/or metals, including the weak-guidance approximation and the scaling laws it implies. - Formulate equations describing the coupling of light into dielectric waveguides. - Describe the definition and implications of the concepts of dispersion, nonlinear coefficient/effective area, and bend loss for waveguides. - Describe the structure of guided modes and waveguiding properties in slab and rectangular waveguides, including dispersion, effective area and bend loss. - Describe the structure of guided modes and waveguiding properties in step-index fibers, including dispersion, effective area and bend loss for given values of core radius and index contrast. - Discuss structure and applications of graded-index fibers, polarization-maintaining fibers, and photonic crystal fibers. - Describe structure, guided modes, propagation loss and applications for various kind of hollow-core optical fibers. - Derive equations for reflection/​transmission/​mode coupling in waveguide-integrated Bragg and long-period gratings. Sketch solutions for uniform Bragg and long-period gratings, understand the meaning of chirp and apodisation. - Derive coupled-mode equations for directional couplers, and sketch their solutions. Use these results to formulate transmission equations for Mach-Zender interferometers and simple ring resonators. - Describe the properties of surface plasmon polaritons (SPP). Set up the wave equation describing SPP, and outline the dispersion diagram for SPP waves at air/metal interfaces. - Describe prism- and grating-assisted coupling of light into SPP modes, and have knowledge of prism-assisted beam-splitting in the THz regime. - Describe waveguidance of broadband signals in the THz range,the properties of dispersion-free as well as dispersive metallic waveguides, and loss mechanisms for THz waves due to finite electrical conductance in waveguides.
34375:
Name English: Access networks and home networks
Danish Title: Access- og hjemmenet
General Course Objectives: The course provides a broad overview of methods and techniques used to connect different types of terminals, for example, private household appliances, entertainment electronics, telemedicine measuring equipment, sensors (and similar M2M devices) to a communications network. The course will focus on wired networks and wireless networks using non-licensed frequency bands but also (to a lesser degree) mobile communication networks using licensed frequency bands. The course will cover both the physical transmission parts focusing on the different methods for multiplexing and capacity sharing generally used to achieve high bandwidth efficiency for media with varying characteristics as well as protocol aspects that ensure integration of different applications with very different quality needs and requirements for network performance.
Content: The course will describe general aspects of access to the Internet and other global communication networks and use concrete standards to exemplify basic trends and differences. Solutions in the public part of the network that reuse the existing infrastructure (e.g. xDSL and Powerline) or require new optical fibre cables (e.g., PONs) will be discussed with a focus on understanding the basic principles and comparison of the advantages and disadvantages of the different solution models. For in-home networks, focus will be on describing and comparing the various prevailing technologies and techniques (such as Bluetooth, ZigBee, Wi-Fi, Ethernet, etc.) and focusing on how home equipment can be integrated using communication technologies.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the fundamental principles of connecting heterogeneous terminals (e.g., household appliances, entertainment devices, and IoT-devices) to modern communication networks. - Compare wired and wireless access technologies, including solutions using both unlicensed and licensed frequency bands, and describe their typical use cases. - Describe and analyse physical-layer transmission techniques, including multiplexing methods and capacity‑sharing mechanisms. - Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of various access technologies such as xDSL, Powerline or PONs, including how they reuse or require new infrastructure. - Compare major in‑home networking technologies (e.g., Bluetooth, ZigBee, Wi‑Fi, Ethernet) in terms of performance, architecture, and suitability for different types of devices. - Assess how communication technologies enable integration of home devices. - Describe general aspects of Internet and global network access, including typical architectural models and standards. - Analyse how different media characteristics influence the choice of transmission methods, including constraints such as noise, range, bandwidth, and cost.
34555:
Name English: Thin Films for Energy and Electronics by Solution Processing
Danish Title: Tyndfilm til energi- og elektronikanvendelser ved opløsningsbaserede metoder
General Course Objectives: Through lecture and lab-integrated sessions, students gain hands-on experience in fabricating thin films and evaluating their properties. They learn how processing parameters, such as solution composition, viscosity, and coating speed, affect the final material performance. The final part of the course focuses on real-world applications of layers from sub-micron to tens of micrometers for solar cells, batteries, sensors, and electronics. Students work on a project where they design and analyze a thin film process for a selected application, linking laboratory methods to scalable manufacturing. The course combines theory, practical work, and project-based learning to provide a strong foundation in solution-based thin film processing as an alternative to conventional vacuum deposition techniques.
Content: In this course, students learn how to fabricate thin functional layers used in technologies such as solar cells, batteries, sensors, and electronic devices using solution-based (liquid) processing methods. Unlike vacuum-based techniques such as physical vapor deposition, this course focuses on how materials can be deposited directly from liquids, enabling simpler, lower-cost, and scalable manufacturing. The course begins with the fundamentals of solution-based thin film formation, including wetting, drying, and film uniformity. Students then explore key coating techniques such as spin-coating, slot-die coating, hydrothermal synthesis, chemical bath deposition, and spray coating, and compare their advantages in terms of precision, scalability, and industrial relevance. Chemical methods such as hydrothermal synthesis are also introduced to demonstrate alternative routes for forming structured films.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain how thin films form from liquid solutions, including wetting, drying, precipitation, nucleation, coalescence, and film uniformity. - Describe and compare deposition methods such as spin-coating, slot-die coating, hydrothermal synthesis, chemical bath deposition, and spray-coating. - Apply solution-based methods to fabricate thin films for energy and electronic applications. - Analyze how processing parameters influence film thickness, morphology, and performance. - Perform basic morphological, compositional, optical characterization of thin films and interpret results. - Design a simple thin film process for a selected application, such as display, solar cell, battery. - Explain how solution processing is used in technologies such as solar cells, batteries, and sensors. - Know and comply with safety procedures for work in the laboratory.
34556:
Name English: Solar Cells: From Fundamentals to Device Engineering
Danish Title: Solceller: Fra fundamentale principper til device-design
General Course Objectives: The course provides a complete introduction to photovoltaics, covering fundamental principles, device engineering, and real-world applications. Students learn how to design, model, and optimize solar cells, explore emerging materials, and examine advanced concepts such as tandem architectures. The course also highlights applications like indoor energy harvesting for IoT and provides hands-on experience with solar cell characterization techniques.
Content: The course covers the fundamental principles of solar energy conversion, including the efficiency limits of single-junction solar cells (~33.7% under standard 1-sun illumination), and progresses to device engineering and practical applications. The course focuses in particular on thin-film solar cells, some of which are already commercialized (e.g., CdTe, CIGS), while others are at the forefront of emerging photovoltaic technologies (e.g., kesterites, chalcogenides, dye-sensitized solar cells (DSSC), halide perovskites). The course includes lectures on the synthesis and processing techniques of thin-film solar cells. Students use simulation tools (e.g., SOLEY) to design, model, and optimize solar cells, evaluate device performance, and identify loss mechanisms, while also exploring emerging photovoltaic materials and fabrication techniques. Through a combination of lectures and practical work, students gain hands-on experience with solar cell characterization methods, including current–voltage (J–V), external quantum efficiency (EQE), and internal quantum efficiency (IQE). Advanced photovoltaic concepts, including multi-junction solar cells such as tandem architectures, are also covered. The course further highlights real-world applications, including indoor energy harvesting under low-light conditions and the use of photovoltaics to power sensors and electronic components in the Internet of Things (IoT). This course builds on the previous course 34551 Thin-Film Photovoltaics.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the physical working principles of photovoltaic conversion in solar cells - Calculate the theoretical efficiency limit of a single p-n junction solar cell, usually referred to as Shockley-Queisser limit. - Apply semiconductor physics to identify key device parameters (e.g., band gap, mobility, recombination, thickness) and use tools such as SOLEY to model, validate, and optimize solar cell performance. - Describe thin-film fabrication methods and emerging materials. - Evaluate how materials synthesis and processing influence material structure and resulting properties. - Apply characterization techniques (e.g., J–V, EQE, IQE) to analyze and interpret solar cell performance. - Evaluate advanced photovoltaic concepts, including tandem and multi-junction solar cells and their advantages. - Analyze indoor photovoltaic applications by evaluating operating conditions, efficiency limitations, and practical use cases.
34692:
Name English: PhD Course - Electro Research Colloquium
Danish Title: Ph.d.-kursus - Electro forskningskollokvium
General Course Objectives: The objective of this course is to provide a structured, recurring forum for PhD students to meet and exchange knowledge. By breaking the isolation between research groups, the course fosters an academic community and provides a dedicated space for the exchange of ideas, methods, and state-of-the-art research. It is designed to expose students to research directions outside or tangential to their specialization while promoting networking and collaboration across laboratories and departments.
Content: The course content centers on broad, shared research themes that are not specific to a single research group. These themes overlap across a wide range of fields, including, but certainly not limited to: machine learning, signal processing, sensors, optimization, and embedded systems. The curriculum is participant-driven and built around regular (weekly/bi-weekly) subgroup meetings. Each session features a rotating mediator who selects a topic and delivers a short introductory presentation. Group members individually find, read, and present their findings from relevant literature to foster a guided group discussion. Additionally, the course provides a forum for constructive peer review, where students receive feedback on their presentations and, when relevant, on draft academic manuscripts.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Independently curate and synthesize relevant scientific literature to prepare for scientific discourse. - Critically discuss the contribution and relevance of diverse academic papers. - Compare and evaluate research methods to determine their transferability across different scientific domains. - Translate complex, domain-specific research concepts into accessible language for a diverse, cross-disciplinary audience - Present research topics and mediate academic discussion within a peer group. - Assess the strengths, limitations, and potential applications of various methodologies. - Provide constructive peer review and feedback on academic papers and presentations. - Contribute to the creation of a PhD student community by actively engaging in interdepartmental knowledge exchange and collaboration.
34766:
Name English: Robotic Manipulation: Perception, Planning, Control and Learning
Danish Title: Robotic Manipulation: Perception, Planning, Control and Learning
General Course Objectives: Robotic systems have advanced significantly in recent years, expanding beyond controlled industrial settings into complex environments such as warehouses, healthcare facilities, and remote exploration. Despite this progress, enabling robots to robustly interact with the physical world and generalize across tasks and environments remains a central challenge in robotics. This course examines these challenges and provides an in-depth introduction to modern robotic manipulation through the study of foundational methods and current research in the field. This course provides an overview of the mathematical models and algorithmic foundations underlying state-of-the-art manipulation systems. Topics include perception for manipulation, motion planning and control, grasping, control in contact, and learning manipulation skills via advanced machine learning techniques including imitation learning and emerging foundation models. Students will gain both conceptual understanding and exposure to current research developments.
Content: Introduction to the robotic framework ROS, Robotic Grasping, Robotc Manipulation, Motion Planning, Robot Control, Robot Learning, Imitation Learning, VLAs The exercise part consists of introductory exercises and a project solved in teams.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Integrate perception, planning, control, and learning components to design complete robotic manipulation pipelines using ROS. - Apply algorithms to process visual data (e.g., images or point clouds) for perception in manipulation. - Apply motion planning algorithms to generate feasible manipulation trajectories under task constraints. - Explain fundamental robot motion control methods, including position, velocity, and torque control. - Implement different control strategies for motion tracking, compliance, and force regulation. - Apply grasp stability principles (e.g., form/force closure, friction models) to evaluate grasp quality. - Discuss the role and challenges of machine learning in robotic manipulation. - Analyze the advantages and limitations of modern learning paradigms such as vision-language-action (VLA) models for generalist manipulation policies. - Propose and implement solutions for manipulation tasks using the techniques covered in the course and scientific literature in robotics.

Name English: Skylab Startup programme - Stage 1
Danish Title: Skylab Startup programme - Stage 1
General Course Objectives: The aim of the course is to deepen the strategy and business development of an early-stage start-up focusing on the validation of their business ideas, value proposition, and problem/solution alignment.
Content: Workshop sessions, coaching and supervised group work on the student’s startups.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Differentiate and contrast the key assumptions behind the startup idea. - Design experiments to test those assumptions applying a more evidence-driven mindset to reduce risk and strengthen their business case. - Compose the different components of the Lean Business Model identifying the un validated assumptions and recognize the need for further confirmation. - Evaluate potential applications of their idea, compare market opportunities, and most promising markets to focus. - Differentiate between Value Proposition and Unique Selling Points. - Create a customer-focused Value Proposition to strengthen their startup idea. - Understand the alignment of personal values, goals, needs and expectations within the founding team to strengthen the startup’s foundation. - Compose and deliver a coherent and convincing pitch for their startup idea. - Reflect on your own network as an emerging entrepreneur and the effect on your development as an entrepreneur.
38312:
Name English: Skylab Startup programme - Stage 2
Danish Title: Skylab Startup programme - Stage 2
General Course Objectives: The aim of the course is to deepen the strategy and business development of an early-stage start-up focusing on the validation and development of their business model and customer base, and develop a MVP of their product/service.
Content: Workshop sessions, coaching and supervised group work on the student’s startups.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Contrast and appraise the different entrepreneurial finance components, enabling them to evaluate the economic​ feasibility of their business ideas. - Understand how to translate customer interactions into actionable sales strategies, gaining the ability to design and refine a repeatable sales process for their startup. - Develop project management skills that will facilitate the development of alignment and prioritization of task within the development of their startup. - Design a go-to-market strategy for their startup. - Understanding of the main types of intellectual property and how to apply them effectively to safeguard their innovations. - Develop the ability to adapt a business pitch to your personal style of communication. - Understand the team dynamics, and analyse competencies to form and expand a functioning team. - Reflect on the importances of peer-to-peer support for the development of their startup idea.
38400:
Name English: Innovation in Engineering (Polytechnical Foundation)
Danish Title: Innovation in Engineering (Polyteknisk grundlag)
General Course Objectives: The course introduces students to apply competencies and methods to enable innovation in engineering within multidisciplinary teams. Students will: - Understand how to follow and apply a structure innovation process to a real-life engineering challenge - Experience the varied innovation landscape by navigating and applying their skills in it - Contribute with collaborative initiatives in a team context to allow new perspectives - Combine their disciplines through various methods in a facilitated innovation process - Acquire the DTU's signature Innovation Mindset and application of multidisciplinary teams - Be able to communicate key findings to relevant stakeholders and adjust from their inputs - Acquire a toolkit of structured methods to increase the innovative probability - Create new solution-oriented ideas and mature these into a final concept proposal
Content: Innovation competencies are crucial for future engineers to invigorate new perspectives, particularly to nurture and drive global change in tackling the societal, environmental and health-related challenges we face. Through the course, students acquire applicable experiences and competencies with a systematic approach to innovation in an engineering context. Students are required to develop unique insights into how integrated innovation is practised. They will experience and face challenges with multidisciplinary collaboration while working on a real industry challenge. Each project team will also be assigned a team facilitator (which are students who are taking the course 'Facilitating Innovation in Multidisciplinary Teams'). These facilitators have attained innovation competencies and will guide the team during all project work. With a facilitator at hand, the team will have a 'catalyst' to increase 'Innovation Height'. The course is organized into two main parts. The first week - the BOOST module - is focused on engaging the students with the topic of innovation by an array of speakers, and introducing students to a systematic approach to innovation, including relevant theory. At the start of the first week, the students will be put into project teams based on their chosen innovation challenge as well as their line of study et al. In the second and third weeks - the EXPERIENCE module - the teams's focus is on developing an innovative solution in collaboration with their facilitator. This should result in a concept that must be presented to the stakeholders at the end of the process. The course consists of lectures, reading material, team exercises, assignments, peer-reviews and multiple-choice quizzes. The learning activities and submissions are team-based experiences and for that reason, it is important to participate in class at DTU Campus
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the importance between Feasibility, Viability, Desirability, Responsibility and Sustainability of an innovation context - Explain the innovation process through the chosen model of the 'Double Diamond' - Explain the different approaches in DTU's Signature Innovation Mindset and practical applications - Explain methods of working in the different stages of an innovation process e.g., exploration, ideation, iteration, designing, and building - Apply an innovation process model that encompasses phases of Discover, Define, Develop, Deliver i.e. Double Diamond - Evaluate and adapt the different phases of the innovation process based on limitations as, resources, time, constraints, data, stakeholders etc. - Contribute activly with your own disciplinary background in the different stages of the innovation process - Give and receive constructive and appropriate feedback to and from team members and other teams - Reflect on how to act constructively and proactively in a context where the decision-making process is characterized by high uncertainty and risk - Make informed and qualified decisions in an innovation process with regards to the Feasibility, Viability, Desirability, Responsibility and Sustainability of a solution - Reflect on their role, ways of working, and impact as an engineer in the innovation process - Review and communicate to the relevant stakeholders the design choices of an explored concept in relation to both the value creation and limitations

Danish Title: Facilitating Innovation in Multidisciplinary Teams
General Course Objectives: The course aims to equip the student with competencies in facilitating innovation in multidisciplinary teams in an engineering context. Students will: - Understand what it takes to facilitate an innovation process in an industry challenge. - Experience the varied innovation landscape by navigating and applying their skills in it given their expanded innovation and facilitation competencies. - Facilitate collaborative initiatives in a group context to develop new perspectives. - Identify value and limitations of new solution-oriented ideas and encourage maturing these into a final concept proposition. - Acquire the DTU's signature Innovation Mindset in the application of multidisciplinary teams and further develop their own approach to innovation. - Expand their toolkit of structured methods to increase the innovative probability.

The learning activities and submissions are team-based experiences and for that reason, it is important to participate in class at DTU Campus.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the importance between Feasibility, Viability, Desirability, Responsibility and Sustainability of an innovation content - Identify different team dynamics and apply relevant iniciatives to their innovation process - Explain relevant approaches in the facilitation of teamwork. - Explain methods for leading and facilitating the different stages of an innovation process e.g., exploration, ideation, iteration, designing, and building - Apply methods to support and maintain a collaborative environment in the processes of exploration, ideation, iteration, designing, and building - Guide team dicussions on group dynamics and teamwork with regards to the division of tasks and responsibilities. - Identify and increase the inclusion of diverse disciplinary backgrounds in the different stages of the innovation process - Apply methods to facilitate constructive teamwork in a context where the decision-making process is characterized by high uncertainty and risk of being led astray - Support the making of informed and qualified decisions in an innovation process with regards to Feasibility, Viability, Desirability, Sustainability, and Responsibility - Reflect on their role, ways of working, and value as an innovation facilitator in the innovation process. - Keep the end in mind with regards to deliver and argue to the relevant stakeholders the design choices of an explored concept in relation to both the value creation and limitations - Give and receive constructive and appropriate feedback to and from team members and other teams

Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the importance between Feasibility, Viability, Desirability, Responsibility and Sustainability of an innovation context, - Explain the innovation process through the chosen model of the 'Double Diamond', - Explain the different approaches in DTU's Signature Innovation Mindset and practical applications, - Explain methods of working in the different stages of an innovation process e.g., exploration, ideation, iteration, designing, and building, - Apply an innovation process model that encompasses phases of Discover, Define, Develop, Deliver i.e. Double Diamond, - Evaluate and adapt the different phases of the innovation process based on limitations as, resources, time, constraints, data, stakeholders etc., - Contribute activly with your own disciplinary background in the different stages of the innovation process, - Give and receive constructive and appropriate feedback to and from team members and other teams, - Reflect on how to act constructively and proactively in a context where the decision-making process is characterized by high uncertainty and risk, - Make informed and qualified decisions in an innovation process with regards to the Feasibility, Viability, Desirability, Responsibility and Sustainability of a solution, - Reflect on their role, ways of working, and impact as an engineer in the innovation process, - Review and communicate to the relevant stakeholders the design choices of an explored concept in relation to both the value creation and limitations.
38405:
Name English: Facilitating Innovation in Multidisciplinary Teams
Danish Title: Facilitating Innovation in Multidisciplinary Teams
General Course Objectives: The course aims to equip the student with competencies in facilitating innovation in multidisciplinary teams in an engineering context. Students will: - Understand what it takes to facilitate an innovation process in an industry challenge. - Experience the varied innovation landscape by navigating and applying their skills in it given their expanded innovation and facilitation competencies. - Facilitate collaborative initiatives in a group context to develop new perspectives. - Identify value and limitations of new solution-oriented ideas and encourage maturing these into a final concept proposition. - Acquire the DTU's signature Innovation Mindset in the application of multidisciplinary teams and further develop their own approach to innovation. - Expand their toolkit of structured methods to increase the innovative probability.
Content: Facilitating the innovation process can be crucial for future engineers to invigorate new perspectives, particularly to nurture and drive global change in tackling the societal, environmental and health-related challenges we face. Students will develop a strong instinct and unique insights into how the facilitation of integrated innovation is practised. Each project team (consisting of students who are taking the course 'Innovation in Engineering') will be assigned a team facilitator.
