Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the importance between Feasibility, Viability, Desirability, Responsibility and Sustainability of an innovation content, - Identify different team dynamics and apply relevant iniciatives to their innovation process, - Explain relevant approaches in the facilitation of teamwork, - Explain methods for leading and facilitating the different stages of an innovation process e.g., exploration, ideation, iteration, designing, and building, - Apply methods to support and maintain a collaborative environment in the processes of exploration, ideation, iteration, designing, and building, - Guide team dicussions on group dynamics and teamwork with regards to the division of tasks and responsibilities, - Identify and increase the inclusion of diverse disciplinary backgrounds in the different stages of the innovation process, - Apply methods to facilitate constructive teamwork in a context where the decision-making process is characterized by high uncertainty and risk of being led astray, - Support the making of informed and qualified decisions in an innovation process with regards to Feasibility, Viability, Desirability, Sustainability, and Responsibility, - Reflect on their role, ways of working, and value as an innovation facilitator in the innovation process., - Keep the end in mind with regards to deliver and argue to the relevant stakeholders the design choices of an explored concept in relation to both the value creation and limitations, - Give and receive constructive and appropriate feedback to and from team members and other teams.
41264:
Name English: Ship Hydrodynamics
Danish Title: Skibshydrodynamik
General Course Objectives: Understanding ship behavior in calm water and accurate estimation of the resistance which is experience by ship, is essential for reliable and optimum design of its propulsion plant including the ship engine. Moreover, determining unsteady ship motions due to ocean waves plays a key role in ship seakeeping properties and its structural response. Both of these subjects are vital for safe and sustainable ship operation, which are becoming increasingly important due to the green transition in maritime transport. The overall objective of this course is that students learn the fundamental concepts of ship resistance, propulsion and seakeeping, and they learn to conduct engineering calculations for these topics with direct application for ship design and operation.
Content: • Fundamental equations of fluid mechanics, dimensional analysis (Pi theorem) • Control volume approach for solving external flow problems • Potential-flow fields and boundary layer theory • Linear wave theory and its engineering properties • Ship resistance components including frictional and residuary resistance • International Towing Tank Committee (ITTC) guidelines • Propeller in open-water and behind-the-hull conditions • wave- and motion-induced forces on ships • Classical strip theory and motion response in the frequency domain
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - describe the flow field around a ship hull including the wave patterns - describe the components of ship resistance and their proportional significance for different ship types - compute ship resistance using empirical approaches and ITTC methods - describe the physics of a ship propeller and its interaction with the ship hull - design a ship propeller and perfrom calculations to optimize the propulsion plant - set up, analyze and solve the equations of motion for a ship in waves - compute the ship response spectrum using a wave spectrum and the response transfer functions - compute added resistance of ship in waves using a wave spectrum and the transfer function - calculate and assess the global structural response due to waves and ship motion
41349:
Name English: Advanced combustion in engines
Danish Title: Avanceret forbrænding i motorer
General Course Objectives: The course aims to give students knowledge on advanced combustion concepts to complement the conventional Spark Ignition (SI) and Compression Ignition (CI) in internal combustion engines. Further, the course introduces the working principles of SI ignition and fuel injection concepts. The students will gain knowledge on the interaction between fuel chemistry, emission formation and thermal efficiency under a range of combustion concepts. Emphasis will be given on advanced combustion concepts such as Partially Premixed Combustion (PPC), Spark Assisted Compression Ignition (SACI), Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) and Prechamber Combustion (PCC). Finally, advanced thermodynamic cycles such as the Double Compression Expansion Engine (DCEE) will be introduced.
Content: The cycle-to-cycle variations with spark ignition combustion is discussed before the advanced ignition and fuel injection systems are introduced. Special emphasis on Gasoline Direct Injection is given. The advanced combustion concept of HCCI is discussed, including emission formation, combustion control and dissecting the fundamentals showing results from laser diagnostics and CFD modelling. The process in between pure HCCI and conventional spark ignition, SACI, is also discussed. The process between conventional compression ignition and HCCI; PPC, is then explained and discussed including the effect of fuel choice; gasoline-like or diesel-like. The concept used in large gas engines with a prechamber, PCC, is also presented and explained. DCEE to further improve engine efficiency is presented using two or three cylinders instead of only one for the engine cycle. Finally, an outlook in engine trends is included. Recent progress will be highlighted, discussed and put into perspective. A real-time simulation model of HCCI is used to get further understanding of the special requirements of HCCI and to extract the response of combustion to input variables like engine speed, engine torque, inlet temperature, inlet pressure, and fuel octane number. Single input, single output response as well as cross-correlations will be studied.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - explain the working principles of advanced SI ignition systems - select the best fuel supply system for an SI engine - discuss the cycle-to-cycle variations in SI combustion and identify the influence of fluctuations in fluid flow, fuel and residual gas concentration. - compare the concept of HCCI combustion to conventional SI and CI combustion, respectively. - explain similarities and differences between SACI, HCCI and SI. - evaluate benefits and drawbacks of PCC and dual fuel combustion - perform simulations of HCCI combustion with supplied software - develop a conceptual model of PPC and relate it to HCCI and conventional CI - discuss the benefits of DCEE and relate it to the theoretical limits for engine thermal efficiency
41518:
Name English: Weight Critical Structures
Danish Title: Vægtkritiske konstruktioner
General Course Objectives: To develop mathematically and physically based methods for analysing the strength and stability of lightweight structures made of stiffened or unstiffened laminated and sandwich composites or light metals, and to dimension such structures for weight critical applications in aerospace, automotive, marine, and space engineering.
Content: 1) Unstiffened and stiffened plates: Differential equations, stiffness behavior of stiffened plate panels, stress calculation, boundary conditions, analysis methods (Navier and Rayleigh-Ritz methods). 2) Layered sandwich beams and plates: Differential equations, stiffness properties and their connection to classic lamination theory, stress calculation, basic sandwich theory with shear deformations and first order sandwich beam and plate theories and their analysis methods. 3) Stability of composite plates: Analytical buckling analysis methods, energy method, stiffened plates, buckling of layered sandwich plates and the influence of imperfections. 4) Progressive failure analysis of laminate and layered sandwich plates. 5) Analysis and design of joints between composite plates and other structural elements. 6) Fracture mechanical analysis of typical damages in laminate and sandwich plates. 7) Design principles and practical application of analytical solutions and FEA for plate structures within typical weight critical constructions such as aircrafts, ships, automotive and space vehicles. 8) Experimental methods for plate structures consisting of composite materials.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Account for the assumptions for first and higher order beam and plate theories for both unstiffened and stiffened layered laminates and sandwich structures. - Formulate relevant boundary conditions for plate fields in lightweight structures. - Perform theoretical stress and deformation analyses of unstiffened and stiffened plates in lightweight structures by use of Navier's, Levy's and Rayleigh-Ritz's solution methods. - Perform theoretical stress and deformation analyses of sandwich beams with shear deformations. - Perform theoretical stress and deformation analyses of layered sandwich plates based on classical lamination theory and basic sandwich theory with shear deformations. - Perform theoretical stability analysis of unstiffened and stiffened laminate and sandwich plates. - Analyze and design cohesive joints in laminate and sandwich constructions. - Calculate progressive failure of rectangular and laterally loaded sandwich plates using failure criteria for composite materials. - Perform fracture mechanics analysis of typical damage scenarios for laminate and sandwich structures. - Use a commercial FEM program to analyze and design both unstiffened and stiffened plate structures consisting of laminate and sandwich composite materials. - Compare analytical, numerical and experimentally achieved results for a given lightweight plate structure and evaluate the quality of the respective results. - Write a technical report containing analysis including the above mentioned points applied on a practical design example from an aircraft, ship, automotive or space vehicle.
41751:
Name English: Metal forming and joining technologies
Danish Title: Metalformgivning og sammenføjningsprocesser
General Course Objectives: The overall objective of the course is to provide students with a physically based and engineering-oriented understanding of sheet metal forming and selected joining technologies, enabling them to analyze, design and integrate manufacturing process chains for industrial sheet metal components. Sheet metal forming includes the basics of metal plasticity and anisotropy to calculate stress and strain in processes, such as deep drawing and stretch forming. The joining processes include joining by plastic deformation (such as hemming and various types of riveting), resistance welding, and laser welding.
Content: Sheet metal forming involves analysis and design of processes such as deep drawing and stretch forming. Content and methods include basic metal plasticity, anisotropy, plastic instability and sheet formability, tribology (friction, lubrication and wear), tool design and introduction to the finite element method (FEM). Joining technologies will be introduced in general and focus will be on those mostly combined with sheet formed parts, i.e., joining by plastic deformation (hemming, riveting, and clinching), resistance welding and laser welding. For the joining technologies, the focus will be on fundamental understanding, possible material combinations, geometrical constraints, process windows, and the relationship between process parameters and joint strength. Combinations of processes will be analyzed as process chains, where one process will influence the next one. Sustainability aspects will be taught by published example calculations that will highlight important aspects to improve. The course will be centered around project work, where the individual lectures, exercises, use of commercial software, and laboratory work all feed into the overall aim of the project.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - explain and compare the fundamentals of sheet metal forming and joining processes - apply simplified analytical models to estimate stresses, strains, forming limits and joining process windows - identify and explain critical process limitations in sheet metal forming, such as wrinkling, fracture, and excessive tool wear - identify and explain critical process limitations in joining processes, such as limited geometrical locking, splash/expulsion of molten metal, or porosity formation - design tools and plan process parameters for sheet metal forming and selected joining processes to stay within the respective process windows - plan and execute experimental work for studying manufacturing processes - apply commercial finite element software packages to simulate sheet metal forming and joining processes while evaluating and using results critically - evaluate process chains involving sheet metal forming and joining processes with respect to material combinations, process robustness, and final product properties - describe sustainability aspects in individual processes and at process chain level with focus on material use, energy use, and the consequences of the manufacturing stage on the environmental impact during the use phase of the product
41B26:
Name English: Emergency Technology
Danish Title: Beredskabsteknik
General Course Objectives: To provide participants with the fire technical prerequisites and competencies to handle analytical case processing of technical matters related to building and emergency law with a focus on relevant scenarios, risks, operational options and limitations as well as an understanding of authorities, including the role and responsibility of emergency services in this context.
Content: The course includes the building code and emergency response legislations, and associated documentation and methodology requirements. The course provides a thorough introduction to case processing, including ATMU (Work Environment, Tactics, Equipment, Training). The course also introduces risk assessment at damage sites as well as emergency response capacity and quality. It also includes principles for extinguishing capacity, including the required amount of water, foam, etc. Methods for damage site investigation and response evaluation (data collection, etc.) are also included in the course. Additional content includes trace preservation, causes of fire, dimensioning of operational conditions (FBIM), rescue tactics, rescue methods, standards (NFPA, BRE, SFPE), fire tests, understanding of and the emergency response team's interaction with installations. Finally, temporary structures such as scaffolding, stands, tents and site covers are included in the course.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the fire engineering and emergency management principles that form the basis for assessing response conditions in building and emergency management law cases. - Explain and apply methodologies for documenting building and emergency response requirements. - Document and compare the building law response requirements in relation to the emergency services' actual equipment and tactics in selected buildings. - Identify and address operational issues in the event of deviations from the pre-accepted solutions in the technical regulations of the emergency response legislation. - Describe and apply risk assessment in emergency preparedness law contexts in relation to technical and preventive provisions. - Analyze the operational capacity of the emergency response in relation to specific tasks, including assessment of scenarios and tactical options and limitations. - Use of methodologies for identifying and treating relevant local planning and societal risks in relation to emergency response efforts - Explain the difference between traditional operational tactics (ITT) and non‑traditional operational tactics
41B28:
Name English: Special Emergency Challenges
Danish Title: Beredskabsudfordringer
General Course Objectives: The overall course objective is that participants acquire knowledge about emergency design, barriers and prerequisites within selected relevant areas. With the acquired skills, to be able to carry out an analytical review and assessment of emergency and response premises and prerequisites.

Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Use the Fire Brigade Intervention Model (FBIM) or similar models to systematically quantify the relevant times (detection, alarm, driving, attack) and response resources in a fire scenario. - Explain the interaction between fixed technical installations in construction and the efforts of the "mobile" rescue service. - Assess the relevance of and use international standards (e.g. NFPA, SFPE) as a basis for tactical dimensioning. - Conduct a quantitative risk analysis of high-rise buildings and complex buildings to dimension the necessary emergency response capacity and response strategy. - Analyze the efforts and extinguishing strategy for fires in Lithium-Ion battery energy storage systems (BESS), including the risk of thermal runaway and the need for specialized equipment. - 41B29:
Name English: Fire and Sustainable Buildings
Danish Title: Brand og bæredygtigt byggeri
General Course Objectives: To provide the students with basic knowledge about fire-related challenges and associated solutions in connection with the sustainable transition in construction.
Content: This course will introduce the students to the fire safety challenges associated with various design components intended to reduce the lifecycle carbon emissions of buildings, including timber elements, biobased insulation, solar cells, and energy storage systems. The students will learn how to evaluate and review designs of such "sustainable" buildings. The course is based on review of the latest research and practice.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - develop and evaluate performance-based fire safety strategies for different kinds of low-carbon buildings - describe the components of a holistic performance-based fire safety strategy, and how they relate to each other. - describe the fire safety challenges related to different aspects of low-carbon buildings, and how they influence the fire safety strategy. - define design objectives and performance criteria for buildings incorporating low-carbon materials and systems. - describe the influence of combustible building elements, and energy production and storage systems, on fire dynamics and the resulting fire risks. - describe the applicability and limitations of standard test methods for new materials and systems. - design ad hoc tests to evaluate the performance of novel materials and systems. - independently search, find, refer to relevant literature to evidence decisions. - describe solutions, including active and passive fire protection systems (and the limitations of these protection systems), to address the risks associated with different components of low-carbon buildings.
46220:
Name English: Green Energy Transition in Emerging and Developing Economies
Danish Title: Grøn energiomstilling i vækst- og udviklingsøkonomier
General Course Objectives: The course provides students with an overview and understanding of the special economic, policy, technological, and social challenges associated with green energy transition in emerging economies. Decarbonizing the energy sector, which globally accounts for three-quarters of emissions, is fundamental in climate change mitigation. Today, emerging economies account for the main share of global carbon emissions, and emissions are projected to increase. They are also among the most vulnerable to climate change. Due to the scale of these challenges, emerging economies have also become large while often risky commercial investment destinations for high-income country firms in green industries. In this course, we will discuss the challenges of green energy transition in emerging economies from different stakeholder perspectives, including national governments, local societies, international organizations, and multinational firms.
Content: In the course, we will discuss and analyze the most pertinent issues related to green energy transition in emerging economies. Emerging economies are distinct from high-income countries with their lower economic and institutional development, financial and entrepreneurial scarcities, greater inequalities, higher institutional diversity, higher extent of state control, higher risks, etc. Decarbonizing the energy sector in emerging economies is a massive and multi-dimensional challenge in technical, financial, economic, policy, and social terms. The challenges we will discuss in the course include the following: wide-ranging economic transformations in industries, business models, capabilities, and markets are required to develop a sustainable energy sector. Operating in the business environments in these economies represents challenges for multinational firms, and conversely, the presence and involvement of multinational firms represent special challenges for the countries’ development goals. The modes of involvement of local firms and institutions have long-term implications for the countries’ upgrading trajectories. Transformation of governance and regulatory frameworks are often highlighted as primary determinants of green energy transition, including supportive institutional frameworks, administrative efficiency, and effective incentive systems. Further development of a range of technologies for generation, transmission and storage of energy is required for cost-efficient decarbonization of the energy sector. Financing needs for green energy transition in emerging economies have been estimated to be seven times the current level of investment by 2030, and huge financing gaps call for innovative and private schemes. Social challenges include maintaining a broad societal coalition and managing the uneven distributions of transition costs and benefits.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain concepts, theories, and methods that are central to green energy transition in emerging economies - Analyze the factors that affect green energy transition in emerging economies - Examine the strengths and weaknesses of theories, models, and frameworks covered in the course on the basis of cases as well as contemporary developments - Operationalize concepts pertaining to green energy transition in emerging economies, using relevant data sources and indicators - Independently analyze issues pertaining to green energy transition deriving from the theories, concepts as well as empirical evidence (data and cases) - Conduct a methodologically robust social science analysis and present it in an academic report - Apply generative AI as a learning tool in a reflective and critical manner, which safeguards learning outcomes - Document and critically evaluate your usage of generative AI
46800:
Name English: Renewable Energy Technologies
Danish Title: Vedvarende Energiteknologier
General Course Objectives: Renewable energy technologies are multidisciplinary topics that require the development of systems that can produce, transport, deliver and store energy reliably, economically and environmentally responsible way. The overall course objective is to introduce students to basic energy engineering concepts and their relationships within 3 different energy technologies, wind energy, solar energy (photovoltaic) and electrochemical energy storage. The students will be able to estimate the performance of the energy technologies and be able to assess the possibilities and limitations of these technologies. In addition, the students will be able to explain commercial aspects associated with the technologies.
Content: The course introduces basic concepts such as energy and power, as well as an introduction to energy technologies. The course then goes more in depth with three selected technologies: wind energy, solar energy (photovoltaics), and electrochemical energy storage (batteries). The goal is to be able to estimate the production/capacity of a system and describe the most important components and their functions. The teaching is based on a central assignment in which students investigate how to meet the electrical energy needs of a small town using different energy technologies. First, each technology is examined individually, and finally students explore what happens when the technologies are combined into a single system. The course consists of lectures and exercises. The exercises can be used directly in the work with the central assignment. There will also be time for questions and feedback on your solutions.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the meaning and difference between energy and power - List different forms of energy and can give examples of each of them - Define an energy technology - List the most common energy technologies including their advantages and disadvantages - Use basic parameters to dimension a system and estimate the monthly and annual energy yield for the following energy technologies: wind turbines, solar cells - Describe the essential subcomponents and their function for the following energy technologies: wind turbines, solar cells, batteries - Estimate Levelized Cost of Energy (LCoE) in the context of wind and solar systems and Levelized Cost of Storage (LCoS) in the context of energy storage - Broadly size a combined energy system that includes both wind and solar energy as well as battery storage, based on a given set of design criteria - Communicate issues and solutions when designing energy systems in the context of a company
46805:
Name English: Materials and manufacturing processes for industrial technology
Danish Title: Materialer og fremstillingsprocesser til industriel teknologi
General Course Objectives: The aim of the course is to give a general understanding of how components are designed and manufactured, and to provide hands-on experience with both theoretical and experimental aspects of design and manufacturing processes. Case examples will include components for wind turbines and solar energy. The course aims to equip students with a structured way of thinking when developing new components, as well as a basic understanding of the overall process and material selection from design to finished product.
Content: The course gives an overall introduction to component design and manufacturing through theory and experiments using wind turbines and solar cells as case examples. It also briefly touches on testing and end-of-life of components, and includes the following elements: • Brief introduction to prerequisite mechanical concepts • Tensile testing and data analysis to measure stiffness and strength of materials • Simplified analytical calculations of stiffness and strength of materials and components • Introduction to Ashby’s material selection method for mechanical design • Brief introduction to material properties relevant for solar modules (optical, thermomechanical and electrical) • Introduction to manufacturing and joining processes for metals, polymers, and composites and selection of suitable processes based on material and product requirements • Demonstration of manufacturing processes for metal components • Combining theory and hands-on experimental work on two cases: (1) Manufacturing and testing a small solar cell panel and (2) manufacturing and testing a small-scale wind turbine blade
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain how selected material properties are measured experimentally - Estimate the stiffness and strength of simplified components - Apply Ashby’s material selection method to component design - Describe relations between materials, manufacturing processes and product properties - Select appropriate manufacturing processes based on material and product requirements - Evaluate component designs regarding feasibility, safety and reliability - Explain typical wind turbine blade and solar photovoltaic (PV) module manufacturing processes - Implement a PV module design in a realistic production environment - Build and test a small-scale wind turbine blade using realistic manufacturing methods
46950:
Name English: Generative AI Tools for Research
Danish Title: Generative AI-værktøjer til forskning
General Course Objectives: The emergence of capable generative AI models presents PhD researchers with both an opportunity and a challenge. The learning objectives, content, and course structure have been designed to promote critical thinking, technical competence, and responsible use of AI in PhD-level research. On one hand, tools such as large language models, code assistants, and multi-modal pipelines can dramatically accelerate research tasks that previously required significant manual effort — literature synthesis, exploratory data analysis, writing, and communication. On the other hand, uncritical adoption carries real risks: hallucinated references, eroded scientific voice, ethical breaches, and institutional policy violations. This course is designed to build genuine competence rather than surface familiarity. Students begin by grounding themselves in the ethical, institutional, and epistemological landscape of AI use in academia, and they progress through progressively more demanding hands-on projects that culminate in producing a short scientific paper from real research data. Each session pairs conceptual input with a concrete task, ensuring that the skills acquired transfer directly to students’ own PhD projects.
Content: Students will develop a working understanding of the generative AI landscape, including the trade-offs between open-source and closed-source models, local and cloud-based deployment, and API-based versus interface-driven interaction. From this foundation, they will acquire hands-on experience designing and implementing multi-step AI workflows in Python, covering tasks such as batch document processing, cross document synthesis, automated translation, and structured output generation. A significant portion of the course is devoted to AI-assisted scientific writing. Students will learn to configure professional writing environments that combine LATEX, VSCode, and AI coding assistants, and will practise using these tools across all stages of manuscript preparation — from outlining and drafting to figure captioning, revision, and peer review. Critically, students will work with real data: either from their own PhD research or from publicly available energy-system datasets retrieved via the ENTSO-E Transparency Platform. This ensures that the skills developed are immediately applicable to their own work. Throughout, the course emphasizes responsible and transparent use of AI. Students will engage with the ethical, epistemological, and institutional dimensions of AI adoption in academia, and will develop criteria for evaluating and disclosing AI contributions in line with publisher and DTU standards.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Navigate the current landscape of generative AI tools - Evaluate AI tools suitability for specific research tasks, taking into account performance, cost, privacy, and licensing considerations - Interact with AI models programmatically through API calls and local deployments - Design multi-step automated workflows tailored to research needs - Integrate AI assistance into professional academic writing environments - Apply AI tools to data analysis, visualization, and scientific communication using data from their own research - Critically assess the quality, accuracy, and limitations of AI-generated text, code, figures, and interpretations - Develop principled strategies for accepting, adapting, or rejecting AI suggestion - Reflect on the broader ethical, epistemological, and societal implications of AI adoption in academic research - Align their practice with DTU policy and evolving publisher standards

62129:
Name English: Innovation and Creative Problem Solving in engineering
Danish Title: Innovation og Kreativ Problemløsning i ingeniørfaget
General Course Objectives: The course aims to develop students’ fundamental innovation competencies, with a focus on identifying and addressing complex engineering problems. The course places innovation within an academic and societal context and provides students with a foundation for working systematically and reflectively on solution development throughout the remainder of their program. Emphasis is placed on strengthening students’ ability to think critically, solve problems creatively, and collaborate, so that they can participate effectively in interdisciplinary and practice-oriented development processes. The course also helps build an awareness of their own role as engineers in relation to users, stakeholders, and society.
Content: The course is structured as a team-based, project-oriented program in which students work on innovation through an iterative process, from problem identification to the development and testing of solutions. The program begins with an introduction to innovation in an engineering context, focusing on innovation as a learnable practice, the development of a growth mindset, and the establishment of a safe learning environment. Students are then introduced to design thinking as a methodological framework, with a particular focus on empathy and problem understanding. They work with user involvement, data collection, and synthesis to formulate relevant and meaningful problems. This forms the basis for the subsequent phase, where students systematically work on idea development through both divergent and convergent processes, as well as the application of structured creative techniques. The course also addresses complex and intractable problems (wicked problems), in which students analyze the interplay between technical, human, and societal factors using systems thinking and stakeholder analysis. Against this backdrop, they develop prototypes of their proposed solutions, which are tested and refined through iterative processes with a focus on user feedback and learning. A recurring element of the course is the focus on team dynamics and collaboration, where students work on role distribution, communication, and reflection on their own and the group’s work processes. The course concludes with a comprehensive project in which students apply the methods and competencies they have acquired to develop and communicate a solution to a real-world problem.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the role and significance of innovation in engineering, as well as its social and economic relevance. - Describe the key phases of design thinking and their purpose and function in a problem-solving process. - Distinguish between well-defined (engineering) problems and complex, open-ended problems (wicked problems) and recognize the characteristics of each type. - Apply design thinking methods and tools (e.g., empathy mapping, problem definition, idea generation, prototyping, and testing) when working on real-world problems. - Generate and develop solution ideas using structured creative techniques. - Analyze complex, real-world problems with a focus on identifying stakeholders, underlying human needs, and constraints. - Evaluate and select proposed solutions based on criteria such as feasibility, desirability, and viability. - Actively participate in teamwork and apply basic collaboration practices, as well as reflect on team dynamics, identify sources of friction or inefficiencies in teamwork, and suggest improvements. - Develop, test, and communicate prototype solutions to real-world challenges through feedback and iterative processes. - Reflect on one’s own role, learning, and development within innovation processes and teamwork. - Contribute to the establishment and development of a high-performing team focused on collaboration and shared goals.
62151:
Name English: Bridging Business and Technology in a Global Context
Danish Title: Bridging Business and Technology in a Global Context
General Course Objectives: The purpose of this course is to introduce students to the Global Business Engineering Programme, clarifying its distinctive features and the professional opportunities it offers. The course also provides an introductory understanding of how technologies—particularly digital technologies—interact with the business and socio-cultural contexts in which they are developed and adopted. In doing so, it highlights the importance of considering not only technical aspects, but also economic, managerial, and behavioural factors that shape the adoption and use of technology in organizations. Additionally, through experiential learning, students will develop key transversal skills required to thrive in a global business environment, including teamwork, effective communication and the ability to collaborate across diverse perspectives.
Content: The course introduces students to the interdisciplinary foundations of Global Business Engineering by exploring how technologies interact with business and socio-cultural contexts. Through a combination of participatory lectures, guest lectures from industry and academia, and collaborative teamwork, students engage with key concepts such as problem framing, technology development and adoption, and the integration of technical, economic and behavioural perspectives in global organizational settings. Particular attention is given to the implications of emerging technologies, including generative AI, especially for organizations operating across national and cultural boundaries. A challenge-based learning approach is used to form the project work, where students work in teams to address a real-life problem by developing a solution or concept grounded in an integrated analysis of business, socio-cultural and technical dimensions. Throughout the course, students progressively build their project through iterative feedback, peer discussions and presentation sessions, culminating in a final poster presentation and a written report. Drawing on experiential learning, the course emphasizes the development of transversal skills essential in global business environments, including teamwork, communication, and constructive engagement with diverse perspectives. Students are encouraged to engage in peer feedback processes, reflect on group dynamics, and develop clear, audience-appropriate communication in both written and oral formats. Active participation in class discussions and activities is strongly encouraged and integral to the learning process. All teaching activities, group work, and assessments are conducted in English in an international classroom environment.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Describe the key characteristics and interdisciplinary foundations of Global Business Engineering as a field of study and professional practice. - Understand the difference between problem solving and problem framing, and the importance of the latter as a critical foundation for effective decision making in global business contexts. - Understand how technology is defined and explain its interactions with various business and socio-cultural aspects. - Collaborate effectively in teams by contributing to joint problem framing, analysis and presentation of a business case. - Develop a solution or a concept to address a real-life challenge based on an integrated analysis of business, socio-cultural and technical dimensions. - Communicate solutions effectively through clear, structured, audience-appropriate written and oral presentations. - Evaluate and reflect on teamwork dynamics, including one’s own role and that of others in the project, with attention to communication, planning, decision-making, problem-solving, and the management of disagreements and interpersonal differences. - Integrate peer feedback to improve one’s work and reflect critically on the process. - Provide constructive feedback on the contributions of other course participants.

Name English: Industrial Programming
Danish Title: Industriel Programmering
General Course Objectives: Based on the analysis and understanding of the context and domain of a practical problem, you can formulate requirements for software solutions in industrial automation and apply fundamental programming principles and AI‑assisted development tools to describe, adapt and test the solution.
Content: • Tools: You use VS Code / JetBrains Rider to develop your programs, and GitLab to maintain a log of your code, share your work with others and organise your project using issue boards. • Methods for specifying and delimiting a product: as‑is/to‑be analysis, in‑scope/out‑of‑scope, use cases, flowcharts, UML and user interface sketches. • Python program structure, syntax, variables, data types and operators: You learn how a program is constructed and how to work with data and calculations. • Program control: You choose control structures such as if‑else, switch, and for/while loops to enable the program to make decisions and repeat processes. • Functions: You reuse code without copy‑paste and write code that calculates or processes data differently depending on the input, e.g., a function that calculates the area of different shapes. • Arrays: You collect data of the same type, for example a list of temperatures or grades, instead of using one variable per value. • Object‑oriented programming (OOP): You learn how to organise code into classes and objects that collaborate to solve a task. • Databases: Industrial process data is often stored in databases, from which it can be retrieved, processed and analysed in other parts of the company’s systems, e.g., for monitoring and reporting. • User interface programming: You create graphical desktop user interfaces for your programs using, e.g., Qt. • Robot arm programming: You program a Universal Robot cobot to automate an industrial task. • AI‑assisted programming: After learning the fundamentals, you begin developing with AI as your assistant. You specify requirements, write tests and iterate until the requirements are met.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Identify and delimit a practical and physical process with the purpose of implementing a solution using industrial automation. - Design, develop and demonstrate a complete solution to a practical industrial task by combining programming with relevant technologies within industrial automation. - Set up and use an appropriate development environment. - Organise code in a Git repository and use basic workflows such as init, add and commit. - Visualise program logic and relationships between software components using diagrams to plan a solution. - Identify and explain fundamental programming concepts, including program structure, syntax, data types, variables and operators. - Apply fundamental programming principles to structure, adapt and further develop software components. - Use debugging tools to analyse and troubleshoot errors in industrial software. - Use a database to store and retrieve industrial process data. - Implement a basic control program for an industrial robot. - Apply aspects such as human‑centred automation, mass customisation, data collection, usability, cyber‑, personal‑ and data security (confidentiality), and robustness, which are often associated with Industry 4.0 and 5.0. - Use AI‑assisted development tools to generate, evaluate and adapt code based on requirements and tests.

62513:
Name English: Telemedicine
Danish Title: Telemedicin
General Course Objectives: Telemedicine concerns healthcare which is provided remotely in such a way so that the patient does not need to travel to the clinic. Telemedicine systems use technology for remote monitoring of patients (i.e. transmitting measurements), algorithms for analysis of patient data, and communication between health care professionals and patients. The course aims to introduce students to telemedicine concepts including examples used in clinical practice. This includes wireless technologies that are used to establish communication. The course contributes to the green transition by enabling the students to develop solutions that reduce transportation and resource use.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Explain the basic organisational and administrative principles of the Danish health-care system. - Explain the medical/physiological principles for establishing a telemedicine system for a given patient group. - Analyse the organizational and economic aspects of establishing a telemedicine system for a given patient group having a chronic disease. - Design and prototype a telemedicine system for a given patient group. - Describe the principles of algorithms for the processing of clinical data which can be monitored by the patient. - Explain the function blocks in a digital wireless communication network, radio wave propagation, antenna principles, modulation and coding methods, including calculating a link budget for a given digital communication link. - Explain protocols for wireless communication and use examples of protocols for wireless communication. - Explain the principles of a short-range ad hoc communication network with minimal energy consumption. - Explain the principles of energy harvesting and the importance of minimising energy consumption. - Explain and apply the above principles when planning a telemedicine system, including identification of the system's personal safety-critical elements.

Name English: Introduction to material's mechanical properties
Danish Title: Introduktion til materialers mekaniske egenskaber
General Course Objectives: The course provides a general introduction to materials selection, from classical to computer-aided (where we utilize the software Ansys EduPack). Special focus is on mechanical material properties related to tensile tests and how to use them in a variety of material selections based on e.g. strength-, stiffness- or fracture toughness-limited design (“design-led approach”). The course offers some basic introduction to the underlying physical properties of materials leading to the discussed material properties, again focusing on the origins of stress and strain and as exemplified by the stress-strain graph.
Content: • The EduPack program, structure and use. The program will be installed on the student's computer (License paid by DTU). EduPack will be used as database for material information and as tool for computer-aided material selection. • Introduction to EngTech’s 3D-print facility and 3D-print in general. The students will print their own dogbones and perform and analyse a tensile test for these dogbones. • The structure of materials, from atomic structure to visible structure, will be outlined. The reaction of materials to stationary forces will be covered. Mechanical material parameters such as Young’s modulus, yield strength and fracture toughness will be treated. • Introduction to the subjects stress and strain as well as the analysis of a stress strain-graph. • Acquisition and analysis of stress strain-curves for various 3D printed polymer dogbones. • Preparation of a poster presenting the experimental results. • Some fundamental differences between metals and polymers and their importance for the measured stress strain-curves. • Selection of the best materials for a given purpose will be treated and supported by EduPack. Focus is on metals and polymers. Various ways for computer-aided material selection will be outlined from simple ranking to usage of material indices. The course expands the mechanical approach to also include energy, economic, and environmental desires and requirements.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - describe the concept of “Design-led material selection”. - describe the concept of “Material classes” based on EduPack’s material property charts. - explain mechanical properties such as strength, stiffness and fracture toughness. - explain the properties' relation to measurable quantities like stress and strain. - conduct laboratory investigations of material parameters (tensile and Charpy testing). - present the experimental results in poster form. - analyse a stress-strain curve and identify the determinable mechanical properties. - relate these mechanical properties to material applications with focus on metals and polymer. - execute the material selection methodology as used in EduPack with focus on translation, screening (constraints) and ranking (objectives). - contrast and execute stiffness-, strength- or fracture toughness-limited material selection strategies. - explain and implement the use of material indices in this process. - explain how this process can be broadened to also reduce embodied energy or carbon footprint.
62713:
Name English: Basic C Programming
Danish Title: Grundlæggende C programmering
General Course Objectives: To develop fundamental programming skills in C so you can write programs in a readable and systematic way and test and analyze their functionality.
Content: Tools: You use VS Code to develop your programs and Git to keep a logbook of your code and share your work with others. Flowcharts: You draw diagrams to design and describe a program before and during coding. Program structure, syntax, variables, data types, operators: You learn how a program is built and how to work with data and calculations. Program control: You choose control structures such as if-else, switch, and for/while loops to let the program make decisions and repeat processes. Functions: You reuse code without copy-paste and write code that calculates or processes data differently depending on what you pass into the function—for example, a function that calculates the area of different shapes. Header files: You build your programs on existing code written by others and write your own code that can be shared across multiple files. Arrays: You collect data of the same type (e.g., a list of temperatures or grades) instead of using one variable per value. Pointers: You work with the memory address where data is stored instead of copying large amounts of data, and because arrays and some functions operate directly with addresses. Structs: You group multiple values of different data types into a single variable—for example, name, age, and weight of a person. Debugging: You handle compilation errors and learn how to investigate errors in your program’s functionality. Strings: Humans communicate with computers through text stored as strings. You learn how to read, write, and manipulate strings. File I/O: You read data from files into your program instead of entering them manually, and store the processed results back to a file. AI-assisted programming: After learning the fundamentals, you try developing with AI as a helper. You specify requirements and write tests, repeating the process until the requirements are met.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Set up a development environment for C programming. - Organize code in a Git repository and use basic workflows such as init, add, and commit. - Visualize program logic with flowcharts to plan a solution. - Recognize, explain, and use fundamental C programming concepts, including program structure, syntax, data types, variables, and operators. - Read data from the keyboard and files, and write data to the screen and files using the standard library. - Use conditions and loops to control program flow. - Break down a large problem into functions. - Integrate and distribute functionality using header files. - Analyze and test functions with a debugger and test cases to solve programming problems. - Use addresses (pointers) together with essential functions for text input, text processing, and file handling. - Use arrays and structs to organize data. - Use AI-assisted development tools to generate, evaluate, and adapt code based on requirements and tests.
62776:
Name English: Applied electrical engineering
Danish Title: Anvendt elteknik for Maskin
General Course Objectives: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to alternating current (AC) power systems. It covers the fundamental principles of AC circuits, including voltage, current, impedance, and power relationships. Students will learn power analysis techniques and how to model key electrical components such as transformers, generators, transmission lines, and the fundamentals of three-phase motors. Emphasis is placed on developing both a strong theoretical foundation and practical analytical skills relevant to modern power systems.
Content: Fundamentals of AC Systems, AC Circuit Elements, Power in Single-Phase AC Systems, Power Factor Correction, Three-Phase AC Systems, Per-Phase Analysis of Three-Phase Systems, Transformer Modeling, Generator Modeling, Per-Unit System Analysis, Transmission Line Modeling, Fundamentals of Three-Phase Motors
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Understand and apply fundamental AC concepts, including waveform analysis and phasor representation. - Analyze AC circuits using impedance, admittance, and circuit laws. - Evaluate power in AC systems, including real, reactive, and apparent power. - Assess and improve power factor in electrical systems. - Analyze balanced three-phase systems and perform per-phase calculations. - Develop equivalent circuit models for transformers and generators. - Use the per-unit system for simplified power system analysis. - Model and analyze transmission lines under different operating conditions. - Explain the working principles of three-phase motors and evaluate their performance. - Develop and simulate AC circuits and power system models using MATLAB.
62812:
Name English: Materials selection
Danish Title: Materialevalg
General Course Objectives: The course provides a general introduction to materials selection, from classical to computer-aided (where we utilize the software Ansys EduPack). Special focus is on mechanical material properties related to tensile tests and how to use them in a variety of material selections based on e.g. strength-, stiffness- or fracture toughness-limited design (“design-led approach”). The course offers some basic introduction to the underlying physical properties of materials leading to the discussed material properties, again focusing on the origins of stress and strain and as exemplified by the stress-strain graph.
Content: • The EduPack program, structure and use. The program will be installed on the student's computer (License paid by DTU). EduPack will be used as database for material information and as tool for computer-aided material selection. • Introduction to EngTech’s 3D-print facility and 3D-print in general. The students will print their own dogbones and perform and analyse a tensile test for these dogbones. • The structure of materials, from atomic structure to visible structure, will be outlined. The reaction of materials to stationary forces will be covered. Mechanical material parameters such as Young’s modulus, yield strength and fracture toughness will be treated. • Introduction to the subjects stress and strain as well as the analysis of a stress strain-graph. • Acquisition and analysis of stress strain-curves for various 3D printed polymer dogbones. • Preparation of a poster presenting the experimental results. • Some fundamental differences between metals and polymers and their importance for the measured stress strain-curves. • Selection of the best materials for a given purpose will be treated and supported by EduPack. Focus is on metals and polymers. Various ways for computer-aided material selection will be outlined from simple ranking to usage of material indices. The course expands the mechanical approach to also include energy, economic, and environmental desires and requirements.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - describe the concept of “Design-led material selection”. - describe the concept of “Material classes” based on EduPack’s material property charts. - explain mechanical properties such as strength, stiffness and fracture toughness. - explain the properties' relation to measurable quantities like stress and strain. - conduct laboratory investigations of material parameters (tensile and Charpy testing). - present the experimental results as a report. - analyse a stress-strain curve and identify the determinable mechanical properties. - relate these mechanical properties to material applications with focus on metals and polymer. - execute the material selection methodology as used in EduPack with focus on translation, screening (constraints) and ranking (objectives). - contrast and execute stiffness-, strength- or fracture toughness-limited material selection strategies. - explain and implement the use of material indices in this process. - explain how this process can be broadened to also reduce embodied energy or carbon footprint.
62813:
Name English: Semesterproject 1: Wind turbine technology
Danish Title: Semesterprojekt 1: Vindmølle-teknologi
General Course Objectives: Project work is one of the most applied working methods within engineering. It is thus to be expected that the mechanical engineer has a first-hand knowledge of working individually as well as in groups, with establishing and clarification of projects, and also application of a wide range of engineering competences in a cross-disciplinary context. This work can be carried out in a traditional fashion with physical attendance, but also through various digital communication tools. The purpose of the course is to introduce project work within the field of engineering, by including aspects such a group dynamics and digital manners as well as the application of traditional engineering competences. During the course, the students will form the basic understanding of a problem in an engineering context. Among these the formation of a professional and scientific vocabulary and application of e.g. mathematics, material knowledge (including the CO2 footprint) and technical drawing/use of an advanced CAD program during the solution of specific engineering problems.
Content: The course focuses on the cross-disciplinary application of engineering competences in the solution of realistic problems. During weekly assignments and a concluding exercise, the students will learn to handle projects with an increasing complexity, such that topics such as (digital) group work, application of basic subjects within natural and engineering science as well as problem understanding in a realistic context are treated: - Digital cooperation, application of mathematics, mechanics, material choice and technical drawing to analyze individual components. - Application of mathematics, strength of materials, material choice and technical drawing to analyze mechanisms or component assemblies. - Application of mathematics and conversion of literature knowledge into practical use by an automated solution of engineering problems, such that manual computational operations are not going to be repeated in an undesired way. After completion of the course, the student will have received an introduction into representative tasks a mechanical engineer can face on a daily basis
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - plan and complete a smaller engineering project, both individually and in project groups - work and cooperate across various engineering interests within the field of mechanical engineering, as well as organizing the cooperation in a project group, including the ability to apply knowledge from other courses to solve an engineering problem - document the results of the project work in a work journal, report or poster with a high-level professional content and in a publication worthy quality - understand the context for a given problem, such that a solution obtained through application of technological opportunities will ensure value creation for an individual or society as a whole - carry out engineering calculations on a simple, mechanical construction, including selection of materials for a mechanical product (e.g. wind turbine) - apply hand drawing and CAD for graphical modeling for usage in communication and problem solving - explain the characteristics of the projection (double-orthogonal and axonometric projection) and choose the most appropriate projection form for a given task - read and apply technical literature - be able to apply study techniques etc. in effectively handling a remote study. This includes knowledge of theory within group dynamics and digital cooperation - perform the drawing types that describe mechanical components’ construction and function and apply them to spatial visual sketches, design drawings and machining drawings - read a mechanical drawing and judge whether it is clear and unambiguous and assess whether it meets relevant standards and norms
62814:
Name English: Mechanics
Danish Title: Mekanik
General Course Objectives: The overall aim of the course is to provide the student with an understanding of the fundamental principles of mechanics. This includes plane statics for statically determinate systems, Newtons Laws, and conservation laws for energy and linear momentum.
Content: Forces and couples. Plane equilibrium equations. Dry friction. Truss and frame structures. Distributed loads. Motion with constant and varying acceleration. Newton's 2nd law for planar/circular motion. Kinetic and potential energy. Conservation of energy. Work of non-conservative forces.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Draw free-body diagrams for planar mechanical systems and system parts with a clear indication of external forces and couples. - State and solve the static equilibrium equations for planar mechanical systems. - Identify dry friction forces (Coulomb friction) on bodies in static equilibrium or in motion. - Find forces in plane truss elements using the method of sections and the method of joints. - Brainstorm on the design of structures (e.g. trusses, frames, mechanisms) with specified behavior. - Identify statically equivalent concentrated loads for linear load distributions including water loads. - Solve kinematic problems for particle motion with constant and varying acceleration. - State and solve Newton's 2nd law for planar and circular motion of particles. - Find the kinetic energy of particles. - Find the work of forces and potential energy of spring and gravity forces. - Apply work-energy relations to particles affected by conservative and non-conservative forces.
62I21:
Name English: Leadership in AI and Digital Transformation
Danish Title: Ledelse med AI og digital udvikling
General Course Objectives: It is the aim that the student acquires knowledge, skills and competencies to be able to lead and develop the management task with artificial intelligence (AI) and other digital technologies.
Content: The course content may vary depending on the type of tender. Contact the course coordinator for further information.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Have knowledge and understanding of theories, concepts and methods related to the management of digital processes. - Reflect on applied practices in relation to the management of digital processes in one's own organization. - Apply methods and tools and master the skills associated with management with artificial intelligence (AI) and digital development. - Analyze, assess and communicate the importance of various theories, concepts and methods related to management with artificial intelligence and digital development. - Handle complex management situations with digital technologies within the framework of professional ethics. - Identify needs for personal and organizational competency development in relation to the specific contexts of the digital management task. - - - -
