MA239:
Name English: Numerical Methods in Structural Mechanics
Danish Title: Numeriske metoder i konstruktionsmekanik
General Course Objectives: To enable the participants to understand and apply computational models for statically determinate and indeterminate elastic beam, frame, membrane and plated structures, including discretization of continuous models for finite element analysis. Furthermore, to make the participants able to operate a commercial Finite Element Method program for analysis of plane and spatial structures.
Content: The course concerns statically indeterminate elastic structures and analysis methods such as the Deformation/Stiffness Method and the Finite Element Method for plane and spatial structures, as well as application and training in the use of a commercial Finite Element Method (FEM) program within the civil engineering and naval architecture fields. The course has the following content: - The Deformation/Stiffness method for trusses and frames. - Distributed loads and equivalent nodal loads for bars and beams. - Element stiffness matrix for plane beam elements, 2D and 3D beam elements. - Transformation of elements in the plane. - Boundary conditions and symmetry conditions. - The Finite Element Method (FEM) - Basic plane and solid continuum element types (formulations, advantages and disadvantages). - Iso-parametric plane and spatial elements. - Equivalent nodal loads for plane and solid continuum elements. - Gaussian integration. - Stress determination and mesh distribution.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Apply the Deformation/Stiffness Method to solve simple beam, truss and frame problems by hand calculations. - Explain the assemblage of the global stiffness matrix and load vector for plane trusses and frames including accounting for boundary conditions. - Explain the equivalence between the Deformation/Stiffness Method and the Finite Element Method. - Use a mathematics program to analyze statically indeterminent truss and frame structures using the Deformation/Stiffness method. - Account for the interpolation functions for simple bar, beam and plane elements. - Account for the transformation of element stiffness matrices. - Account for the solution of the global finite element system. - Use a commercial finite element program to solve truss, frame, membrane and plate problems. - Perform convergence analysis for a finite element analyses. - Analyze and evaluate deformations and stress distributions in a commercial finite element program. - Critically evaluate the importance of the choice of element types, size and boundary conditions in finite element analysis. - Perform finite element analysis of selected applied structural design problems.
MA263:
Name English: Experimental and numerical methods for ship resistance and propulsion
Danish Title: Eksperimentel og numerisk bestemmelse af skibsmodstand og fremdrivning
General Course Objectives: To train the participants to predict the hydrodynamic resistance of a ship using model tests, empirical calculation methods, and numerical simulations, and to use these predictions to specify an optimal bulbous bow and a highly-efficient propulsion system for the ship.
Content: Experimental and computational methods to predict resistance and propulsion in calm water. Froude scaling. Resistance model tests (ITTC-1978) with optimization of a bulbous bow. Power prognosis on the basis of the model tests, and calculation of the optimum combination of main engine and propeller (B-series). It is emphasised that the students must take an active part in the planning, preparation, testing, and analysis of the model tests.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - describe the assumptions associated with theoretical models and calculation methods associated with the resistance and propulsion of ships - explain the theory behind model testing for resistance and propulsion (Froude scaling) - organize and execute a series of ship model tests - perform calculations that transform data from model to full scale by ITTC-1978 or a similar procedure - calculate and assess the flow, including the generated wave system, around the ship with commercial software - describe the function of ship propellers, and explain the use of propeller diagrams (for instance the B-series propellers) - apply propeller diagrams to identify an optimum propeller - explain the interaction between ship, propeller, and main engine - specify the propulsive main engine that performs best with the ship and its propeller - collect experimental and numerical results in a high-quality technical report
MA264:
Name English: Ship Hydrodynamics
Danish Title: Skibshydrodynamik
General Course Objectives: Understanding ship behavior in calm water and accurate estimation of the resistance which is experience by ship, is essential for reliable and optimum design of its propulsion plant including the ship engine. Moreover, determining unsteady ship motions due to ocean waves plays a key role in ship seakeeping properties and its structural response. Both of these subjects are vital for safe and sustainable ship operation, which are becoming increasingly important due to the green transition in maritime transport. The overall objective of this course is that students learn the fundamental concepts of ship resistance, propulsion and seakeeping, and they learn to conduct engineering calculations for these topics with direct application for ship design and operation.
Content: • Fundamental equations of fluid mechanics, dimensional analysis (Pi theorem) • Control volume approach for solving external flow problems • Potential-flow fields and boundary layer theory • Linear wave theory and its engineering properties • Ship resistance components including frictional and residuary resistance • International Towing Tank Committee (ITTC) guidelines • Propeller in open-water and behind-the-hull conditions • wave- and motion-induced forces on ships • Classical strip theory and motion response in the frequency domain
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - describe the flow field around a ship hull including the wave patterns - describe the components of ship resistance and their proportional significance for different ship types - compute ship resistance using empirical approaches and ITTC methods - describe the physics of a ship propeller and its interaction with the ship hull - design a ship propeller and perfrom calculations to optimize the propulsion plant - set up, analyze and solve the equations of motion for a ship in waves - compute the ship response spectrum using a wave spectrum and the response transfer functions - compute added resistance of ship in waves using a wave spectrum and the transfer function - calculate and assess the global structural response due to waves and ship motion
MA270:
Name English: Economic and environmental performance of ships
Danish Title: Grøn Skibsfart
General Course Objectives: The aim of the course is to provide tools for an economic and environmental evaluation of ship transportation. During the course an optimal ship design is sought for a specific trade through minimization of the total life cycle cost including production of the vessel, operation and maintenance and, finally, scrapping. The total cost includes environmental and political issues and a risk assessment is made to quantify the effects of uncertainties in the input parameters. The course will give the students a commercial and strategic understanding of the governing parameters in running a shipping company.
Content: The course content is the following • Freight market for shipping • Cost involved in ship design, production, operation, maintenance and scrapping • Life cycle analysis • Energy consumption for propulsion, cooling, heating etc • Exhaust emissions from ships • Energy Efficiency Design Index (EEDI) • Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan (SEEMP) • Cost benefit analysis The students will be divided into groups. Each group will be given a specific trade in terms of cargo type, amount of cargo and route. An optimal conceptual ship design shall be made by each group including a risk assessment taking into account the uncertainties in the input parameters.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Select and optimize a conceptual ship design for a specific trade route. - Perform a SWOT analysis of a conceptual ship design. - Explain the basic principles in a life cycle analysis of a ship. - Explain the basic physics of exhaust emissions from ships. - Perform a Net Present Value estimation for a ship. - Perform a cost benefit analysis of a ship including environmental issues. - Explain the rules and regulations regarding operation and scrapping of ships. - Perform a Energy Efficiency Design Index (EEDI) calculation of a ship.
MA271:
Name English: Ship design
Danish Title: Skibsprojektering
General Course Objectives: To give the student a thorough knowledge and experience in the design of different types of ships. In this to give the student knowledge about the arrangement of ships and their function.
Content: Ship owner, shipping, ship types, main dimensions, hull lines, general arrangement, propulsion, loading conditions, hydrostatics, intact and damage stability, international and national rules and regulations, environmental protection including energy efficiency design index (EEDI), machinery, aesthetics. The subjects are treated by application of methods within hydromechanics and CAD/CAE. The methods learned are applied in the design of a ship to given ship owner's specification. Commercial CAD/CAE programs are applied including dedicated programs for hydrostatic and hydrodynamic analyses of ship hulls.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - describe all common ship types and their technical characteristics as functions of their mission, - explain all the most important rules and regulations that apply to the arrangement and equipment of ships, - describe the arrangement of a ship and the different systems on board, - from a naval architect's point of view outline the different types of operations, such as anchoring, mooring, cargo handling and fire fighting, - do calculations (with commercial computer programs) of stability, loading conditions and propulsion, - do calcuations of (specific) energy consumption, smoke emissions and energy efficiency design index (EEDI), - describe the process of ship design, - design a ship, - draw a general arrangement plan to a professional standard, - write a technical report with main body report, outline specification, general arrangement plan and appendices.
MA534:
Name English: Dimensioning and strength 2
Danish Title: Dimensionering og styrke 2
General Course Objectives: To enable the student to analyze and calculate how a given structure ie. machine components, pressure vessels, shrinkage joints, structures, frames, etc. deform and when plastic deformation or fatigue occurs. The content of the course constitute a necessary prerequisite for the use and understanding of the finite element method (FEM), and not least, the ability to provide qualified assessment and interpretation of results obtained through FEM calculations.
Content: The course is taught in Danish. Three-dimensional stresses and strains. Principal stresses / strains and the associated principal coordinate systems. Hooke's generalized law. Plane stress and plane strain. Deformation of thick-walled pipes and circular discs. Plastic deformation mechanisms and yield hypotheses. Dimensioning against fatigue fractures. As part of the course, the student is introduced to multidimensional elastic stress and deformation analysis. Dimensioning is introduced against permanent deformation (plasticity) as well as fatigue fractures.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Determine the stress and strain state in a loaded continuum using Hooke's generalized law as well as any strain gauge measurements. - Perform analyses of principal stresses and strains and corresponding principal directions for general 3D-states. - Identify and account for special stress states as for instance uniaxial, plane, cylindrical or hydrostatic - Calculate stresses based on strains and conversely, as a result of mechanical and thermal loading, for e.g. thin-walled pressure vessels. - Analyze the stress and strain state in circular in-plane loaded plates and thick walled pipes. - Utilize von Mises' and Tresca's yield hypotheses to dimension against plastic deformation in structures. - Dimension against fatigue and establishing reduced Haigh/Goodman diagrams. - Determine safety factors while taking plastic deformation and fatigue into account, i.e. enabling the minimization of material consumption to ensure sustainability in accordance with the UN World Goals. - Describe the mechanical properties of time-independent materials under static uniaxial tensile loading.
MA604:
Name English: Thermodynamics and energy technology
Danish Title: Termodynamik og energiteknik
General Course Objectives: To provide a theoretical and practical background in formulating and solving thermodynamic problems in the field of energy and mechanical engineering, including energy storage and renewable energy in relation to Sustainable Development Goals.
Content: Thermodynamics: The basic concepts, definitions and applications of thermodynamics, including system, universe, thermodynamic equilibrium, processes, states and control volume. Phases: solid, liquid and gas. Thermodynamic properties of substances: density, specific heat capacity, coefficient of thermal expansion, compressibility and thermal conductivity. Thermodynamic coordinates, including pressure, temperature and specific volume. Ideal gas and real gas as well as state equations. Heat and work as well as energy quality. Triple point, PvT-relation, critical point, phase change processes and the lever rule. The 1st law of thermodynamics for closed systems and internal energy. The 1st law of thermodynamics for open systems and enthalpy. The 2nd law of thermodynamics, reversibility and irreversibility. The concepts of entropy and exergy, the direction of rotation of cycles, including the Carnot process and the Stirling machine as both engine and cooling. Energy technology: Internal combustion engines including the Otto process and the Diesel engine. Thermodynamic efficiency of a cycle. Brayton cycle process. Rankine cycle process. The cycle process for 1-stage cooling and heat pump systems. Components in systems including, boilers, evaporators, condensers, throttle valves, nozzles, diffusers, heat exchangers as well as pumps, compressors, turbines with associated isentropic efficiencies. Renewable energy and energy storage. T-s , h-s , log (p)-h diagrams as well as thermodynamic tables. Gas mixtures, combustion and humid air including Mollier diagram. Fluid mechanics: Introduction to calculating pressure loss in pipes. Heat transfer: Introduction to heat conduction, convection and radiation. Project: During the 3-week period, a small CDIO project is prepared, which is carried out as group work with a written methodological report, and contains significant matters from CDIO, ie. definition / description of plant and its boundaries, design supported by relevant technical calculations, description of most important conditions for installation, start-up and operation of the plant. The choice of plant must be relevant to the components and plants that are covered in the course.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - explain the basic concepts of thermodynamics. - describe the different phases and physical properties of substances. - describe state equations for ideal gas, ideal gas mixtures (including humid air) and real gas. - use tables, diagrams and the EEA to determine the different thermodynamic properties and state sizes of substances. - formulate the 1st law and 2nd law of thermodynamics as well as mass conservation for sub-processes and cycles. - apply thermodynamics to describe the principles behind energy engineering machines such as steam power plants, gas turbines, internal combustion engines, refrigeration systems and heat pumps. - apply simplifications of real plants so that they can be subjected to thermodynamic calculation. - use the concept of entropy to assess the efficiency of a thermodynamic process and its useable energy. - describe the application function of the individual components in systems. - conduct experimental studies, analyze measurement results and prepare technical reports. - apply basic principles of heat transfer, fluid mechanics and combustion. - Explain the concepts of energy storage and renewable energy as well as their applications and possibilities.
MA646:
Name English: Modeling and Programming
Danish Title: Modellering og Programmering
General Course Objectives: This course provides a basic introduction to MATLAB programming and the application of physical and electrical laws to develop mathematical models in mechanical or electrical engineering.
Content: MATLAB programming: conditions, loops, functions, arrays, plots, file handling. Physical and electrical laws: Newton's 2nd law, Kirchhoff's circuit law. Numerical methods: Euler's method, ODE45, Simulink. State-space formulation. Linearization.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Write MATLAB programs using conditional statements, loops, functions, and arrays. - Solve differential equations in the time domain using MATLAB's ODE45 solver. - Use Simulink to model and solve differential equations graphically. - Apply the MATLAB Symbolic Math Toolbox to manipulate and solve equations. - Describe governing equations for electrical or mechanical systems. - Convert higher-order differential equations into sets of first-order equations. - Determine if a system is linear or nonlinear and perform linearization of nonlinear systems. - Collaborate on programming projects in teams. - Write technical reports with clear structure, graphics, and well-documented MATLAB code.
MA657:
Name English: Fluid Mechanics
Danish Title: Fluid Mekanik
General Course Objectives: To give a theoretical and practical background for the formulation and the solution of flow problems within energy and mechanical field, including turbomachinary.
Content: Classification and properties of fluids. Fluid statics. Control volume. Fluid kinematics and vector fields including velocity and acceleration field, divergence and rotation. Conservation of mass, momentum, angular momentum and energy for fluid mechanical systems. Bernoulli's equation. Static and dynamic pressure. Dimensional analysis, modeling and similarity. Introduction to measurement techniques in fluid mechanics. Intern and Extern flows. Head loss calculations in pipes and pipe systems. Archimedes' principle including buoyancy and stability. Drag and lift. Boundary layer theory, including velocity profiles. Turbo machinery, including centrifugal pumps, windmills, gas, steam, Pelton, Francis and Kaplan turbines. Application of velocity triangles.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Analyze flows and parts of flows as laminar/turbulent, viscous/inviscid, steady/unsteady and compressible/​incompressible and use properties of fluids and find values for the properties using tables, equations of state and EES. - Analyze static pressures, forces and buoyancy forces. - Evaluate whether Bernoulli’s equation or Energy equation is valid for a given flow. - Use the control volume method for mass, momentum, angular momentum and energy. - Use dimensional analysis and understand the physical significance of certain dimensionless numbers for given flows. - Use rough estimates in fluid mechanics for pump systems and hydropower. - Use flow components and measuring techniques. - Use efficiencies and calculate energy consumption for flow processes and components. - Understand and use principles, performance curves and velocity diagrams for flow machines such as fans, pumps, turbines and propellers. - Understand the function of rotor and stator in compressors and turbines and understand the principles in different pumps and turbines, including Betz-limit for windmills. - Use the computer software EES (Engineering Equation Solver) for the solution of flow problems. - Read engineering literature about fluid mechanics.
MA678:
Name English: Introduction to material's mechanical properties
Danish Title: Introduktion til materialers mekaniske egenskaber

Special focus is on mechanical material properties related to tensile tests and how to use them in a variety of material selections based on e.g. strength-, stiffness- or fracture toughness-limited design (“design-led approach”). EduPack will be used as database for material information and as tool for computer-aided material selection. • Introduction to EngTech’s 3D-print facility and 3D-print in general. The students will print their own dogbones and perform and analyse a tensile test for these dogbones. • The structure of materials, from atomic structure to visible structure, will be outlined. The reaction of materials to stationary forces will be covered. Mechanical material parameters such as Young’s modulus, yield strength and fracture toughness will be treated. • Introduction to the subjects stress and strain as well as the analysis of a stress strain-graph. • Acquisition and analysis of stress strain-curves for various 3D printed polymer dogbones. • Preparation of a poster presenting the experimental results. • Some fundamental differences between metals and polymers and their importance for the measured stress strain-curves. • Selection of the best materials for a given purpose will be treated and supported by EduPack. Focus is on metals and polymers. Various ways for computer-aided material selection will be outlined from simple ranking to usage of material indices. The course expands the mechanical approach to also include energy, economic, and environmental desires and requirements.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - describe the concept of “Design-led material selection”. - describe the concept of “Material classes” based on EduPack’s material property charts. - explain mechanical properties such as strength, stiffness and fracture toughness. - explain the properties' relation to measurable quantities like stress and strain. - conduct laboratory investigations of material parameters (tensile and Charpy testing). - present the experimental results in poster form. - analyse a stress-strain curve and identify the determinable mechanical properties. - relate these mechanical properties to material applications with focus on metals and polymer. - execute the material selection methodology as used in EduPack with focus on translation, screening (constraints) and ranking (objectives). - contrast and execute stiffness-, strength- or fracture toughness-limited material selection strategies. - explain and implement the use of material indices in this process. - explain how this process can be broadened to also reduce embodied energy or carbon footprint.
MA694:
Name English: Dynamics
Danish Title: Dynamik
General Course Objectives: To provide the student with a fundamental understanding of phenomena related to dynamics of rigid bodies and mechanical vibrations.
Content: 1D impact. Vector description of rigid body kinematics. Kinetic energy, linear and angular momentum for rigid bodies and systems of particles. General equations of motion. Work and power. Work-energy relations. Conservation principles for linear and angular momentum and energy. Vibrations of systems with one degree-of-freedom; undamped and damped free vibrations; forced vibrations, frequency response and resonance; energy methods.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Draw free-body and kinetic diagrams for plane motion of rigid bodies. - Apply vector-description for plane motion of rigid bodies in inertial and non-inertial coordinate systems. - State the general plane equations of motion for rigid bodies and systems of rigid bodies and determine linear and angular accelerations. - Find center of gravity and mass moment of inertia for simple bodies. - Use the principle of linear momentum conservation to solve simple 1D impact problems. - Apply the principle of linear momentum conservation for rigid bodies and systems of particles. - Apply the principle of angular momentum conservation for rigid bodies and systems of particles. - Determine the natural frequency and damping ratio for systems with one degree-of-freedom. - Find the response of damped and undamped systems with one degree-of-freedom subjected to a harmonic load. - Determine work and power of external forces and couples. - Apply work-energy relations for plane motion of rigid bodies. - Use the energy method to set up the general equations of motion for particles and rigid bodies.
MA722:
Name English: Linear control design 1
Danish Title: Reguleringsteknik 1
General Course Objectives: The purpose is to provide a basis for analysing, designing and optimising most commonly used control systems. Regulatory systems are used to improve the performance and efficiency of e.g. power plants, factory production, vehicles, heating, cooling, drones, aircraft and many other places. Regulatory knowledge therefore contributes to many of the UN's goals for sustainable development, for example: 11: Sustainable Cities and Communities, 12: Responsible Consumption and Production and 9: Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure.
Content: Fundamental concepts in control systems with feedback. Formulation of models of physical systems. Linearisation. Differential equations Laplace transformation and transfer functions. Frequency analysis. Stability. Basic design methods. Application of standard controllers and compensators. The theory and methods reviewed are supported by many practical examples and exercises. E-learning is used in the form of e.g. on-line quiz (home assignments), online discussions or blog and digital exam.
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Apply heuristic methods for PID controller design - Derive models of simple dynamic systems based on physics or measurements, and linearize the system to a transfer function in a single operating point - Analyze transfer functions in the frequency domain (primarily Bodeplot) - Apply block diagrams to describe models for both open- and closed-loop control systems - Design PID controllers based on open loop frequency analysis - Apply the concepts of stability and stability margin from open loop design - Understand the consequences of disturbance and noise sensitivity - Evaluate controller performance in terms of overshoot, settling time, steady state error, bandwidth and control limitations - Apply analysis, design and simulation software - Apply analysis and design of controllers for an energy producing system
MA776:
Name English: Applied electrical engineering
Danish Title: Anvendt elteknik for Maskin
General Course Objectives: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to alternating current (AC) power systems. It covers the fundamental principles of AC circuits, including voltage, current, impedance, and power relationships. Students will learn power analysis techniques and how to model key electrical components such as transformers, generators, transmission lines, and the fundamentals of three-phase motors. Emphasis is placed on developing both a strong theoretical foundation and practical analytical skills relevant to modern power systems.
Content: Fundamentals of AC Systems, AC Circuit Elements, Power in Single-Phase AC Systems, Power Factor Correction, Three-Phase AC Systems, Per-Phase Analysis of Three-Phase Systems, Transformer Modeling, Generator Modeling, Per-Unit System Analysis, Transmission Line Modeling, Fundamentals of Three-Phase Motors
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Understand and apply fundamental AC concepts, including waveform analysis and phasor representation. - Analyze AC circuits using impedance, admittance, and circuit laws. - Evaluate power in AC systems, including real, reactive, and apparent power. - Assess and improve power factor in electrical systems. - Analyze balanced three-phase systems and perform per-phase calculations. - Develop equivalent circuit models for transformers and generators. - Use the per-unit system for simplified power system analysis. - Model and analyze transmission lines under different operating conditions. - Explain the working principles of three-phase motors and evaluate their performance. - Develop and simulate AC circuits and power system models using MATLAB.
MA922:
Name English: Linear Algebra and Modelling
Danish Title: Lineær Algebra og Modellering
General Course Objectives: The course is a direct continuation of course 01911, Mathematical Analysis and Modelling. The goal is to provide the students with the ability to apply fundamental mathematical concepts and modern computer tools solving classical problems of engineering on a slightly higher taxonomical level than in 01911. Relevant topics from linear algebra are introduced as a methodical basis for treating multi-dimensional problems arising from engineering applications. The scope and form of the course supports application of the modelling circle aiming at the treatment of relevant problems within the different study lines at increasing taxonomical levels. The digital formation and "computational thinking" of the students is further strengthened compared to course 01911 by working with modern computational tools (currently Maple).
Content: Systems of linear equations, Gaussian elimination, matrix algebra, determinants, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, systems of linear differential equations, engineering applications of linear algebra
Learning Objectives: A student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to: - Solve systems of linear equations by, among other things, Gaussian elimination, both by hand and using a computer and explain the structure of the resulting solution. - Identify different types of matrices and carry out basic calculations with matrices, both by hand and using a computer. - Apply the concept of the determinant of a quadratic matrix and calculate determinants, both by hand and using a computer. - Determine whether a square matrix is invertible, and if so, calculate its inverse, both by hand and using a computer. - Explain the concept of eigenvalues and eigenvectors for square matrices and calculate these, both by hand and using a computer. - Solve simple systems of linear differential equations, both by hand and using a computer. - Apply the symbolic software tool Maple to solve and graphically display mathematical/engineering problems and solutions. - Use linear algebra to model and solve engineering problems such as encryption, systems of linear differential equations, over-determined systems of equations, and finding extremal points for functions of two variables.
